ch01/prob-1-41a.description: An atom-by-atom drawing labeled “Indole” shows a six-membered carbon ring fused to a five-membered ring containing N–H, with double bonds and hydrogens explicitly shown. It is presented as a structure to convert into a skeletal drawing.

ch01/fig-1.12.description: Three views of methane show a space-filling model, a central bond drawing, and a ball-and-stick model. The drawing marks an H–C–H bond angle of 109.5° and a C–H bond length of 109 pm.

ch02/prob-2-23a.description: A ball-and-stick model labeled Adenine shows a fused two-ring structure with black carbon, blue nitrogen, and gray hydrogen atoms. The drawing includes bonds between the atoms but does not mark lone pairs.

ch01/p027.description: Two separate hydrogen 1s orbitals, each containing one electron with opposite spin, are shown overlapping to form an H₂ molecule. The drawing illustrates formation of the H–H bond by orbital overlap.

ch05/fig-5.12.description: A wedge-and-dash structure and a ball-and-stick model of meso-tartaric acid show a blue symmetry plane passing through the bond between the two central carbons. The plane divides the molecule into mirror-image halves, illustrating why it is achiral.

ch06/fig-6.4.description: A two-step mechanism shows ethylene’s double bond attacking the hydrogen of HBr as the H–Br bond breaks, producing a carbocation and bromide ion. A curved arrow then shows bromide attacking the positively charged carbon to form bromoethane; a colored orbital illustrates the vacant orbital on the carbocation.

ch03/table-3.1a.description: A table entry shows a generic alkene structure: two carbon atoms joined by a pink double bond, with two unlabeled single bonds extending from each carbon. The nearby text identifies the functional group as an alkene.

ch12/fig-12.14.description: The mass spectrum of butyrophenone plots relative abundance against m/z, with its tallest peak at 105, a prominent peak at 77, and a molecular-ion peak near 148. An inset shows the molecule’s skeletal structure, formula C₁₀H₁₂O, and molecular weight 148.20.

ch07/p243c.description: A curved-arrow scheme shows 3,3-dimethyl-1-butene reacting with HCl to form a secondary carbocation, which can undergo a methyl shift to a tertiary carbocation. Chloride attack on each carbocation leads to the two labeled chloro products.

answer_key/ans-1-6c.description: Two representations of CH₃NH₂ appear side by side: a Lewis dot structure showing shared electron pairs and a lone pair on nitrogen, and a structure drawn with bonds as lines.

front_matter/p003.description: The OpenStax logo appears as five colored horizontal bars beside the gray wordmark “openstax™.”

front_matter/p013.description: A close-up portrait shows a smiling man with short brown hair wearing a light blue collared shirt. The text beneath the photo identifies him as Peter McMurry.

front_matter/p005.description: The image shows the Rice name in large blue letters beside a blue shield bearing chevrons and owl emblems. It functions as an institutional logo.

ch01/fig-1.2.description: A partial periodic table highlights elements commonly found in organic compounds with their typical molecular-model colors, including hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, sulfur, phosphorus, and several halogens. Other elements appear in uncolored boxes, with group numbers marked above the columns.

ch01/fig-1.4.description: Three side-by-side orbital models show a spherical s orbital, a two-lobed p orbital, and a four-lobed d orbital, each centered on a small green dot. The p and d lobes are colored pink and blue.

ch01/fig-1.3.description: The left schematic shows a small nucleus within a diffuse blue region labeled as the volume occupied by orbiting electrons. The right view shows a dark blue electron-density surface inside a larger gray mesh surface, illustrating that electron density increases toward the nucleus.
labels_in_image: Volume around nucleus occupied by orbiting electrons

ch01/p020.description: Three labeled skeletal structures are shown side by side: oxycodone (OxyContin), cholesterol, and benzylpenicillin. The drawings illustrate how different organic molecules are represented with bonds, rings, atom labels, and wedge and dashed stereochemical bonds.

ch01/fig-1.1.description: A ribbon model of the enzyme HMG–CoA reductase shows intertwined blue, reddish-brown, purple, and yellow-green folded regions against a white background. The caption links this enzyme to a crucial step in the body's synthesis of cholesterol.

front_matter/p017.description: A color-coded academic integrity chart places original work and credited quotations under “Approved,” five activities including group work and AI chatbot apps under “Ask Instructor,” and posting questions and answers, plagiarism, and having others do your work under “Not Approved.” Icons along a horizontal line illustrate each activity.
labels_in_image: Getting Others To Do Your Work

ch01/fig-1.5.description: An upward arrow marks increasing energy beside three electron shells with capacities of 2, 8, and 18 electrons. Horizontal orbital levels labeled 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, and 3d show paired up-and-down arrows for the electrons each orbital can hold.

ch01/we-1.2.description: Two representations of chloromethane are shown: a Lewis dot structure with shared electron pairs and chlorine’s lone pairs, and a line-bond structure with carbon bonded to three hydrogens and one chlorine.

ch01/p026b.description: The figure shows line bonds and lone-pair dots around H, C, N, O, F, Cl, Br, and I. Braces beneath them indicate that hydrogen and the halogens form one bond, carbon four, nitrogen three, and oxygen two.

ch01/p023.description: A diagonal-arrow chart arranges atomic orbitals in rows from 1s through 6s, 6p, 6d, and 6f. The pink arrows show the order in which the orbitals are filled, including 4s before 3d.

ch01/fig-1.7.description: Two pink tetrahedron sketches are compared with a carbon bonded to four hydrogens, shown both as a wedge-and-dash drawing and a ball-and-stick model. Arrows identify bonds in the plane of the page, a dashed bond receding behind it, and a solid wedge projecting toward the viewer.

ch01/p026c.description: Three representations of ammonia show nitrogen bonded to three hydrogens: an electron-dot drawing, a line-bond drawing with the nitrogen lone pair shown, and a bracketed line-bond drawing that omits it. An arrow labels the dots as “Nonbonding, lone-pair electrons.”

ch01/fig-1.6.description: Three diagrams show mutually perpendicular 2p orbitals aligned along the x, y, and z axes. Each has two dumbbell-shaped lobes colored blue and pink to indicate opposite signs of the wave function, separated by a node at the center.

ch01/p026a.description: The figure compares electron-dot (Lewis) structures with line-bond (Kekulé) structures for methane, ammonia, water, and methanol. Colored dots show bonding electron pairs and lone pairs, while lines replace the bonding pairs in the lower row.

ch01/prob-1-4.description: A ball-and-stick model labeled Ethane shows two dark carbon atoms bonded together, each surrounded by three light hydrogen atoms. The model illustrates the three-dimensional arrangement of atoms around the carbons.

ch01/fig-1.8.description: A pink, elongated H–H bonding region surrounds two hydrogen nuclei, with a vertical plane cutting through it to show a circular cross-section. The drawing illustrates the cylindrical symmetry of the σ bond in an H₂ molecule.

ch01/table-1.1b.description: An orbital diagram shows paired electrons in the 1s, 2s, 2p, and 3s orbitals, with one electron in each of three 3p orbitals. The nearby text identifies the element as phosphorus (15).

ch01/p030.description: Three side-by-side representations of ethane show an electron-dot structure, a line-bond structure, and the condensed formula CH₃CH₃. Each shows two bonded carbon atoms with three hydrogens attached to each carbon.

ch01/prob-1-9.description: A ball-and-stick model labeled “Hexane” shows six black carbon atoms in a zigzag chain with gray hydrogen atoms attached. The problem asks readers to convert the model into a line-bond structure.

ch01/fig-1.11.description: A spherical 2s orbital and three red-and-blue 2p orbitals are shown combining through hybridization to produce four green sp³ orbitals directed toward the corners of a tetrahedron. A separate enlarged sp³ orbital shows its two unequal lobes.

ch01/fig-1.9.description: An energy diagram places two separate hydrogen atoms above an H₂ molecule, with electron arrows on their respective energy levels. The 436 kJ/mol difference is marked as energy released when the bond forms and absorbed when it breaks.

ch01/fig-1.13.description: Two green sp³ carbon orbital diagrams point to an sp³–sp³ σ bond; below, a structural drawing and ball-and-stick model show ethane. The structural drawing marks a 153 pm carbon–carbon bond and a 111.2° bond angle.

ch01/fig-1.10.description: An energy-versus-internuclear-distance plot for two hydrogen atoms falls to a minimum at a 74 pm bond length, then rises toward zero as the atoms move farther apart. Small drawings show the atoms too close, bonded at the minimum, and too far apart.

ch01/fig-1.14.description: Side and top views show three green sp² hybrid orbitals arranged 120° apart in a plane, with a red-and-blue p orbital perpendicular to that plane at 90°. Dashed axes and pink arrows mark the angles.

ch01/we-1.3.description: The figure shows an electron-dot structure and a line-bond structure for formaldehyde, each with carbon bonded to two hydrogens and double-bonded to oxygen. It illustrates two ways to represent the same bonding arrangement.

ch01/prob-1-12.description: A ball-and-stick model labeled “Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid)” shows a six-carbon ring with a carboxylic acid group and an oxygen-linked acetyl group. Black spheres represent carbon, red oxygen, and gray hydrogen.

ch01/fig-1.16.description: The left diagram shows two green sp hybrid orbitals pointing in opposite directions, marked 180° apart. The right diagram adds two perpendicular p orbitals in blue and pink/red, illustrating their orientation relative to the sp orbitals.

ch01/table-1.1a.description: This cropped table entry shows an orbital diagram labeled 1s, 2s, and 2p. Pink arrows mark electrons on horizontal orbital lines, illustrating how a ground-state electron configuration is represented.

ch01/p035a.description: The figure shows methylamine as a bond drawing beside a ball-and-stick model. A blue lobe marks the nitrogen lone pair, and pink arcs label two bond angles, 107.1° and 110.3°.

ch01/p035c.description: A structural formula and ball-and-stick model show methyl phosphate, with a pink arrow marking an approximately 110° angle around the central phosphorus atom.

ch01/p036.description: Side-by-side structural drawings and ball-and-stick models of methanethiol and dimethyl sulfide show two lone pairs on each sulfur atom, with bond angles labeled 96.5° and 99.1°, respectively.

ch01/fig-1.17.description: Colored orbital diagrams show two carbon atoms’ sp and p orbitals combining to form the carbon–carbon triple bond in acetylene, with one σ bond and two π bonds. Below are space-filling and ball-and-stick models and a linear H–C≡C–H drawing marked 180°, 106 pm, and 120 pm.

ch01/p035b.description: Methanol is shown as an O–H and O–CH₃ structure with two pink lobes marking oxygen’s lone pairs, alongside a ball-and-stick model. A curved arrow marks the 108.5° bond angle at oxygen.

ch01/fig-1.15.description: Two sp²-hybridized carbon atoms are shown combining to form ethylene’s carbon–carbon double bond: green orbitals overlap head-on for the σ bond, while red and blue p orbitals overlap above and below it for the π bond. Below are space-filling and ball-and-stick models and a structural drawing marked with bond lengths of 108.7 pm and 134 pm and angles of 121.3° and 117.4°.

ch01/fig-1.18.description: Two hydrogen 1s orbitals combine to form a lower-energy, filled s bonding molecular orbital and a higher-energy, unfilled s antibonding molecular orbital. The antibonding orbital has a node between the nuclei, and an upward arrow indicates increasing energy.

ch01/prob-1-14a.description: The drawing shows a nitrogen atom bonded to three methyl groups, with one group on each side and one below. It is the structure of trimethylamine in a problem asking about the indicated nitrogen atom.

ch01/table-1.3a.description: A line-bond drawing of isoprene shows a four-carbon chain with two double bonds and a methyl branch; each carbon and hydrogen is explicitly labeled.

ch01/table-1.3d.description: The image shows a skeletal structure of a six-membered ring with a single line extending from one vertex, representing a methyl substituent. It illustrates the skeletal drawing of methylcyclohexane in a table comparing structural representations.

ch01/table-1.3f.description: A skeletal structure shows a six-membered ring with alternating double bonds and an OH group attached, illustrating the line-bond representation of phenol.

ch01/table-1.3b.description: A skeletal structure shows a branched five-carbon chain with two double bonds and a short branch rising from the second carbon. It illustrates the skeletal notation for isoprene in a table comparing line-bond and skeletal structures.

ch01/prob-1-14b.description: The drawing shows methionine as CH₃–S–CH₂–CH₂–CH(NH₂)–C(=O)OH, with sulfur linking a methyl group to the rest of the chain. It accompanies a problem about the sulfur atom.

ch01/we-1.4a.description: A skeletal structure labeled Carvone shows a six-membered ring with a carbonyl group, a double bond and a methyl substituent, plus a branched side chain containing another double bond. The worked example asks readers to count the hydrogens bonded to each carbon and determine the molecular formula.

ch01/table-1.3e.description: A line-bond drawing shows a six-membered ring with alternating double bonds, explicit hydrogen atoms, and an OH group attached to one carbon. It illustrates the line-bond structure of phenol in a table comparing structural drawing styles.

ch01/p038.description: An expanded bond drawing of 2-methylbutane is shown alongside two equivalent condensed structures, illustrating how the same carbon connectivity can be written without drawing every bond.

ch01/table-1.3c.description: A line-bond drawing shows a six-carbon ring with a methyl group attached to one ring carbon; every carbon and hydrogen is written out. It is the methylcyclohexane entry in a table comparing ways to draw chemical structures.

ch01/fig-1.19.description: Two carbon p orbitals combine to form a lower-energy, filled π bonding orbital with continuous lobes and a higher-energy, unfilled π antibonding orbital with a node between the carbons. An upward energy arrow and orbital-level lines show their relative energies.

ch01/fig-1.20.description: A yellow crop-dusting airplane flies low over a field, releasing a yellowish spray beneath its wings. The caption asks how dangerous the pesticide being sprayed on the crop is.

ch01/prob-1-15a.description: A skeletal structure labeled “Adrenaline” shows a benzene ring with two hydroxyl groups and a side chain bearing another hydroxyl group and an NHCH₃ group. It is presented as one of the structures in a problem about counting carbon-bonded hydrogens and determining molecular formulas.

ch01/prob-1-15b.description: The figure shows the skeletal structure of estrone: four fused rings, with an HO group on the left-hand ring, a carbonyl group on the five-membered ring, and a short unlabeled bond extending upward. It accompanies a problem asking readers to determine the hydrogens bonded to each carbon and the molecular formula.

ch01/p040.description: The figure shows atrazine’s structural formula: a nitrogen-containing six-membered ring with chlorine, an ethylamino group, and an isopropylamino group attached. It illustrates the molecular structure of the herbicide discussed in the surrounding text.

ch01/prob-1-17.description: A ball-and-stick model labeled para-Aminobenzoic acid (PABA) shows a six-carbon ring with an amino group and a carboxylic acid group attached on opposite sides. Black spheres represent carbon, red oxygen, blue nitrogen, and gray hydrogen; the drawing does not mark the multiple bonds.

ch01/we-1.4b.description: A skeletal structure labeled Carvone (C₁₀H₁₄O) has colored annotations marking how many hydrogens are attached to each carbon: 0 H, 1 H, 2 H, or 3 H. It illustrates counting implicit hydrogens in a line-angle drawing.

ch01/prob-1-18b.description: A ball-and-stick model labeled “Alanine (an amino acid)” shows a central carbon bonded to a methyl group, an amino group, a hydrogen, and a carboxyl group. Carbon atoms are dark gray, nitrogen is blue, oxygen is red, and hydrogen is pale.

ch01/prob-1-20.description: A ball-and-stick model of acetaminophen shows a benzene ring with a hydroxyl group and, opposite it, an amide group bearing a methyl group. Carbon is black, oxygen red, nitrogen blue, and hydrogen light gray; the problem asks which atoms have lone pairs.

ch01/prob-1-28a.description: The figure shows dimethyl disulfide as H₃C–S–S–CH₃, with two sulfur atoms bonded to each other and each bonded to a methyl group. No nonbonding electrons are drawn.

ch01/prob-1-28b.description: A structural formula labeled “Acetamide” shows a CH₃ group bonded to a carbonyl carbon, which is also bonded to NH₂. The drawing is part of a problem asking for missing nonbonding valence electrons.

ch01/prob-1-28c.description: The figure shows the acetate ion as H₃C–C(=O)–O⁻, with no nonbonding electrons drawn on the oxygen atoms. It is presented in a problem asking the reader to fill in missing nonbonding valence electrons.

ch01/prob-1-18a.description: A ball-and-stick model of coniine shows gray carbon atoms, a blue nitrogen atom, and white hydrogen atoms in a ring with a carbon chain extending to the right. The caption identifies coniine as the toxic substance in poison hemlock.
labels_in_image: Coniine (the toxic substance in poison hemlock)

ch01/prob-1-29a.description: A line-bond structure shows a six-membered ring with alternating double bonds, an O–C(=O)–CH₃ group, and a C(=O)–OH group. It is labeled “Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid)” and appears in a problem asking for molecular formulas.

ch01/prob-1-29d.description: A line-bond drawing shows a six-membered glucose ring with one oxygen in the ring, a CH₂OH group, and several OH and H groups attached. The label beneath it reads “Glucose.”

ch01/prob-1-29b.description: A line-bond structure labeled Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) shows a five-membered ring with a carbonyl, two hydroxyl groups on a carbon–carbon double bond, and a hydroxyl-bearing side chain ending in CH₂OH.

ch01/prob-1-35b.description: The figure labels acetic acid and shows its structural formula, CH₃–C(=O)–OH, with the carbonyl oxygen drawn above the carbon.

ch01/prob-1-29c.description: A line-bond structure labeled “Nicotine” shows a six-membered ring containing one nitrogen attached to a five-membered ring containing a nitrogen bonded to CH₃. Several carbon-bound hydrogens are drawn explicitly.

ch01/prob-1-36.description: A six-carbon ring with alternating single and double bonds has one hydrogen attached to each carbon. The drawing is labeled “Benzene” and accompanies a question about its shape and carbon hybridization.

ch01/prob-1-35a.description: The figure shows 2-methylpropene as a displayed formula: a central carbon bonded to two CH₃ groups and double-bonded to CH₂. It is presented as a structure for the carbon-hybridization question.

ch01/prob-1-37a.description: The figure shows H₂N—CH₂—C(=O)—OH, labeled “Glycine (an amino acid).” The carboxyl-group atoms are highlighted in pink.

ch01/prob-1-19.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a six-carbon structure with three oxygen-bearing terminal groups and a central oxygen bearing hydrogen; carbon is black, oxygen red, and hydrogen gray. The drawing leaves multiple bonds and lone pairs unspecified for the problem.

ch01/prob-1-37b.description: A six-membered ring labeled Pyridine has one nitrogen and five carbon atoms, alternating double bonds, and a hydrogen attached to each carbon. The nitrogen and its two neighboring carbons are highlighted in pink.

ch01/prob-1-37c.description: The figure shows the structural formula CH₃–CH(OH)–C(=O)–OH, labeled “Lactic acid (in sour milk).” The CH₃–CH–C portion is highlighted in pink.

ch01/prob-1-41b.description: An expanded structural drawing shows a five-carbon chain with alternating single and double bonds, labeled “1,3-Pentadiene.” It is presented as a structure to convert into a skeletal drawing.

ch01/prob-1-40.description: The figure shows the skeletal structure of pyridoxal phosphate: a nitrogen-containing ring bearing hydroxyl, methyl, aldehyde, and phosphate-linked side groups. The phosphate group is drawn with two negatively charged oxygens.

ch01/prob-1-41c.description: An expanded structural drawing shows a five-carbon ring with two chlorine atoms attached to adjacent ring carbons; the hydrogens and bonds are drawn explicitly. The structure is labeled “1,2-Dichlorocyclopentane” in a problem asking for conversion to a skeletal drawing.

ch01/prob-1-39a.description: A structural formula labeled “Procaine” shows an amino-substituted benzene ring attached to an ester and a two-carbon chain ending in a positively charged nitrogen with two ethyl groups; Cl⁻ appears nearby. The problem asks about carbon hybridization, but the drawing does not mark any answers.

ch01/prob-1-41d.description: A six-membered ring has carbonyl groups at opposite positions, double bonds on two sides, and one explicitly drawn hydrogen on each of the other four carbons. It is labeled “Benzoquinone.”

ch01/prob-1-39b.description: The figure shows the drawn structure of Vitamin C (ascorbic acid): a five-membered oxygen-containing ring with a carbonyl, a carbon–carbon double bond, several hydroxyl groups, and a CH₂OH-bearing side chain. It is presented as a structure for the problem asking about carbon hybridization.

ch01/prob-1-42b.description: A skeletal structure shows a six-membered saturated ring fused to a benzene ring, with Br attached to the saturated ring and a –C(=O)OH group attached to the benzene ring. It is one of the structures in a problem asking for the number of hydrogens on each carbon and the molecular formula.

ch01/prob-1-42a.description: A benzene ring bears adjacent isopropyl and cyano groups; the cyano group is drawn as C≡N. The figure is one of the structures in a problem asking for hydrogen counts and a molecular formula.

ch01/prob-1-44a.description: A skeletal structure of oseltamivir (Tamiflu) shows a substituted cyclohexene ring with an ether side chain, an ethyl ester, an acetamide group, and an amino group. Solid and dashed bonds indicate stereochemistry at several ring positions.

ch01/prob-1-44b.description: A skeletal chemical structure labeled “Clopidogrel (Plavix)” shows a sulfur-containing fused ring, a nitrogen-containing ring, a methyl ester group, and a chlorinated benzene ring.

ch01/prob-1-48.description: A skeletal structure labeled Caffeine shows a fused nitrogen-containing ring with two carbonyl groups and three methyl groups. Pink arrows point to a carbonyl carbon and to a carbon and nitrogen in the five-membered ring; lone pairs are not shown.

ch01/prob-1-45.description: A five-membered ring is drawn with a triple bond along its bottom edge and labeled “Cyclopentyne.”

ch01/prob-1-42c.description: The line-angle structure shows two fused five-membered rings, with a methyl branch on one ring and a carbonyl group and carbon–carbon double bond on the other. The problem asks for the number of hydrogens bonded to each carbon and the molecular formula.

ch01/prob-1-49.description: A carbon atom bonded to three hydrogen atoms bears a positive charge. The structure is labeled “A carbocation,” illustrating a carbon atom with three bonds.

ch01/prob-1-21.description: A ball-and-stick model of aspartame shows a chain containing red oxygen atoms and blue nitrogen atoms, with a six-membered carbon ring at the right. The problem asks the reader to complete the bonds and mark the multiple bonds; the atom colors are specified as black for carbon, red for oxygen, blue for nitrogen, and gray for hydrogen.

ch02/fig-2.1.description: A close-up photograph shows a pink opium poppy flower with a green seed capsule at its center, alongside another seed capsule and a blurred flower. The caption identifies the opium poppy as the source of morphine.

ch01/prob-1-50.description: The figure shows a carbon bonded to three hydrogens, with a lone pair and a negative charge beside the carbon. It is labeled “A carbanion.”

ch01/prob-1-56.description: Three labeled skeletal structures appear side by side: ibuprofen, naproxen, and acetaminophen. They illustrate the molecular structures of common over-the-counter pain relievers.

ch02/fig-2.2.description: Three electron-cloud drawings compare a covalent X–X bond with evenly shared electrons, a polar covalent X–Y bond with δ+ on X and δ− on Y, and separated X+ and Y− ions. An arrow labeled “Ionic character” increases from left to right, showing the continuum from covalent to ionic bonding.

ch01/prob-1-43.description: An atom-labeled structural drawing of quetiapine (Seroquel) shows a sulfur- and nitrogen-containing fused-ring system attached to a six-membered ring with two nitrogen atoms. A chain labeled OCH₂CH₂OCH₂CH₂OH extends from the upper nitrogen; the problem asks readers to convert the drawing to a skeletal structure and give its molecular formula.

ch02/prob-2-4.description: The figure pairs a wedge-and-dash structure of methylamine with an electrostatic potential map of the same molecule, showing colored regions around its C–N bond. It asks the reader to determine the bond’s direction of polarization.

ch02/fig-2.3.description: A color-coded periodic table lists electronegativity values for elements, ranging from Cs at 0.7 to F at 4.0. The colors illustrate the general increase from left to right and decrease from top to bottom.

ch02/fig-2.4.description: Two panels compare methanol’s C–O bond and methyllithium’s C–Li bond using ball-and-stick models, colored electrostatic potential maps, and structures marked with partial charges. Methanol shows δ− on oxygen and δ+ on carbon (electronegativity difference 1.0); methyllithium shows δ− on carbon and δ+ on lithium (difference 1.5).

ch02/table-2.1b.description: The table shows drawings of water, methanol, and ammonia with colored lone-pair regions, pink dipole arrows, and dipole moments of 1.85 D, 1.70 D, and 1.47 D, respectively. It compares the directions and magnitudes of their molecular dipoles.

ch02/table-2.1c.description: The table shows structural drawings of carbon dioxide, methane, ethane, and benzene, each labeled with a dipole moment of μ = 0. It illustrates that these molecules have zero overall dipole moments.

ch02/p054a.description: The figure shows a Lewis structure and an electrostatic-potential molecular model of dimethyl sulfoxide. Arrows mark the oxygen as formally negative and the sulfur as formally positive; the model shows red near oxygen and blue near sulfur.

ch02/table-2.1a.description: A table of compound dipole moments shows a six-membered ring with alternating double bonds labeled “Benzene,” with a dipole moment of 0 D.

ch02/we-2.1.description: A wedge-and-dash drawing of methylamine shows the nitrogen lone pair in a blue lobe and a pink dipole arrow pointing from the methyl group toward it. The figure labels methylamine with μ = 1.31.

ch02/p055b.description: Two equivalent equations define formal charge as an atom’s free-atom valence-electron count minus its bonded-atom electron count. The second expands the bonded-atom count into half the bonding electrons plus the nonbonding electrons.
labels_in_image: Number of valence electrons in free atom
Number of valence electrons in bonded atom

ch02/table-2.2a.description: A table entry shows a phosphorus atom labeled P⁺ with four single bonds radiating upward, downward, left, and right, illustrating a common positive formal charge on phosphorus.

ch02/table-2.2c.description: A carbon atom marked with a positive charge has three single bonds extending left, right, and downward, illustrating a common formal-charge pattern in the table.

ch02/p054b.description: The figure compares an isolated carbon atom with four pink valence-electron dots to a methane Lewis structure showing four C–H bonds as shared electron pairs. Arrows and text indicate that carbon owns four valence electrons in both drawings.
labels_in_image: An isolated carbon atom owns 4 valence electrons.
This carbon atom also owns 8/2 = 4 valence electrons.

ch02/table-2.2b.description: A nitrogen atom marked with a positive charge is shown with four single bonds extending upward, downward, left, and right, illustrating a common formal-charge pattern.

ch02/p055a.description: A Lewis structure shows sulfur bonded to oxygen and two carbon groups, with a positive charge on sulfur and a negative charge on oxygen. Beside it, electron counts and formal-charge calculations give +1 for sulfur and −1 for oxygen.

ch02/table-2.2e.description: A sulfur atom is shown with three single bonds, one lone pair of electrons, and a positive formal charge, as an entry in a table of common formal charges.

ch02/p054c.description: The figure compares an isolated nitrogen atom with five valence-electron dots to nitrogen in ammonia, drawn with three N–H bonds and one lone pair. It shows the calculation 6/2 + 2 = 5 for nitrogen’s assigned valence electrons in ammonia.
labels_in_image: An isolated nitrogen atom owns 5 valence electrons.
This nitrogen atom also owns 6/2 + 2 = 5 valence electrons.

ch02/table-2.2f.description: A table entry shows an oxygen atom with one lone pair, three single bonds to unspecified groups, and a positive formal charge.

ch02/table-2.2d.description: A table entry shows a carbon atom with three single bonds to unspecified groups, a lone pair, and a negative formal charge.

ch02/p056b.description: Two line-bond drawings of the acetate ion are linked by a double-headed resonance arrow. The C=O double bond and negative charge switch between the upper and lower oxygen atoms, with callouts asking which oxygen should have the double bond.

ch02/p056a.description: A bracketed Lewis structure of methyl phosphate dianion shows a CH₃–O–P group with one double-bonded oxygen and two singly bonded oxygens, with lone pairs marked by dots and an overall 2− charge.

ch02/table-2.2h.description: A table entry shows a nitrogen atom with two single bonds, one extending to each side, and two lone pairs of electrons, one above and one below.

ch02/p057a.description: An electrostatic potential map of benzene appears beside two hexagonal structures with alternating double bonds in different positions, connected by a double-headed arrow. The figure illustrates benzene’s two resonance forms.

ch02/p057c.description: Two benzene ring drawings are connected by a double-headed arrow. Pink curved arrows on the left show the double bonds shifting positions while the carbon and hydrogen atoms remain in place.

ch02/p056c.description: An electrostatic potential model of the acetate ion shows red regions around both oxygen atoms. Beside it, two line-bond resonance forms are connected by a double-headed arrow, with the C=O double bond and negative charge on opposite oxygens in the two drawings.

ch02/table-2.2g.description: The cropped table entry shows a carbon atom bonded by three single lines, with a dot above the C. It appears in a table summarizing common formal charges.

ch02/p057b.description: Two resonance forms of the acetate ion are shown with a double-headed arrow between them. Curved arrows show a lone pair on the upper oxygen forming a C=O bond while the original C=O bond electrons move onto the lower oxygen as a lone pair.

ch02/p058a.description: Acetone is shown converting under “Base” to an acetone anion with two resonance forms, connected by a double-headed arrow. Curved arrows depict electron movement; one form has a negative charge on carbon, and the other has it on oxygen.

molecules.name: Acetone anion

labels_in_image: This resonance form has the negative charge on carbon.
This resonance form has the negative charge on oxygen.

ch02/p058b.description: The acetate ion is drawn beside a proposed resonance form in which the carbon bonded to the two oxygens has double bonds to both; a crossed-out resonance arrow separates them. The proposed form is labeled invalid, with an arrow pointing to that carbon and noting it has 10 electrons.

ch02/p058c.description: A generic X–Y–Z three-atom grouping is shown in two resonance forms, X=Y–Z* and *X–Y=Z, with the multiple bond and asterisk shifting between the ends. Colored p-orbital lobes flank the formulas, and an annotation says the asterisk represents 0, 1, or 2 electrons.

ch02/p059a.description: The drawing shows 2,4-pentanedione reacting with a base to give an anion after removal of one hydrogen from the central carbon. The remaining central hydrogen is highlighted in pink, and a lone pair and negative charge are shown on that carbon.

ch02/we-2.2a.description: A Lewis structure labeled “Carbonate ion” shows a central carbon double-bonded to one oxygen and single-bonded to two negatively charged oxygens, with lone-pair dots around the oxygens.

ch02/p059c.description: Three resonance structures of the 2,4-pentanedione anion are linked by double-headed arrows. Pink curved arrows show electron pairs shifting from the central carbon toward either carbonyl, placing the negative charge on an oxygen in the other two structures.

ch02/p060.description: A five-carbon chain with two alternating double bonds is drawn with an unpaired electron marked by a dot on the terminal carbon. The figure labels it “Pentadienyl radical” and points to the dot with an “Unpaired electron” arrow.

ch02/we-2.2b.description: Three Lewis structures of the carbonate ion are connected by double-headed resonance arrows; the C=O double bond moves among the three oxygens, while the other two oxygens bear negative charges. Pink brackets and arrows labeled “Three-atom groupings” highlight the groups used to draw the resonance forms.

ch02/we-2.3b.description: Two resonance forms of the pentadienyl radical are connected by a double-headed arrow. The unpaired electron moves from the central carbon to an end carbon as a double bond shifts; pink brackets mark the three-atom groupings.

ch02/prob-2-10.description: A benzene ring with alternating double bonds is bonded to a CO₂⁻ group, depicting the benzoate anion as a structure for the resonance-form problem.

ch02/we-2.3c.description: Three resonance forms of the pentadienyl radical are connected by double-headed arrows. The carbon skeleton stays the same while the double bonds shift and the unpaired electron appears at the right end, center, or left end.

ch02/we-2.3a.description: Two resonance forms of a five-carbon radical are connected by a double-headed arrow. The double bonds and unpaired electron shift positions, with pink brackets highlighting a three-atom grouping in each form.

ch02/prob-2-9a.description: Two structures are shown side by side: a benzene ring bonded to a positively charged CH₂ group, and a six-membered ring with an exocyclic CH₂ double bond and a positive charge on a ring carbon. The problem presents them as a pair to compare for resonance.

ch02/table-2.3b.description: A vertical arrow points upward from “Weaker base” to “Stronger base,” illustrating the direction of increasing base strength.

ch02/p061b.description: A generic acid H–A reacts reversibly with a base :B to form the conjugate base :A⁻ and conjugate acid H–B⁺. The diagram illustrates proton transfer in a Brønsted–Lowry acid–base reaction.

ch02/table-2.3a.description: A vertical arrow fades from blue at the top to pink at the bottom, pointing from “Weaker acid” toward “Stronger acid.” It illustrates increasing acid strength downward.

ch02/p061c.description: Two reversible acid–base reactions show acetic acid transferring a proton to hydroxide to form acetate and water, and water transferring a proton to ammonia to form hydroxide and ammonium. The reactants and products are labeled acid, base, conjugate base, and conjugate acid, illustrating that water can act as either an acid or a base.

molecules.name: hydroxide
molecules.role: base in upper reaction; conjugate base in lower reaction

molecules.name: water
molecules.role: conjugate acid in upper reaction; acid in lower reaction

ch02/p061a.description: A reversible reaction shows H–Cl and water forming chloride ion and hydronium ion, with colored molecular models above each structure. The four species are labeled acid, base, conjugate base, and conjugate acid, respectively.

ch02/prob-2-12.description: The problem shows the structures of phenylalanine and tryptophan side by side, each with a positively charged amino group and a carboxylic acid group. Their printed pKa values are 1.83 and 2.83, respectively, for comparing acid strength.

ch02/prob-2-9b.description: Two hydrocarbon structures are shown side by side, separated by “and”: CH₂=C(CH₃)–CH=C(CH₂CH₃)–CH₃ on the left and CH₃–C(CH₃)=CH–C(CH₂CH₃)=CH₂ on the right. The problem presents them as a pair to compare, without indicating an answer.

ch02/p059b.description: Two resonance structures are connected by a double-headed arrow. The highlighted double bond is between carbon and oxygen in the left structure and between two carbons in the right, while a labeled lone pair appears on the adjacent carbon in the left structure and on oxygen in the right.

ch02/p064a.description: An equilibrium reaction shows acetic acid and hydroxide ion forming acetate ion and water, with colored molecular models above the corresponding structures. The labels give pKa = 4.76 for acetic acid and pKa = 15.74 for water, illustrating an acid–base reaction compared by pKa values.

ch02/p064b.description: An equilibrium reaction shows acetic acid and hydroxide forming water and acetate. The reactants are labeled “Stronger acid” and “Stronger base,” while the products are labeled “Weaker acid” and “Weaker base.”

ch02/we-2.4.description: The worked example shows acetylene reacting with hydroxide ion in a proposed reaction to form an acetylide ion and water. A question mark above the arrow asks whether the reaction occurs to a significant extent.

ch02/p066c.description: Three labeled structural formulas show acetic acid, pyruvic acid, and citric acid, with the hydrogen in each carboxylic acid group highlighted in pink. They illustrate examples of organic acids.

ch02/prob-2-14a.description: An acid–base reaction is shown with HCN and sodium acetate on the left and sodium cyanide and acetic acid on the right. A question mark above the arrow asks whether the reaction proceeds significantly as written.

ch02/prob-2-15.description: The problem shows acetone reacting with sodium amide, with a question mark over the reaction arrow. The structures drawn on the right are a negatively charged carbon adjacent to acetone’s carbonyl group, a sodium ion, and ammonia; the figure asks whether this reaction occurs to a significant extent.

ch02/p065.description: Three side-by-side examples show colored molecular surfaces above structural formulas for methanol, acetic acid, and acetone, with pKa values of 15.54, 4.76, and 19.3, respectively. Pink hydrogen labels mark the O–H hydrogens in methanol and acetic acid and the carbon-bound hydrogens next to the carbonyl group in acetone.

ch02/p066b.description: Acetone loses H⁺ from a methyl group to form an anion shown in two resonance forms, with the negative charge on carbon or oxygen. The figure states that resonance and placement of charge on electronegative oxygen stabilize the anion.

molecules.name: acetone enolate
molecules.role: product, shown in two resonance forms

labels_in_image: Anion is stabilized both by resonance and by having negative charge on a highly electronegative atom.

ch02/p066a.description: The upper drawing shows methanol losing H⁺ to form methoxide, with its negative charge on oxygen. Below, acetic acid loses H⁺ to form acetate, shown in two resonance forms; the accompanying text links anion stabilization to oxygen's electronegativity and, for acetate, resonance.

ch02/prob-2-14b.description: The reaction diagram shows ethanol and sodium cyanide on the left of an arrow, with sodium ethoxide and hydrogen cyanide on the right. A pink question mark above the arrow asks whether the reaction occurs.

ch02/p067c.description: A Lewis base labeled B has a filled orbital containing an electron pair, while a Lewis acid labeled A has a vacant orbital. The diagram shows them combining to form a B—A bond, illustrating donation of the electron pair.

ch02/p067b.description: Two structural drawings of alanine are connected by opposing arrows: the uncharged form has an NH₂ group and a COOH group, while the zwitterion form has NH₃⁺ and COO⁻ groups.

ch02/fig-2.5.description: Three side-by-side electrostatic potential maps show the conjugate bases of methanol, acetic acid, and acetone, with their structural formulas underneath. Red regions around the oxygen atoms indicate substantial negative charge.

ch02/p067a.description: Three labeled organic bases—methylamine, methanol, and acetone—are shown as structural formulas beneath color-shaded molecular surface models. Blue dots mark lone electron pairs on nitrogen or oxygen in the formulas.

ch02/fig-2.6.description: Electrostatic potential models and structural drawings show boron trifluoride reacting with dimethyl ether to form an acid–base complex. A curved arrow shows an oxygen lone pair moving toward boron; in the product map, boron is redder and oxygen bluer.

ch02/p067d.description: Mg²⁺, labeled a Lewis acid, reacts with an organodiphosphate ion labeled a Lewis base. The product drawing shows Mg²⁺ associated with two negatively charged oxygens of the diphosphate in an acid–base complex.

ch02/p069c.description: Acetic acid reacts with H₂SO₄ by protonation at its doubly bonded oxygen; curved arrows and two resonance structures show the resulting cation. A bracketed structure protonated at the other oxygen is marked “not formed.”

ch02/fig-2.7.description: Two panels depict polar molecules as pink-to-blue ovals marked δ− and δ+. In (a), they line up with opposite partial charges adjacent, illustrating attraction; in (b), their orientations place like charges near one another, illustrating repulsion.

ch02/fig-2.8.description: Four space-filling models of pentane are arranged side by side, each with blue δ+ labels on the left and pink δ− labels on the right. The aligned temporary dipoles illustrate attractive dispersion forces between nonpolar molecules.

ch02/p069a.description: Water’s oxygen donates a lone pair to the hydrogen of H–Cl as the H–Cl bond electrons move to chlorine. A reversible arrow connects the acid and base to the hydronium ion and chloride ion.

ch02/prob-2-18.description: The figure shows the five-membered imidazole ring as a structural formula beside a colored electrostatic potential map. A bracketed structure of histidine shows the same ring attached to a side chain with NH₃⁺ and COO⁻ groups.

ch02/p068.description: A bracket labeled “Some Lewis acids” groups neutral proton donors, cations, and metal compounds. The proton donors include formulas and drawings of a carboxylic acid, a phenol, and an alcohol, with their hydrogen atoms highlighted in pink.

ch02/we-2.6.description: Curved arrows show the oxygen lone pair of acetaldehyde bonding to H in a generic H–A acid while the H–A bond electrons move to A. An equilibrium arrow leads to protonated acetaldehyde and A⁻, illustrating acetaldehyde acting as a Lewis base.

ch02/p071b.description: Two views of a deoxyribonucleic acid segment show its coiled double-strand shape: a space-filling model on the left and a skeletal model on the right. An arrow in the skeletal model points to hydrogen bonds between the strands.

ch02/fig-2.9.description: A photograph shows a coca bush with oval green leaves and small green, yellow, and red fruits. The caption identifies it as Erythroxylon coca, the source of the alkaloid cocaine.

ch02/p071a.description: Two water molecules and two ammonia molecules are each shown with a dotted hydrogen bond between a hydrogen and a neighboring oxygen or nitrogen. Below, electrostatic potential maps show the same pairs, with positively polarized hydrogens in blue and negatively polarized oxygens or nitrogens in red.

ch02/p073.description: Three labeled skeletal structures show the alkaloids morphine, ephedrine, and cocaine side by side, with wedge and dashed bonds indicating three-dimensional arrangement at some atoms.

ch02/prob-2-19.description: Two labeled structural formulas appear side by side: vitamin A (retinol) has a ring attached to a long carbon chain ending in CH₂OH, while vitamin C (ascorbic acid) has a five-membered ring with several OH groups. The accompanying problem asks which vitamin is water-soluble and which is fat-soluble.

ch02/p072.description: The figure shows sucrose as two linked rings with several OH groups, alongside animal fat as a triester with three ester-linked R chains. The animal-fat label specifies that R, R′, and R″ are C₁₁–C₁₉ chains.

ch02/p074a.description: Two labeled skeletal structures are shown side by side: Procaine (Novocain) on the left and Lidocaine (Xylocaine) on the right. Each has an aromatic ring and a nitrogen-containing side chain.

ch02/p069b.description: A chart of eleven Lewis-base examples shows alcohol, ether, carbonyl, amine, sulfide, and organotriphosphate structures, with blue dots marking lone pairs on oxygen, nitrogen, or sulfur atoms. The examples are grouped under a bracket labeled “Some Lewis bases.”

ch02/prob-2-23b.description: A ball-and-stick model labeled Cytosine shows a six-membered ring with blue nitrogen atoms, an attached blue nitrogen with two gray hydrogens, and a red oxygen. The problem asks for multiple bonds and lone pairs to be added and a skeletal structure to be drawn.

ch02/p074b.description: Three side-by-side skeletal structures are labeled Mepivacaine (Carbocaine), Bupivacaine (Marcaine), and Prilocaine (Citanest). Each shows an aromatic ring, an amide group, and a nitrogen-containing portion, with different substituents.

ch02/prob-2-22.description: The figure compares cis-1,2-dichloroethylene and trans-1,2-dichloroethylene using structural drawings, ball-and-stick models, and colored molecular surfaces. The chlorine atoms are on the same side of the double bond in the cis form and opposite sides in the trans form.

ch02/prob-2-20.description: A ball-and-stick model of naphthalene shows two fused six-membered carbon rings, with dark spheres for carbon and light spheres for hydrogen. The drawing leaves the placement of multiple bonds unspecified.

ch02/prob-2-24b.description: An acid–base reaction is shown with HI and acetone as reactants, followed by an arrow toward an unspecified product. No curved arrows or products are drawn.

ch02/prob-2-25b.description: A skeletal structure shows a carbonyl group bonded to a methyl group and to an N–H group bearing another methyl group. No curved arrows or protonated form are shown.

ch02/prob-2-24c.description: An acid–base reaction prompt shows acetic acid plus trimethylamine, with a right-pointing arrow and no product drawn. Lone pairs are shown on the oxygen and nitrogen atoms.

ch02/prob-2-25c.description: A six-membered ring with alternating double bonds and one nitrogen atom is shown as a Lewis base in a protonation problem. No curved arrows or protonated product are drawn.

ch02/prob-2-25a.description: A five-membered ring has an oxygen atom at the top and four unlabeled carbon vertices. The drawing shows the Lewis base before protonation; no curved arrows or protonated product are shown.

ch02/prob-2-24a.description: A five-membered ring containing an oxygen atom is shown reacting with BF₃; an arrow points to an unspecified product. The drawing is an acid/base reaction prompt and does not show the product or curved arrows.

ch02/prob-2-25d.description: A benzene ring is bonded to a carbonyl carbon that also bears a hydrogen, showing the structure of benzaldehyde. No protonation or curved arrows are drawn.

ch02/prob-2-26a.description: Two resonance forms of a five-carbon chain bearing an NH₂ group are connected by a double-headed arrow. The left structure has a positive charge on a carbon and a C=C bond near the NH₂ group; the right has two C=C bonds and a positive charge on the NH₂ group.

ch02/prob-2-27.description: A six-membered carbon ring is drawn with a double bond along its left side, depicting cyclohexene as one of the problem structures.

ch02/prob-2-30a.description: A six-membered benzene ring with alternating double bonds has an OH group attached to one carbon, depicting the structure of phenol.

ch02/prob-2-30d.description: A benzene ring is drawn with two hydroxyl groups at opposite positions. The image shows only this structure, with no dipole arrows or other annotations.

ch02/prob-2-30b.description: A benzene ring is drawn with two OH groups attached to adjacent carbon atoms. The structure is presented as one of the molecules in a dipole-moment problem.

ch02/prob-2-26b.description: Two resonance structures of an enolate are connected by a double-headed arrow: the left has a negatively charged oxygen and a carbon–carbon double bond, while the right has a carbonyl double bond and a negative charge on the adjacent carbon. The figure asks for curved arrows showing the electron flow between them.

ch02/prob-2-30c.description: A benzene ring is drawn with two hydroxyl groups attached at the upper-left and upper-right positions, separated by one ring carbon.

ch02/prob-2-26c.description: Two resonance structures of a methyl-substituted six-membered ring are connected by a double-headed arrow. The double bonds and positive charge occupy different positions in the two drawings.

ch02/prob-2-35a.description: A structure shows an H₂C carbon with a pair of dots above it, single-bonded to a phosphorus atom that is also bonded to three CH₃ groups. The carbon and phosphorus are highlighted in red for a formal-charge exercise.

ch02/prob-2-35b.description: A six-membered ring with alternating double bonds has a red nitrogen at one vertex, bonded to a red oxygen below it. Dots around the oxygen represent lone-pair electrons; the highlighted atoms are the subject of a formal-charge problem.

ch02/prob-2-37b.description: Two six-membered ring structures are shown side by side: the left has a negatively charged, singly bonded oxygen and a double bond within the ring; the right has a carbonyl group and a negative charge on the adjacent ring carbon.

ch02/prob-2-36.description: The drawing shows a central nitrogen atom bonded to three methyl groups and a singly bonded oxygen atom with three lone pairs. It is presented as a structure for a formal-charge assignment problem, with no charges marked.

ch02/prob-2-38a.description: The drawing shows a three-carbon structure with a central carbonyl group, a CH₃ group on one side, and a CH₂ group bearing a lone pair and negative charge on the other. It is presented as a species for which the reader is asked to draw resonance structures.

ch02/prob-2-37c.description: Two structures are shown side by side: a benzene ring fused to a four-membered ring, and a six-membered ring with two internal double bonds and two adjacent exocyclic double bonds.

ch02/prob-2-37d.description: Two skeletal structures are shown side by side: a benzene ring bonded to an O⁻ group, and a six-membered ring with a double-bonded oxygen at the top and a negatively charged carbon at the bottom. They illustrate two drawn arrangements of bonds and charge for the same species.

ch02/prob-2-38c.description: A carbon atom is single-bonded to two NH₂ groups, each shown with a lone pair, and double-bonded to an NH₂ group bearing a positive charge. This is one resonance structure of the guanidinium ion in a problem asking for additional resonance structures.

ch02/prob-2-37a.description: Two ring structures are shown side by side: a benzene ring bonded to a negatively charged oxygen, and a ring with a carbonyl oxygen, a negative charge on the adjacent carbon, and shifted double bonds. The drawing compares alternative placements of bonds and charge.

ch02/prob-2-21.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a carbon framework with a six-membered ring, a branching chain with a double bond on the left, and a carboxylic acid group on the right. Black spheres represent carbon, red oxygen, and pale spheres hydrogen; the problem asks where the multiple bonds are and for a skeletal structure.

ch02/prob-2-41.description: The figure shows the structural formula of acetic acid, with three hydrogens attached to a carbon and one hydrogen attached to an oxygen in the –COOH group. It accompanies a question comparing the acidity of the O–H hydrogen with the C–H hydrogens.

ch02/prob-2-39.description: Two rectangular ring structures are shown side by side: the left has double bonds on its top and bottom edges, while the right has double bonds on its left and right edges. A double-headed arrow between them is crossed by a pink slash, indicating they are not resonance forms.

ch02/prob-2-38b.description: A six-membered ring has two double bonds and a lone pair on the upper-right carbon, which is bonded to a labeled H; the adjacent lower-right carbon bears two labeled H atoms. The drawing is one resonance structure of a cyclohexadienyl anion in a problem asking for additional resonance structures.

ch02/prob-2-47.description: A structural formula shows a central carbon bonded to three CH₃ groups and an O⁻, with K⁺ beside the oxygen. The figure labels the compound “Potassium tert-butoxide.”

ch02/prob-2-44.description: Four labeled structures—acetone, 2,4-pentanedione, phenol, and acetic acid—are shown with pKa values of 19.3, 9, 9.9, and 4.76, respectively. The figure presents their structures and acidity values for a ranking problem without giving the ranking.

ch02/prob-2-53.description: Two structural formulas show maleic acid with both carboxylic acid groups on the same side of a carbon–carbon double bond, and fumaric acid with the groups on opposite sides. The accompanying problem states that maleic acid has a dipole moment whereas fumaric acid does not.

ch02/prob-2-48.description: The figure shows pyridine, drawn as a six-membered ring with a nitrogen lone pair, plus acetic acid, followed by a reaction arrow pointing to a question mark. It asks for the product of their reaction without showing that product.

ch02/prob-2-38d.description: The structure shows H₃C–S–CH₂⁺, with two lone pairs drawn on sulfur and a positive charge on the CH₂ carbon. It is one of the species in a problem asking for resonance structures.

ch02/prob-2-55a.description: Acetone and TiCl₄ are shown reacting to form an oxygen–titanium adduct. In the product, acetone’s oxygen bears a positive charge and the TiCl₄ group a negative charge.

ch02/prob-2-57b.description: The figure labels ozone and shows one resonance structure, O=O–O, with a positive charge on the central oxygen, a negative charge on the singly bonded terminal oxygen, and lone-pair dots.

ch02/prob-2-55b.description: A reaction drawing shows cyclohexanone and NaH forming a ring with a negative charge on the carbon next to the carbonyl, alongside Na⁺ and H₂. It illustrates removal of a hydrogen from the carbon adjacent to the carbonyl.

ch02/prob-2-57a.description: The figure shows a Lewis structure labeled “Nitromethane”: H₃C is bonded to N⁺, which is double-bonded to one oxygen and single-bonded to an O⁻. Lone pairs are marked as dots on both oxygens.

ch02/prob-2-58a.description: A three-carbon carbocation bearing a positively charged central carbon reacts with H₂O to form the corresponding alcohol, with OH attached to the central carbon, plus H⁺. The diagram illustrates the general conversion of a carbocation to an alcohol by reaction with water.

ch02/prob-2-56a.description: Two structures are shown side by side: CH₃–C(=O)–O⁻ and ⁻CH₂–C(=O)–OH, with lone pairs and negative charges marked. The problem asks whether the pair represents resonance structures.

ch02/prob-2-56b.description: Two benzene-ring amides are shown side by side: the left has a carbonyl group and a positively charged NH₃ group, while the right has a positively charged OH group double-bonded to carbon and an NH₂ group. The drawing presents these structures as subjects of a resonance-structure problem.

ch02/prob-2-59a.description: A generic ketone is drawn with a carbonyl group (C=O) and two single bonds extending from the carbonyl carbon to unlabeled groups. The drawing is labeled “Ketone.”

ch02/prob-2-58b.description: A drawn allylic carbocation reacts with H₂O to give two alcohol structures: one has OH on the carbon that bore the positive charge, and the other has OH at the opposite end of the allylic group, with the double bond shifted.

ch02/prob-2-55c.description: A six-membered ring containing NH and O reacts with BH₃ to form an adduct with a new N–B bond. The product shows a positive charge on nitrogen and a negative charge on BH₃.

ch02/prob-2-59d.description: A generic nitrile group is drawn as a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen, with a single bond extending from the carbon to the left. The structure is labeled “Nitrile.”

ch02/prob-2-61.description: The figure shows the structures of phenol, a benzene ring bearing an –OH group, and methanol, CH₃OH. Their printed pKa values, 9.89 and 15.54 respectively, compare their acidity.

ch02/prob-2-59b.description: A line drawing shows a central carbon bonded to an OH group and three unlabeled carbon branches. The structure is captioned “Alcohol.”

ch02/prob-2-60.description: The figure shows one drawn structure of azidobenzene: a benzene ring bonded to a chain of three nitrogen atoms, with lone-pair dots shown on the nitrogens. It is the starting structure for a problem asking for additional resonance structures and formal charges.

ch02/prob-2-59c.description: A structure labeled “Amide” shows a carbonyl carbon double-bonded to oxygen, single-bonded to NH₂, and bonded to an unlabeled line ending on the left. It illustrates the amide functional group.

ch02/prob-2-56c.description: Two charged carbon–nitrogen–oxygen structures are shown side by side: CH₂=N⁺ bonded to two O⁻ atoms, and :CH₂⁻–N⁺ double-bonded to one oxygen and single-bonded to O⁻. Lone-pair dots and formal charges are drawn on the atoms.

ch02/prob-2-63.description: The figure shows a positively charged C(CH₃)₃ group, one of the species in a problem asking which compounds or ions have a dipole moment.

ch02/prob-2-62.description: A bracketed thiamin diphosphate (TPP) structure, marked 2−, has a highlighted ring hydrogen labeled pKₐ = 18. An arrow labeled “Base” leads to a 3− structure in which that hydrogen is absent and a pair of dots appears on the ring carbon.

ch02/prob-2-64a.description: The figure shows phenol and benzoate ion on one side of an equilibrium arrow, and phenoxide ion and benzoic acid on the other. It presents an acid–base equilibrium without indicating which direction is favored.

ch02/prob-2-64b.description: An equilibrium arrow connects CH₃CH₂CH₂OH and NH₂⁻ on the left with CH₃CH₂CH₂O⁻ and NH₃ on the right. The drawing presents the acid–base equilibrium without indicating which direction is favored.

ch03/fig-3.1.description: A photograph shows two weathered bristlecone pines with twisted trunks in a snowy, shrub-covered landscape. The caption links the trees' needles to alkanes in their waxy coating; no chemical structures are shown.

ch03/table-3.1c.description: The table entry shows a six-membered ring with alternating double bonds, labeled “Benzene.” It illustrates the arene (aromatic ring) functional group.

ch03/p085.description: Three colored molecular models sit above line drawings labeled “Alkene,” “Alkyne,” and “Arene (aromatic ring).” The drawings compare a carbon–carbon double bond, a triple bond, and a six-membered ring with alternating double bonds.

ch02/prob-2-64c.description: An equilibrium reaction shows CH₃⁻ and CH₃NO₂ on the left, and CH₄ and CH₂NO₂⁻ on the right. The drawing illustrates transfer of a proton from CH₃NO₂ to CH₃⁻.

ch03/table-3.1b.description: A pink six-membered ring with three alternating double bonds has black single bonds extending outward from each vertex. It illustrates the arene (aromatic ring) functional group.

ch03/table-3.1d.description: A generic halide functional group is shown: a carbon bonded to X, with its other three bonds drawn as plain, solid-wedge, and dashed-wedge lines. The nearby text defines X as F, Cl, Br, or I.

ch03/fig-3.2.description: Side-by-side reactions show ethylene and the larger ring molecule menthene each reacting with Br₂: bromine adds across the highlighted carbon–carbon double bond, leaving one Br on each formerly double-bonded carbon. Molecular surface models and arrows emphasize that the same functional group reacts similarly in both molecules.

ch03/table-3.1e.description: A generic carbon is bonded to an OH group and three unlabeled bonds; solid and dashed wedges show the bonds extending toward and away from the viewer. It illustrates the three-dimensional arrangement around a carbon bearing an alcohol group.

ch03/table-3.1f.description: A generic ether functional group is drawn with a pink oxygen atom bonded between two carbon atoms. Wedge and dashed bonds extend from each carbon, showing their three-dimensional bond directions.

ch03/table-3.1g.description: This table excerpt shows methyl phosphate: a carbon group bonded through oxygen to phosphorus, which is double-bonded to one oxygen and single-bonded to two negatively charged oxygens. Wedge and dashed bonds show the carbon's three other bonds.

ch03/table-3.1k.description: The table entry shows acetone imine, with a central carbon bonded to two CH₃ groups and double-bonded to NH. The C=NH group illustrates an imine functional group.

ch03/table-3.1l.description: A generic tetrahedral carbon is bonded to an –SH group, with its other three bonds shown as a plain line, a solid wedge, and a dashed wedge. The drawing illustrates a thiol functional group.

ch03/table-3.1h.description: The table shows a carbon group connected through oxygen to two linked phosphate groups. Three oxygen atoms are marked with negative charges, illustrating the diphosphate functional group.

ch03/table-3.1p.description: The figure shows the structure CH₃–S⁺(O⁻)–CH₃, labeled “Dimethyl sulfoxide,” illustrating a sulfoxide functional group.

ch03/table-3.1o.description: A generic sulfoxide structure shows sulfur bonded to oxygen and two carbon groups, with a positive charge on sulfur and a negative charge on oxygen.

ch03/table-3.1r.description: The table entry shows ethanal as CH₃–CH=O, with the carbonyl group highlighted in pink. It illustrates an aldehyde functional group.

ch03/table-3.1q.description: This table entry shows a generic aldehyde group: a carbon double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded to hydrogen and an unlabeled carbon chain.

ch03/table-3.1i.description: A carbon atom is bonded to a nitrogen atom with a lone pair. Solid and dashed wedges depict the three-dimensional arrangement of their other bonds, illustrating the amine entry in the functional-group table.

ch03/table-3.1j.description: A generic imine (Schiff base) structure shows nitrogen double-bonded to a carbon attached to two carbon groups. Wedge and dashed bonds on the outer carbons indicate three-dimensional bonding.

ch03/table-3.1s.description: The drawing shows a ketone functional group: a carbonyl carbon double-bonded to oxygen and bonded to a carbon on each side. Wedge-and-dash bonds extend from the neighboring carbons.

ch03/table-3.1t.description: The table entry shows propanone as CH₃–C(=O)–CH₃, illustrating a ketone with a carbonyl group between two carbon groups.

ch03/table-3.1n.description: The drawing shows two carbon atoms joined by an S–S linkage, with solid and dashed wedge bonds indicating the other bonds around each carbon. It illustrates the disulfide functional group in the nearby example of dimethyl disulfide.

ch03/table-3.1v.description: The table entry shows the structural formula CH₃C(=O)OH, labeled “Ethanoic acid,” illustrating a carboxylic acid functional group.

ch03/table-3.1x.description: A table entry shows the condensed structure of methyl ethanoate, with a carbonyl group bonded to an oxygen and a methyl group, illustrating an ester functional group.

ch03/table-3.1w.description: The table entry shows a generic ester group: a carbonyl carbon double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded through another oxygen to a carbon group. Solid and dashed wedge bonds appear on the carbon groups on either side.

ch03/table-3.1m.description: A sulfide functional group is shown as a sulfur atom single-bonded to two carbon atoms. Solid and dashed bonds extend from each carbon to indicate its other attachments.

ch03/table-3.1z.description: The table entry shows the structure CH₃C(=O)SCH₃, with the oxygen double bond and sulfur linkage highlighted in pink. It is labeled “Methyl ethanethioate” and illustrates a thioester functional group.

ch03/table-3.1y.description: A thioester functional group is drawn as a carbonyl carbon double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded to sulfur, with carbon groups on either side; wedge and dashed bonds show their three-dimensional attachments.

ch03/table-3.1-28.description: A table example shows ethanamide as CH₃–C(=O)–NH₂, with its carbonyl oxygen and NH₂ group highlighted in pink. It illustrates the structure of an amide functional group.

ch03/table-3.1-29.description: A generic acid chloride is drawn with a carbonyl carbon double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded to chlorine and an adjacent carbon group. Solid and dashed wedge bonds extend from the adjacent carbon.

ch03/table-3.1-32.description: The table entry shows the structure CH₃–C(=O)–O–C(=O)–CH₃, labeled “Ethanoic anhydride,” as an example of a carboxylic acid anhydride.

ch03/table-3.1u.description: A generic carboxylic acid group is drawn with a carbon double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded to OH, attached to a carbon shown with line, wedge, and dashed bonds. It illustrates the carboxylic acid entry in a table of common functional groups.

ch03/table-3.1-30.description: A structural formula shows CH₃ bonded to a carbonyl carbon that is also bonded to chlorine, with “Ethanoyl chloride” printed beneath it. It illustrates an acid chloride example in a table of common functional groups.

ch03/table-3.1-31.description: The table shows a generic carboxylic acid anhydride group: two carbonyl carbons linked by an oxygen atom, with each carbonyl bonded to a carbon group. The terminal carbons have solid and dashed wedge bonds indicating three-dimensional orientation.

ch03/p088.description: Two rows pair colored molecular models with skeletal drawings of eight functional groups: alkyl halide, alcohol, ether, phosphate, amine, thiol, sulfide, and disulfide. The drawings highlight the characteristic chlorine, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus, or sulfur atoms in pink.

ch03/prob-3-1c.description: The image shows the skeletal structure of capsaicin, with a methoxy- and hydroxy-substituted aromatic ring linked through an amide to a branched carbon chain containing a double bond.
labels_in_image: Capsaicin, the pungent substance in chili peppers:

ch03/p089.description: A molecular model and structural drawing of acetone show its carbonyl group, with partial negative charge on oxygen and partial positive charge on the carbonyl carbon. Below are generic structural examples labeled aldehyde, ketone, carboxylic acid, ester, thioester, amide, and acid chloride.

ch03/table-3.1-27.description: This table fragment shows an amide functional group: a carbonyl carbon bonded to a nitrogen, with additional bonds extending from the nitrogen and an adjacent carbon. The carbonyl and nitrogen are highlighted in pink.

ch03/prob-3-1a.description: The problem shows methionine as a condensed structure, CH₃SCH₂CH₂CH(NH₂)C(=O)OH, beneath the heading “Methionine, an amino acid.” It asks the reader to identify functional groups without marking them on the structure.

ch03/prob-3-1b.description: The drawing labeled “Ibuprofen, a pain reliever” shows a benzene ring with a branched carbon chain on one side and a carbon bearing CH₃ and CO₂H on the other. It is presented as a structure for a functional-group identification problem.

ch03/p090a.description: Displayed structures show methane, ethane, propane, and butane, with carbon atoms joined by single bonds and hydrogens filling the remaining bonds. The series ends with “... and so on,” illustrating progressively longer alkane chains.

ch03/p090b.description: The drawing shows a glycerol backbone attached through three ester groups to long chains of CH₂ units ending in CH₃. Captioned “A typical animal fat,” it illustrates the long carbon chains mentioned in the nearby text.

ch03/fig-3.3.description: The figure shows five representations of butane: two structures with every carbon and hydrogen shown, and three condensed formulas. They illustrate the same continuous four-carbon chain drawn in different ways, without specifying its geometry.

ch03/p091.description: Ball-and-stick models and condensed formulas show methane, ethane, propane, the two four-carbon alkanes, and the three five-carbon alkanes. The grouped models illustrate straight-chain and branched arrangements with the same molecular formula.

ch03/p095b.description: The left structure shows the general class of tertiary alcohols, R₃COH, with an OH group attached to a carbon bonded to three R groups. The right structure shows citric acid as a specific tertiary alcohol.
labels_in_image: General class of tertiary alcohols, R₃COH

ch03/p092.description: Three pairs of structures with the same molecular formula compare different carbon skeletons (2-methylpropane and butane), different functional groups (ethanol and dimethyl ether), and different positions of a functional group (isopropylamine and propylamine). The figure illustrates three ways constitutional isomers can differ.

ch03/p095a.description: Four generic diagrams show a central carbon bonded to one, two, three, or four R groups, with hydrogen atoms filling the remaining bonds. The captions classify these carbons as primary (1°), secondary (2°), tertiary (3°), and quaternary (4°), respectively.

ch03/we-3.1.description: The diagram combines two carbon pieces, one nitrogen piece, and seven hydrogens to show two isomeric structures: one with a C–C–N connection and the other with a C–N–C connection.

ch03/fig-3.4.description: Ball-and-stick models and condensed formulas compare propane with propyl and isopropyl, and butane and isobutane with four butyl groups. Pink zigzag marks show the attachment points of the alkyl groups.

ch03/p094.description: Four side-by-side ball-and-stick models and structural formulas show methane, a methyl group with an open bond marked by a pink squiggle, methyl alcohol (methanol), and methylamine. They illustrate the methyl group as part of the two molecules on the right.

ch03/prob-3-3.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a six-membered nitrogen-containing ring with one double bond, a methyl group attached to the nitrogen, and a methyl ester group attached to the ring. The colors distinguish oxygen (red), nitrogen (blue), carbon (black), and hydrogen (gray).

ch03/p096a.description: A condensed structure and an expanded hydrogen-bond drawing of the same branched five-carbon alkane use arrows and colors to distinguish primary hydrogens on CH₃ groups, secondary hydrogens on CH₂, and the tertiary hydrogen on CH.

ch03/p096b.description: A color-coded naming diagram breaks a compound name into Locant, Prefix, Parent, and Suffix, with arrows linking each part to the question it answers: where substituents and functional groups are, what the substituents are, how many carbons there are, and what the primary functional group is.
labels_in_image: Where are the substituents and functional groups?
What is the primary functional group?

ch03/prob-3-8a.description: The image shows the condensed structure CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₃, with a CH₃ group drawn above the second carbon of the horizontal chain.

ch03/prob-3-8c.description: A condensed structural formula shows a five-carbon chain with one methyl branch on a CH group and two methyl branches on a carbon farther along the chain. The drawing is presented for classifying its carbon and hydrogen atoms.

ch03/prob-3-8b.description: A branched alkane is drawn with a CH₃–CH–CH₃ unit above a CH₃–CH₂–CH–CH₂–CH₃ chain, joined by a vertical bond between their central CH groups. The problem asks readers to classify the carbon atoms, but the drawing does not mark the classifications.

ch03/p097c.description: Two drawings of the same branched alkane compare numbering its seven-carbon parent chain from opposite ends. The left numbering puts the first branch at carbon 3; the right puts it at carbon 4 and is marked “NOT.”

ch03/p097b.description: Two drawings of the same branched alkane highlight different six-carbon parent chains in magenta. The left chain has two substituents and is marked as the correct naming choice; the right has one substituent and is marked “NOT.”
labels_in_image: Named as a hexane with two substituents
as a hexane with one substituent

ch03/p098a.description: A numbered six-carbon chain is shown with a methyl group on C2 and both methyl and ethyl groups on C4, each color-coded to match the substituent list. The figure illustrates choosing hexane as the parent chain and locating its substituents.

ch03/p097e.description: A numbered nine-carbon chain is shown with an ethyl substituent on carbon 3 and methyl substituents on carbons 4 and 7. Colored labels match each branch to its position on the nonane parent chain.

ch03/p097a.description: Two branched alkane structures are shown, one labelled “Named as a substituted hexane” and the other “Named as a substituted heptane.” Their layouts illustrate that the longest carbon chain may turn corners rather than follow a straight horizontal line.

ch03/p098c.description: Two condensed structural formulas show branched alkanes with their parent chains numbered in pink and substituents highlighted in blue. The labels beneath them are 4-Ethyl-3-methylheptane and 4-Ethyl-2,4-dimethylhexane, illustrating how numbered substituents appear in alkane names.

ch03/p098b.description: Three condensed alkane structures show numbered parent chains and colored branches, with their full names beneath: 3-methylhexane, 3-ethyl-4,7-dimethylnonane, and 3-ethyl-2-methylhexane. They illustrate how branch positions and repeated substituents appear in alkane names.

ch03/p097d.description: Two drawings of the same branched alkane show opposite directions for numbering its nine-carbon parent chain. The left drawing is highlighted in pink; the right is marked “NOT,” illustrating the choice of numbering when branches are equally distant from the chain ends.

ch03/p098e.description: A numbered, ten-carbon chain is drawn with methyl branches at carbons 2 and 3 and a blue branched substituent at carbon 6. The color-coded name beneath it is 2,3-Dimethyl-6-(2-methylpropyl)decane, illustrating how the branched substituent is named in parentheses.

ch03/p098d.description: The drawing numbers a ten-carbon main chain from 1 to 10, with methyl branches at carbons 2 and 3 and a blue branched substituent at carbon 6. A separate bracketed drawing numbers that substituent from its attachment point and labels it “A 2-methylpropyl substituent.”

ch03/p099b.description: The figure compares seven branched alkyl groups, showing each condensed structure with a pink wavy bond at its attachment point. Brackets sort isopropyl as a 3-carbon group; sec-butyl, isobutyl, and tert-butyl as 4-carbon groups; and isopentyl, neopentyl, and tert-pentyl as 5-carbon groups, with alternate common names printed beneath some structures.

ch03/p099a.description: The figure shows a numbered, branched nine-carbon chain labeled 5-(1,2-Dimethylpropyl)-2-methylnonane, with its 1,2-dimethylpropyl branch highlighted in pink. A separate bracketed drawing shows the same group and its attachment bond.

ch03/p099c.description: A condensed structural formula shows a seven-carbon chain with a CH₃CHCH₃ branch attached to its central carbon. Beneath it, the same molecule is named “4-(1-Methylethyl)heptane” or “4-Isopropylheptane,” illustrating two names for the branch.

ch03/we-3.2a.description: A condensed alkane structure shows a seven-carbon horizontal chain with a CH₂CH₃ branch on the second carbon and a CH₃ branch on the second carbon from the right. The drawing is presented as a naming exercise.

ch03/we-3.2b.description: A condensed structural formula is numbered in pink along its eight-carbon chain, with methyl branches at carbons 2 and 6. The name printed below is 2,6-dimethyloctane, illustrating how the numbered parent chain determines the name.

ch03/prob-3-11a.description: A condensed alkane structure shows a five-carbon chain with a CH₃ group attached above one CH and another CH₃ group attached below the adjacent CH. It is presented as a structure to be named.

ch03/we-3.3b.description: A condensed structural formula shows a six-carbon chain with a methyl branch at carbon 2 and an isopropyl branch at carbon 3. The colored name beneath it reads “3-Isopropyl-2-methylhexane,” illustrating the completed structure for the worked naming example.

ch03/prob-3-11b.description: A condensed hydrocarbon structure shows a five-carbon chain with a methyl group attached to each of its second and fourth carbons.

ch03/we-3.3a.description: A six-carbon chain numbered 1–6 has an isopropyl group attached at carbon 3 and a methyl group at carbon 2. Arrows and colored labels show where each substituent is placed before hydrogens are added.

ch03/fig-3.5.description: A bar chart plots melting points (blue) and boiling points (magenta) against the number of carbon atoms from 1 to 14 for straight-chain alkanes. Both temperatures generally rise as the carbon count increases, with boiling points higher than melting points throughout.

ch03/fig-3.8.description: A graph of ethane’s potential energy versus bond rotation shows repeating peaks at eclipsed conformations and valleys at staggered conformations, with Newman projections beneath the curve. A vertical arrow marks the eclipsed conformations as 12 kJ/mol higher in energy.

ch03/prob-3-11c.description: A condensed structural formula shows a branched alkane, (CH₃)₃C–CH₂–CH₂–CH(CH₃)₂, with methyl groups attached at both ends of the central chain.

ch03/fig-3.7.description: Side-by-side ball-and-stick models and drawings show ethane as an oblique sawhorse representation and an end-on Newman projection. In the Newman projection, the front carbon and its three green hydrogens appear in front of the back carbon and its three red hydrogens.

ch03/fig-3.6.description: Structural drawings and ball-and-stick models show ethane before and after rotation around its carbon–carbon single bond. A “Rotate” arrow and curved arrows indicate that the hydrogen atoms change their relative positions.
