ch03/p101a.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a branched alkane, with dark carbon spheres linked to smaller pale hydrogen spheres. Several short carbon branches extend from the central chain.

ch03/fig-3.9.description: Newman projections and ball-and-stick models show staggered propane becoming eclipsed propane when the rear carbon rotates 60°. The eclipsed view marks one 6.0 kJ/mol CH₃–H interaction and two 4.0 kJ/mol H–H interactions; the caption says the staggered conformer is lower in energy by 14 kJ/mol.

ch03/p103.description: Newman projections and ball-and-stick models show ethane in staggered and eclipsed conformations, with an arrow indicating a 60° rotation of the rear carbon between them. Three brackets mark 4.0 kJ/mol contributions alongside the eclipsed projection.

ch03/p101b.description: A stepped reaction scheme shows CH₄ reacting with Cl₂ under light to form CH₃Cl and HCl, followed by successive reactions with Cl₂ that produce CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, and CCl₄, with HCl formed at each step. It illustrates successive chlorine substitution.

ch03/p105b.description: Ball-and-stick models and Newman projections show butane changing from an eclipsed conformation to a gauche conformation after a 60° rotation. The figure labels the conformations 16 kJ/mol and 3.8 kJ/mol, respectively, and marks steric strain between the gauche methyl groups.

molecules.name: Butane
molecules.role: depicted in eclipsed and gauche conformations

ch03/fig-3.11.description: A ball-and-stick model of decane appears above a matching structural drawing of its zigzag carbon chain. The figure shows a conformation in which substituents are staggered and the carbon–carbon bonds are arranged anti.

ch03/p105a.description: Ball-and-stick models and Newman projections show butane changing from an anti conformation (0 kJ/mol) to an eclipsed conformation (16 kJ/mol) after a 60° rotation. The eclipsed projection marks interactions of 6.0 and 4.0 kJ/mol.

ch03/fig-3.12.description: A black-and-white historical photograph shows a tall wooden oil derrick beside a low building, with two men in the foreground and several others near a fence. The caption uses the image to illustrate that gasoline is a finite resource.

ch03/fig-3.10.description: A magenta energy curve plots rotation about butane’s C2–C3 bond, with Newman projections beneath it showing anti, gauche, and eclipsed arrangements of the methyl groups. The anti positions at 180° are lowest in energy, while the methyl-on-methyl eclipse at 0° is highest.

ch03/p110.description: The figure compares the condensed structural formulas of straight-chain heptane and branched 2,2,4-trimethylpentane, labeled with octane numbers of 0 and 100, respectively.

ch03/prob-3-19a.description: A ball-and-stick model labeled “Phenylalanine” shows a six-membered carbon ring attached to a chain bearing a blue nitrogen atom and two red oxygen atoms. The figure presents a structure for identifying functional groups and deriving a molecular formula.

ch03/p105c.description: Ball-and-stick models and Newman projections show butane rotating 60° from a gauche conformation (3.8 kJ/mol) to an eclipsed conformation (19 kJ/mol). The eclipsed projection marks an 11 kJ/mol CH₃–CH₃ interaction and two 4.0 kJ/mol H–H interactions.

ch03/prob-3-18.description: A ball-and-stick model shows the indicated conformation of 2,3-dimethylbutane, with dark carbon spheres, light hydrogen spheres, and methyl branches extending above and below the central C2–C3 bond. The problem asks for a Newman projection along that bond and a total strain energy calculation.

ch03/prob-3-19b.description: A ball-and-stick model labeled “Lidocaine” shows an aromatic ring with two methyl groups connected through an amide group to a chain bearing a nitrogen with two ethyl groups. Oxygen is red and nitrogen atoms are blue.

ch03/we-3.4.description: Two Newman projections of 1-chloropropane compare a staggered conformation labeled “Most stable,” with Cl and CH₃ opposite, to an eclipsed conformation labeled “Least stable,” with Cl and CH₃ aligned.

ch03/prob-3-21.description: A ball-and-stick model shows the pictured conformation of 2-butanol, with its four-carbon chain, an OH group on the second carbon, and the hydrogens visible. The problem asks for a Newman projection looking along the C2–C3 bond.

ch03/prob-3-22c.description: The drawing shows a benzene ring bonded to an NH group, which is bonded to a carbonyl carbon bearing CH₃. It is one of the structures presented in a problem asking readers to identify functional groups.

ch03/prob-3-22b.description: A six-membered carbon ring has an oxygen double-bonded to one ring carbon and a carbon–carbon double bond on the adjacent side of the ring.

ch03/prob-3-22a.description: A six-membered ring with alternating double bonds has adjacent CH₂OH and NHCH₃ substituents.

ch03/prob-3-20b.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a branched alkane: a central carbon is bonded to two methyl groups and to another carbon that connects to two two-carbon branches. Dark spheres represent carbon atoms and pale spheres represent hydrogen atoms.

ch03/prob-3-22d.description: A condensed structural formula shows CH₃–CH(NH₂)–C(=O)OH, with the amino group attached to the middle carbon and the carboxylic acid group at the end. It is presented as a structure for identifying functional groups.

ch03/prob-3-22e.description: The drawing shows two fused six-membered rings: one contains a ketone and a carbon–carbon double bond. Two methyl branches extend upward, and an alkene-containing branch extends from the right-hand ring.

ch03/prob-3-20d.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a branched carbon chain, with dark spheres for carbon atoms and pale spheres for attached hydrogens. Several branches extend from the central chain.

ch03/prob-3-38b.description: The drawing shows a central carbon bonded to an ethyl group on the left and three CH₃ groups above, below, and to the right. It is one of the structures in an IUPAC naming problem.

ch03/prob-3-20a.description: A ball-and-stick drawing shows a branched alkane with dark carbon atoms and light hydrogen atoms. Two short branches extend from a central carbon, and another branch extends from a carbon farther along the chain.

ch03/prob-3-29a.description: Three condensed structural formulas are shown side by side, each with a four-carbon chain and attached Br and CH₃ groups. The substituents are placed above or below the chain in different arrangements for comparison.

ch03/prob-3-38a.description: The drawing shows a five-carbon chain, CH₃–CH–CH₂–CH₂–CH₃, with a CH₃ branch attached to the second carbon.

ch03/prob-3-20c.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a branched alkane, with dark carbon spheres and light hydrogen spheres. Its carbon chain has methyl branches near both ends.

ch03/prob-3-38c.description: A condensed structural formula shows a six-carbon chain with one methyl branch on the second carbon and two methyl branches on the third carbon. It is one of the structures presented for an IUPAC naming problem.

ch03/prob-3-38d.description: A condensed alkane structure shows a seven-carbon chain with an ethyl branch on the third carbon from the left and a methyl branch on the sixth. The figure is presented as a compound to name.

ch03/prob-3-22f.description: The skeletal structure shows a branched carbon chain with a carbon–carbon triple bond leading to a carbonyl chloride group, –C(=O)Cl.

ch03/prob-3-29b.description: Three benzene-ring drawings each have two hydroxyl groups. In the first two, the groups are attached to neighboring ring carbons; in the third, one ring carbon lies between them.

ch03/prob-3-48c.description: A six-membered carbon ring is drawn with an OH group attached to one carbon, representing cyclohexanol.

ch03/prob-3-48a.description: A condensed structural formula shows a four-carbon chain with a methyl branch on the second carbon and bromine at the opposite end. It is presented as a compound for which an isomer with the same functional groups should be drawn.

ch03/prob-3-48d.description: A benzene ring is bonded to a CH₂CO₂H group, showing the structure of phenylacetic acid.

ch03/prob-3-54.description: Two labeled drawings compare nonplanar cyclohexane, shown as a puckered ring, with planar cyclohexane, shown as a flat ring in brackets. Both drawings include the hydrogen atoms attached to the ring.

ch03/prob-3-48b.description: A five-membered carbon ring bears an OCH₃ group attached to one ring carbon, depicting methoxycyclopentane as a structure in an isomer-drawing problem.

ch03/prob-3-38e.description: A condensed structural formula shows a branched hydrocarbon chain with a methyl group attached to a CH unit and both a methyl and an ethyl group attached to a later carbon. The drawing shows only single bonds.

ch03/prob-3-29c.description: Three condensed structural formulas of branched alcohols are shown side by side. The left structure has a CH2OH branch on its carbon chain; the middle has HOCH2 at one end with methyl and ethyl branches, and the right has CH2OH at one end with two methyl branches.

ch03/prob-3-551.description: A cyclohexane ring is drawn with a CH₃ group and an H attached to each of two adjacent carbons. The structure is labeled “1,2-Dimethylcyclohexane.”

ch03/prob-3-38f.description: A condensed structural formula shows two adjacent carbon atoms, each bonded to two methyl groups; one end bears another methyl group and the other extends into a three-carbon chain. It illustrates a branched alkane structure presented in a naming problem.

ch04/p118b.description: A skeletal structure labeled Prostaglandin E₁ shows a pink-highlighted five-membered ring bearing a carbonyl and hydroxyl group, with two long side chains extending from it. Solid and dashed wedges indicate the three-dimensional arrangement of some bonds.

ch04/p118d.description: Four cycloalkanes are shown as ball-and-stick models above their skeletal polygon drawings: a triangle, square, pentagon, and hexagon. The pairs illustrate how carbon rings are represented by polygons.

ch03/prob-3-53.description: Side-by-side structural drawings of simvastatin (Zocor) and pravastatin (Pravachol) show their similar fused-ring frameworks and differing attached groups. The figure invites comparison of the two structures without showing a reaction.

ch04/p118c.description: The figure shows the skeletal structure of cortisone, with three fused six-membered rings and one five-membered ring highlighted in pink. It also shows attached oxygen-containing groups and stereochemical wedge and dashed bonds.

ch04/fig-4.1.description: A dark brown musk deer stands on snow against a gray background, facing the camera. The caption connects the male deer’s musk gland to a substance containing cycloalkanes, but no chemical structures are shown.

ch04/p119a.description: Two drawings of a cyclohexane ring with methyl groups at the same positions compare opposite numbering directions. The image favors the lower locants, 1,3-dimethylcyclohexane, over 1,5-dimethylcyclohexane, with “NOT” between them.

ch04/p118a.description: A skeletal structure labeled “Chrysanthemic acid” shows a pink cyclopropane ring bearing methyl groups, an alkenyl side chain, and a CO₂H group. Solid wedge and dashed bonds indicate its three-dimensional arrangement.

ch04/p119c.description: Two numbered cyclopentane rings with adjacent ethyl and methyl groups compare naming choices: the left is labeled “1-Ethyl-2-methylcyclopentane,” while the reversed numbering on the right is marked “NOT” and labeled “2-Ethyl-1-methylcyclopentane.”

ch04/p118e.description: Two structures compare a cyclopentane ring bearing a methyl group, labeled Methylcyclopentane, with a cyclopropane ring attached to a four-carbon chain, labeled 1-Cyclopropylbutane. Braces mark the latter’s ring as “3 carbons” and its chain as “4 carbons,” illustrating which part supplies the parent name.

ch04/p119d.description: Two drawings show a cyclobutane ring with CH₃ and Br on adjacent carbons. The left numbering and name, “1-Bromo-2-methylcyclobutane,” are contrasted with the right numbering and name, “2-Bromo-1-methylcyclobutane,” separated by “NOT.”

ch04/prob-4-1a.description: A six-membered ring is drawn as a hexagon, with a CH₃ group attached to the top vertex and another to the opposite, bottom vertex.

ch04/p119b.description: Three drawings of the same ethyl- and dimethyl-substituted cycloheptane show different ring-numbering choices. The left drawing labels 2-Ethyl-1,4-dimethylcycloheptane with “Lower” arrows, while a “NOT” bracket groups two alternatives on the right marked “Higher.”

ch04/prob-4-1c.description: A four-membered ring is attached to a branching carbon that leads to two two-carbon chains. The figure presents an unlabeled skeletal structure for a cycloalkane naming problem.

ch04/prob-4-1e.description: A six-membered carbon ring has a CH₃ group and a CH(CH₃)₂ group attached to adjacent ring carbons. The drawing is part of a problem asking for IUPAC names.

ch04/prob-4-1b.description: A five-membered carbon ring has a CH₂CH₂CH₃ group attached at the top and a CH₃ group attached at the lower right. The drawing is part of a cycloalkane-naming problem.

ch04/fig-4.3.description: Side-by-side structural drawings and ball-and-stick models show cis-1,2-dimethylcyclopropane with both methyl groups on the same face of the ring and trans-1,2-dimethylcyclopropane with them on opposite faces. The comparison illustrates two distinct isomers that do not interconvert.

ch04/prob-4-1d.description: A ten-membered carbon ring is drawn with a CH₂CH₃ group attached near the upper right and a Br attached near the lower right. The two substituents are separated by three ring bonds along the shorter path.

ch04/fig-4.2.description: Panel (a) shows ethane as a structural drawing and ball-and-stick models, with a curved arrow and “Rotate” arrow showing rotation around its carbon–carbon bond. Panel (b) shows cyclopropane as a three-carbon ring and a ball-and-stick model, illustrating that its ring bonds cannot rotate without opening the ring.

ch04/p120.description: Three skeletal structures show a substituted cyclohexane, cyclobutane, and cyclopentane. Colored substituents and ring numbers accompany printed names illustrating how cycloalkanes are named.

ch04/p121b.description: Two numbered ring drawings show cis-1,3-dimethylcyclobutane, with both methyl groups on the same side, and trans-1-bromo-3-ethylcyclopentane, with bromine and ethyl on opposite sides. Colored substituent labels and hydrogen labels mark their positions around the rings.

ch04/prob-4-1f.description: A seven-membered carbon ring has Br at the top, CH₃ on the lower right, and C(CH₃)₃ on the adjacent bottom-right carbon. The drawing is an unlabeled cycloalkane structure in a naming problem.

ch04/p121a.description: The upper pair shows two four-carbon structures with different atom connections, labeled constitutional isomers. The lower pair shows two 1,2-dimethylcyclopropane structures with the same connections but different three-dimensional arrangements, labeled stereoisomers.
labels_in_image: Stereoisomers (same connections but different three-dimensional geometry)

ch04/p123.description: Four polygon drawings labeled cyclopropane, cyclobutane, cyclopentane, and cyclohexane show interior angles of 60°, 90°, 108°, and 120°, with pink markings indicating their deviations from the 109° tetrahedral angle: 49°, 19°, 1°, and 11°, respectively.

ch04/we-4.1.description: Two ring structures are shown for a naming exercise: (a) a cyclopentane with methyl groups on two ring carbons, one on a solid wedge and the other on a dashed bond; (b) a cyclohexane with chlorine atoms on adjacent carbons, both on dashed bonds. Hydrogen atoms are also shown on the corresponding solid or dashed bonds.

ch04/prob-4-4a.description: A cyclohexane ring has Cl and CH₃ substituents at opposite ring positions. Cl and the H at the methyl-bearing carbon are shown on solid wedges, while CH₃ and the H at the chlorine-bearing carbon are on dashed bonds.

ch04/prob-4-6.description: The drawing shows prostaglandin F₂α as a cyclopentane ring bearing two hydroxyl groups and two carbon chains, one ending in CO₂H and the other in CH₃ with an additional hydroxyl group. Solid wedges and dashed bonds indicate the three-dimensional orientations of the ring substituents.

ch04/prob-4-4b.description: A seven-membered ring has methyl and ethyl substituents on carbons separated by one ring carbon. Both substituents are drawn on solid wedges, with the corresponding hydrogens on dashed bonds.

ch04/fig-4.5.description: Part (a) shows space-filling and ball-and-stick models of cyclopropane. Part (b) shows a Newman projection along a C–C bond, with neighboring C–H bonds marked as eclipsed to illustrate torsional strain.

ch04/fig-4.4.description: A bar chart plots cycloalkane strain energy against ring size from 3 to 14, with energy scales in kJ/mol and kcal/mol. Three- and four-membered rings have the highest bars, while ring sizes 6 and 14 are marked at zero.

ch04/prob-4-3.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a five-carbon ring with an ethyl group on one ring carbon and two methyl groups on another. Dark spheres represent carbon atoms, and light spheres represent hydrogen atoms.

ch04/fig-4.7.description: Three views show cyclopentane as a ball-and-stick model, a numbered puckered ring with carbon 5 bent out of the plane, and a Newman projection looking along the C1–C2 bond. The projection shows neighboring C–H bonds nearly staggered.

ch04/fig-4.6.description: Three views of cyclobutane show a ball-and-stick model, a slightly bent four-carbon ring with a marked viewing direction, and a Newman projection along a C–C bond. The projection shows neighboring C–H bonds that are “not quite eclipsed.”

ch04/p124.description: The left diagram shows orbital overlap along typical alkane C–C bonds at a labeled 109° angle; the right shows bent C–C bond overlap around a three-carbon cyclopropane ring. Dashed lines mark the bond directions, highlighting the contrast between the two bonding arrangements.

ch04/fig-4.8.description: Three views of cyclohexane in its chair conformation show a ball-and-stick model, a numbered bond drawing with colored hydrogen labels and observer sightlines, and an end-on projection. The figure illustrates the chair's near-tetrahedral C–C–C angles and staggered neighboring C–H bonds.

ch04/p126b.description: A chair-shaped cyclohexane ring is drawn with arrows identifying an upper bond as “in back” and the heavily shaded lower bond as “in front.” The shading shows which bond is nearer the viewer.

ch04/p125.description: A stereochemical line drawing and a ball-and-stick model show menthol’s six-membered ring with hydroxyl, methyl, and branched carbon substituents. Wedge and dashed bonds in the drawing indicate their three-dimensional orientations.

ch04/prob-4-7a.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a five-carbon ring with methyl groups attached to adjacent ring carbons; the attached hydrogen atoms are also visible. The drawing is presented as a cis–trans naming problem.

ch04/p126a.description: A step-by-step drawing shows black dots connected by pink and black lines to form the chair-shaped six-membered ring of cyclohexane. Downward arrows lead to the completed outline, where two slanted bonds are highlighted in blue.

ch04/p127b.description: Side-by-side ball-and-stick models and structural drawings show cyclohexane and glucose in chair conformations. The glucose drawing highlights its oxygen atom and hydroxyl groups in pink, illustrating a carbohydrate's chair-shaped structure.

ch04/p127a.description: A twist-boat cyclohexane is shown as a hydrogen-labeled bond drawing alongside a ball-and-stick model. A dashed arc marks steric strain between two hydrogens, while colored hydrogen pairs indicate torsional strain; the model is labeled “23 kJ/mol strain.”

ch04/fig-4.11.description: Chair cyclohexane drawings show how to add six pink axial bonds, which alternate up and down, and six blue equatorial bonds, arranged in three parallel pairs. A completed chair combines both sets of bonds.

ch04/prob-4-11b.description: A ball-and-stick model shows one conformation of cis-1,3-dimethylcyclobutane, with a four-carbon ring and methyl groups attached at opposite ring positions. The problem compares two conformations of this molecule, though only one model is visible in this crop.

ch04/fig-4.9.description: A ball-and-stick model and a line drawing show chair cyclohexane with six axial hydrogens oriented parallel to the ring axis and six equatorial hydrogens arranged around the ring equator. Pink marks the axial positions and blue marks the equatorial positions.

ch04/fig-4.12.description: Two chair drawings and matching ball-and-stick models show a cyclohexane ring-flip, with arrows indicating that one carbon moves up and another moves down. Pink and blue bonds illustrate how axial and equatorial positions interchange.

ch04/prob-4-11a.description: A ball-and-stick model shows one conformation of cis-1,3-dimethylcyclobutane, with two methyl groups attached to opposite carbons of a puckered four-membered ring. The model shows how the carbon and hydrogen atoms are arranged in space.

ch04/fig-4.10.description: Two models show chair cyclohexane viewed down the ring axis: a space-filling view on the left and a ball-and-stick view on the right. The left model labels the alternating red and blue positions as axial and equatorial, respectively.

ch04/p129.description: Two ball-and-stick models and matching chair drawings show a ring flip between axial bromocyclohexane, with Br pointing upward, and equatorial bromocyclohexane, with Br pointing outward from the ring.

ch04/fig-4.13.description: A graph plots the equilibrium percentages of two isomers against their energy difference, with energy scales in kJ/mol and kcal/mol. Both start at 50%; as the energy difference grows, the more stable isomer approaches 100% and the less stable one approaches 0%.

ch04/we-4.2.description: A cyclohexane chair has two methyl groups attached to the same carbon: one points upward in an axial position, while the other extends outward in an equatorial position. Arrows label the axial and equatorial methyl groups.

ch04/prob-4-14.description: A ball-and-stick cyclohexane chair on the left has three positions marked red, blue, and green. A double-headed arrow labeled “Ring-flip” points to a second chair drawing with empty circles where the colored positions can be marked after the flip.

molecules.name: cyclohexane
molecules.role: structure shown in two chair conformations

ch04/fig-4.14.description: Chair drawings, ball-and-stick models, and space-filling models compare methylcyclohexane with an axial CH₃ group on the left and an equatorial CH₃ group on the right, linked by a ring-flip arrow. Pink dashed arrows highlight steric interference in the axial form; the caption states that the equatorial form is more stable by 7.6 kJ/mol.

ch04/fig-4.16.description: Two chair drawings and corresponding ball-and-stick models show the ring-flip conformations of cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane. Each has one axial and one equatorial methyl group, with the same listed strain total of 11.4 kJ/mol.
labels_in_image: Two CH₃ ↔ H diaxial interactions (7.6 kJ/mol)

ch04/fig-4.15.description: Newman projections and ball-and-stick models compare gauche butane with axial methylcyclohexane, highlighting the close approach of methyl groups to nearby atoms. The figure labels gauche butane as having 3.8 kJ/mol of strain and axial methylcyclohexane as having 7.6 kJ/mol, illustrating the two 1,3-diaxial interactions of the axial methyl group.

ch04/fig-4.17.description: The figure compares two chair conformations of trans-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane, with numbered structural drawings and matching molecular models connected by a ring-flip arrow. The top, diequatorial form shows one gauche interaction (3.8 kJ/mol), while the bottom, diaxial form shows four CH₃–H diaxial interactions (15.2 kJ/mol).
labels_in_image: Four CH₃ ↔ H diaxial interactions (15.2 kJ/mol)

ch04/table-4.1a.description: A table entry shows a cyclohexane chair with axial H and generic substituent Y connected by a double-headed arrow, illustrating a 1,3-diaxial interaction. The listed strain is 0.63 kJ/mol (0.15 kcal/mol).

ch04/p134.description: Side-by-side ball-and-stick models and chair structures labeled Glucose and Mannose show their ring substituents. A pink OH and arrows highlight the hydroxyl group whose orientation differs between the two structures.

ch04/prob-4-7b.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a three-carbon ring with a red-brown bromine atom attached to one ring carbon and a two-carbon chain attached to another. The remaining visible atoms are hydrogens.

ch04/p135.description: A structural drawing of decalin shows two six-membered rings sharing a central bond, with their carbon positions numbered 1–10 in pink. Hydrogen atoms are shown at the top and bottom of the shared bond, illustrating the two fused cyclohexane rings.

ch04/table-4.1b.description: A table headed “Steric Strain in Monosubstituted Cyclohexanes” includes a cyclohexane chair with axial H and generic substituent Y connected by a double-headed arrow. It illustrates the 1,3-diaxial interaction, with strain columns labeled in kJ/mol and kcal/mol.

ch04/p137.description: A line-bond structure labeled Camphor appears beside a ball-and-stick model of the same molecule. The drawings show its bridged ring framework, three methyl groups, and a carbonyl oxygen.

ch04/p136a.description: Three depictions of testosterone show its fused-ring structure as a flat drawing, a perspective conformation, and a ball-and-stick model. The views illustrate the three-dimensional shape of a steroid ring system.

ch04/p136b.description: A labeled skeletal drawing and a ball-and-stick model show norbornane (bicyclo[2.2.1]heptane). Colored highlights and arrows identify its bridgehead carbons, a 1-carbon bridge, and a 2-carbon bridge.

ch04/fig-4.18.description: Two rows show cis-Decalin and trans-Decalin, each as a fused-ring drawing, a chair conformation, and a ball-and-stick model. The highlighted bridgehead hydrogens are on the same face in cis-Decalin and opposite faces in trans-Decalin.

ch04/fig-4.19.description: A person sits at a computer displaying a colorful three-dimensional ball-and-stick molecular model. The photo illustrates the use of computer programs to represent molecular geometry.

ch04/prob-4-19.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a cyclohexane chair with two methyl substituents and a green chlorine substituent. The problem asks the reader to classify the substituents as axial or equatorial and assess the chair’s relative stability.

ch04/prob-4-21.description: The figure shows two drawings of estrone: a flat ring structure with wedge-and-dash bonds and a three-dimensional conformation. Two ring-fusion bonds are highlighted in pink in the three-dimensional drawing for the cis-or-trans question.

ch04/prob-4-26.description: Two side-by-side ball-and-stick molecular models are labeled α-Glucose and β-Glucose. They show similar six-membered rings with differently oriented groups on one ring carbon.

ch04/prob-4-24.description: A ball-and-stick cyclohexane chair bears green, red, and blue substituents. A double arrow labeled “Ring-flip” points to an alternate chair drawing with empty circles for the positions to be filled in.

ch04/prob-4-28b.description: A five-membered carbon ring has methyl groups attached at the two upper side vertices on solid wedges; hydrogens at those vertices are shown on dashed bonds. The drawing illustrates the spatial arrangement of the substituents without naming the compound.

ch04/prob-4-22a.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a five-membered carbon ring with a one-carbon branch and a two-carbon branch separated by one ring carbon. Dark spheres represent carbon atoms and pale spheres represent hydrogen atoms.

ch04/prob-4-28a.description: A seven-membered ring has a CH₃ group attached at one vertex.

ch04/fig-4.20.description: A labeled skeletal structure of Tamiflu (oseltamivir) appears beside a color-coded ball-and-stick model showing its calculated minimum-energy conformation. The two views illustrate how the drawn chemical structure corresponds to a three-dimensional arrangement.

ch04/we-4.3.description: Two chair conformations of a cyclohexane bearing tert-butyl and chlorine substituents are connected by a ring-flip arrow. The left shows equatorial tert-butyl and axial chlorine with 2.0 kJ/mol steric strain; the right shows axial tert-butyl and equatorial chlorine with 22.8 kJ/mol steric strain, with dashed arrows marking interactions.

ch04/prob-4-28d.description: A four-membered ring has two substituents on adjacent carbons: a solid wedge leads to a branched carbon bearing two terminal bonds, and a dashed bond leads to CH₃. The wedge and dash show the substituents on opposite sides of the ring.

ch04/prob-4-28c.description: A six-membered carbon ring has CH₃ and H groups on each of two adjacent carbons. Dashed bonds place the upper CH₃ and lower H behind the ring, while solid wedges place the upper H and lower CH₃ in front.

ch04/prob-4-44.description: A flat six-membered ring drawing of galactose shows an oxygen atom in the ring, a HOCH₂ substituent, and four OH groups attached with solid or dashed wedge bonds. The OH group at the lower left is highlighted in pink.

ch04/prob-4-28e.description: A cyclohexane ring has one methyl group attached at the left vertex and two methyl groups attached at the opposite vertex. The drawing shows connectivity only, without stereochemical wedges or dashes.

ch04/prob-4-45.description: A skeletal cyclohexane structure labeled Menthol shows a CH₃ group and an HO group on dashed bonds and a CH(CH₃)₂ group on a solid wedge. The wedge and dashes indicate how the three substituents are oriented relative to the ring.

ch04/prob-4-34.description: The figure shows a skeletal drawing of hydrocortisone with four fused rings, two methyl groups, hydroxyl groups, carbonyl groups, and a CH₂OH-containing side chain. Selected hydrogens and bonds are drawn to show the three-dimensional arrangement of the rings and substituents.

ch04/prob-4-32.description: A ring structure labeled Glucose shows a CH₂OH group and four OH groups colored pink, green, blue, and black. The OH groups are drawn above or below the ring for a problem asking about their cis–trans relationships.

ch04/prob-4-22b.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a cyclohexane ring with two methyl groups attached to one ring carbon and a third methyl group on the opposite ring carbon, illustrating a cycloalkane naming problem.

ch04/prob-4-52.description: Two skeletal structures are shown side by side: trans-decalin has two fused six-membered rings with ring-junction hydrogens on opposite faces, while cis-bicyclo[4.1.0]heptane has fused six- and three-membered rings with its ring-junction hydrogens on the same face.

ch04/prob-4-55.description: A flat hexagonal ring labeled myo-Inositol has an OH group at each carbon; solid and dashed wedge bonds show which hydroxyl groups project toward or away from the viewer. The problem asks for its most stable chair conformation.

ch04/prob-4-59.description: A line drawing labeled “Amantadine” shows a bridged cage-like carbon framework with an NH₂ group attached at the right. The accompanying problem asks for a three-dimensional representation showing the chair cyclohexane rings.

ch04/prob-4-54.description: Three labeled skeletal structures—simvastatin (Zocor), pravastatin (Pravachol), and atorvastatin (Lipitor)—are shown side by side, with stereochemical wedges and dashes and selected bonds highlighted in pink. The drawing invites comparison of the indicated bonds without showing an answer to the cis-or-trans question.

ch04/prob-4-571.description: A skeletal drawing labeled “1-Norbornene” shows a bridged bicyclic framework with a double bond extending from a bridgehead carbon. The figure illustrates the strained bridgehead double bond referenced in the problem.

ch04/prob-4-30.description: Two five-membered rings are shown side by side, each bearing two chlorine substituents at 1,3 positions. The rings are drawn from different orientations, with their front edges thickened.

ch04/prob-4-62.description: A reaction diagram shows 2-tert-butylcyclohexanol, drawn as a cyclohexane ring bearing OH and tert-butyl groups on adjacent carbons, converting with CrO₃ to 2-tert-butylcyclohexanone. The ring's OH-bearing carbon becomes a carbonyl, while the tert-butyl group remains attached.

ch05/fig-5.1.description: A mountain range and forested slopes are reflected in the still surface of a lake. The reflection illustrates the idea of mirror-image counterparts.

ch05/p148.description: An upright left hand is shown beside its mirror image, which appears as a right hand. The illustration uses the reflection to show handedness.

ch04/prob-4-25.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a cyclohexane chair with three differently colored substituents: red on the left, green at the upper right, and blue at the lower right. Dark spheres represent the ring atoms, with pale spheres attached around them.

ch05/fig-5.3.description: Two pairs of wedge-and-dash drawings show attempts to superimpose mirror-image forms of lactic acid. Arrows mark the substituents that remain mismatched: CH3 and CO2H in (a), and H and OH in (b).

ch05/fig-5.4.description: Two panels compare a coffee mug and an upright hand against blue-tinted planes, each with a blue line running through the object. The mug’s halves mirror one another across the plane, while the hand’s halves do not, illustrating the presence or absence of a symmetry plane.

ch04/prob-4-58.description: A series of fused cyclohexane chair outlines has two upward CH₃ groups and several explicitly labeled hydrogens. Pink dots and numbers mark positions 3, 7, and 11, which the problem text specifies for substituents.

ch04/prob-4-23.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a cyclohexane chair with a methyl group extending upward from one ring carbon and a green chlorine atom extending to the right from another. Dark gray spheres represent carbon, and pale spheres represent hydrogen.

ch04/prob-4-61.description: A wedge-and-dash drawing shows a tert-butyl-substituted cyclohexanediol reacting with acetone under acid catalysis to form a ring-bridged product labeled “An acetal,” plus water. The two hydroxyl groups become the oxygen atoms of the new acetal ring.

ch05/fig-5.2.description: Three rows show generic tetrahedral carbon structures, their colored ball-and-stick models, and reflections in a mirror. The CH₃X and CH₂XY arrangements match their mirror images, while the CHXYZ arrangement does not.

ch05/p149.description: A lactic acid structure is paired with a generic CHXYZ tetrahedral carbon. Below, wedge-and-dash structures and colored molecular models show (+)-lactic acid and (−)-lactic acid on opposite sides of a mirror, illustrating their nonsuperimposable mirror-image relationship.

ch05/fig-5.5.description: Side-by-side molecular models and structural formulas compare propanoic acid, labeled achiral with a symmetry plane, and lactic acid, labeled chiral with a dashed line marked “Not a symmetry plane.” The figure illustrates how a symmetry plane distinguishes the two molecules.

ch05/p152c.description: A skeletal structure of dextromethorphan is shown with a methoxy-substituted aromatic ring, fused rings, and an N-methyl group. Solid and dashed bonds indicate its three-dimensional arrangement.

ch05/p152b.description: A skeletal structure of menthol shows a six-membered ring with hydroxyl, methyl, and branched alkyl substituents; solid wedges and dashed bonds indicate their three-dimensional orientations. The caption reads “Menthol (flavoring agent).”

ch05/p152a.description: A six-membered ring containing an N–H group has a CH₂CH₂CH₃ substituent on the carbon next to the nitrogen. The structure is labeled “Coniine (poison hemlock).”

ch05/p151a.description: Ball-and-stick models and numbered ring drawings compare methylcyclohexane, labeled achiral with a dashed symmetry plane, and 2-methylcyclohexanone, labeled chiral with a starred carbon. The comparison illustrates how the symmetry plane distinguishes the two structures.

ch05/p151b.description: Two skeletal structures labeled Carvone (spearmint oil) and Nootkatone (grapefruit oil) are shown side by side. Pink asterisks mark one chirality center in carvone and three in nootkatone.

ch05/we-5.1.description: A structural formula shows a central carbon bonded to OH, H, CH₃, and CH₃CH₂, with a pink asterisk marking that carbon. The figure labels the molecule “2-Butanol (chiral).”

ch05/p150.description: The structure of 5-bromodecane highlights carbon 5, bonded to H, Br, a blue butyl chain, and a pink pentyl chain. A color-coded list of these four substituents illustrates why the marked carbon is chiral.

ch05/prob-5-3.description: A condensed structure shows CH₃–CH–CO₂H with NH₂ bonded above the central CH, labeled “Alanine.” The drawing uses ordinary lines, with no stereochemical wedges or dashes.

ch05/prob-5-4a.description: A ball-and-stick model of threose shows a four-carbon chain with red oxygen atoms in hydroxyl groups and at one end of the chain. The drawing is presented as a chirality-center identification problem; gray spheres represent hydrogen and black spheres carbon.

ch05/fig-5.6.description: A schematic polarimeter shows light from a bulb passing through a polarizer, a sample tube containing organic molecules, and an analyzer before reaching an observer. Red arrows and an angle α illustrate the rotation of the light’s plane of polarization through the sample.

ch05/we-5.2.description: A skeletal structure labeled “Cocaine” shows a bridged nitrogen-containing ring with methyl, methyl ester, and benzoyloxy groups. It accompanies a worked example about the observed optical rotation of a cocaine solution.

ch05/prob-5-4b.description: A ball-and-stick model labeled “Enflurane (an anesthetic)” shows three black carbon atoms, one red oxygen atom, gray hydrogens, a green chlorine atom, and yellow-green fluorine atoms. The drawing accompanies a problem asking readers to identify chirality centers.

ch04/prob-4-60.description: Two methyl-substituted cyclopentane drawings appear side by side. Both show a methyl group extending upward from the front ring carbon; the second methyl group extends downward from the right side in one drawing and the left side in the other.

ch05/fig-5.7.description: Two blue crystal drawings are mirror images, with slanted faces on opposite sides and dashed lines showing hidden edges. Beside them is a structural formula labeled sodium ammonium tartrate; the caption states that one crystal is dextrorotatory.

ch05/p155a.description: A horizontal ranking chart places Br > Cl > S > P > O > N > C > ²H > ¹H from higher to lower rank, with atomic numbers shown above each symbol. It illustrates the priority order for these atoms and hydrogen isotopes.

ch05/fig-5.8.description: Two mirror-image generic tetrahedral centers have groups numbered 1–4; after reorientation with group 4 pointing away, pink arrows trace 1 → 2 → 3 clockwise for R and counterclockwise for S. Steering wheels on either side illustrate the corresponding right and left turns.

ch05/p155b.description: Four bracketed pairs of substituent structures attached by wavy bonds compare priority: methyl versus ethyl, hydroxyl versus methoxy, a carbon bearing two methyl groups versus one bearing a methyl and two hydrogens, and a carbon bearing methyl and amino groups versus one bearing chlorine and two hydrogens. Each structure is marked “Higher” or “Lower” to illustrate how attached atoms determine ranking.

ch05/fig-5.10.description: Two rows show wedge-and-dash structures, numbered substituent priorities with curved arrows, and ball-and-stick models for (S)-glyceraldehyde and (S)-alanine. Both are labeled S, while their displayed optical rotations have opposite signs: −8.7 and +8.5, respectively.

ch05/we-5.3a.description: Two drawings, (a) and (b), show a tetrahedral carbon bonded to four groups marked by priority numbers 1–4. Solid wedges and dashed bonds distinguish groups projecting toward and away from the viewer for an R/S configuration exercise.

ch05/fig-5.9.description: Two mirror-image models and wedge–dash drawings of lactic acid flank a vertical mirror. Numbered OH, CO₂H, and CH₃ groups and curved arrows show a clockwise sequence for the labeled R configuration of (−)-lactic acid and a counterclockwise sequence for the S configuration of (+)-lactic acid.

ch05/p156b.description: Two pairs of drawings show carbon–carbon double and triple bonds beside equivalent expanded representations with color-coded carbon and hydrogen labels. Arrows identify each carbon and list the atoms counted as bonded to it, illustrating how multiple bonds are treated when ranking attached groups.
labels_in_image: This carbon is bonded to H, C, C.
This carbon is bonded to H, H, C, C.
This carbon is bonded to C, C, C.
This carbon is bonded to H, C, C, C.

ch05/we-5.3b.description: A generic tetrahedral carbon with substituents ranked 1–4 is shown from an observer’s viewpoint, then redrawn with group 4 pointing away. Pink arrows trace the clockwise order 1 → 2 → 3, labelled R configuration.

ch05/we-5.3c.description: Two views of a tetrahedral center C show substituents numbered 1–4, with an observer indicated beside the first view. In the second view, pink arrows trace 1 → 2 → 3, and the figure labels the arrangement “R configuration.”

ch05/p156a.description: A carbonyl group is shown alongside an equivalent expanded drawing used to count atoms across the double bond. Arrows indicate that the carbon is counted as bonded to H, O, and O, while the oxygen is counted as bonded to C and C.
labels_in_image: This carbon is bonded to H, O, O.
This oxygen is bonded to C, C.

ch05/prob-5-9a.description: A central tetrahedral C is bonded to four numbered groups: 1 above and 3 to the right by plain bonds, 2 at the lower left by a solid wedge, and 4 to the left by a dashed wedge. The drawing shows their spatial arrangement for assigning configuration.

ch05/we-5.4.description: Two wedge-and-dash drawings of the same tetrahedral carbon are connected by a rotation arrow. The first marks chlorine, ethyl, and methyl as priorities 1, 2, and 3; the rotated drawing is labeled (R)-2-Chlorobutane.

ch05/prob-5-9b.description: A central tetrahedral carbon is bonded to four numbered groups: 3 above and 4 to the right on plain bonds, 2 to the left on a dashed bond, and 1 at the lower left on a solid wedge. The numbered groups provide the ranking for a stereochemistry problem.

ch05/prob-5-9c.description: A central carbon is bonded to four numbered groups: 4 above and 2 to the right by plain bonds, 1 to the left by a dashed bond, and 3 below-left by a solid wedge. The drawing shows a three-dimensional arrangement for a configuration exercise.

ch05/prob-5-12.description: A ball-and-stick model of methionine shows a central carbon bonded to a blue nitrogen, a hydrogen, a carboxyl group, and a carbon chain leading to a yellow sulfur. The problem asks for the configuration of that chirality center; no configuration is marked in the image.

ch05/prob-5-10b.description: A tetrahedral carbon is bonded to OH, CH₃, CO₂H, and H, with dashed and solid wedge bonds showing their spatial arrangement. The drawing is presented as a stereochemistry problem asking for the center’s configuration.

ch05/prob-5-10a.description: A tetrahedral carbon is bonded to CH₃ above, CO₂H to the right, H on a dashed bond to the left, and HS on a solid wedge toward the lower left. The drawing presents a chirality center for an R/S configuration exercise without giving its answer.

ch05/table-5.2.description: Two steroid structures labeled Cholestanol and Coprostanol are shown side by side, with C5 highlighted as S and R, respectively. A bracket labeled “Epimers” indicates that the structures differ in configuration at that center.

ch05/prob-5-10c.description: A tetrahedral drawing shows a central carbon bonded to H on the left and OH on the right by solid wedges, with dashed bonds to an aldehyde group above and CH₂OH below. It is one of the structures presented for assigning a chirality-center configuration.

ch05/fig-5.11.description: Four wedge-and-dash structures and matching ball-and-stick models show the stereoisomers of 2-amino-3-hydroxybutanoic acid. Blue mirror planes and brackets group 2R,3R with 2S,3S and 2R,3S with 2S,3R as enantiomer pairs.

ch05/prob-5-13a.description: A vertical stereochemical structure shows an aldehyde at the top and a CH₂OPO₃²⁻ group at the bottom. Both central carbons have H on the left and OH on the right, illustrating the stereochemistry of D-erythrose 4-phosphate.

ch05/prob-5-14.description: The figure shows the labeled structural formula of morphine, with fused rings, an oxygen bridge, hydroxyl groups, and a nitrogen bearing a CH₃ group. Solid and dashed wedge bonds show the three-dimensional arrangement at several atoms; the accompanying problem asks about chirality centers and possible stereoisomers.

ch05/prob-5-13b.description: The drawing shows an erythrose 4-phosphate structure with an aldehyde at the top and a CH₂OPO₃²⁻ group at the bottom. At both tetrahedral centers, HO is drawn on the left and H on the right, with dashed vertical bonds and solid wedges for the horizontal bonds.

ch05/prob-5-13c.description: A four-carbon chain is drawn with an aldehyde at the top and a CH₂OPO₃²⁻ group at the bottom. At the two central stereocenters, the upper OH points left and the lower OH points right, with horizontal wedge bonds and dashed vertical bonds showing their arrangement.

ch05/p162c.description: Two wedge-and-dash drawings of tartaric acid are labeled 2R,3S and 2S,3R. A 180° rotation arrow and a bracket labeled “Identical” show that the drawings represent the same structure.

ch05/prob-5-13d.description: A four-carbon chain is drawn with an aldehyde at the top and a CH₂OPO₃²⁻ group at the bottom. At its two central stereocenters, H and OH project toward the viewer on opposite sides: H left and OH right at the upper center, HO left and H right at the lower center.

ch05/p162a.description: A ball-and-stick model shows isoleucine, with a carboxylic acid group, an amino group, and a branched carbon chain attached to its central carbon. The three-dimensional arrangement highlights the molecule’s tetrahedral centers.

ch05/p162b.description: Four wedge-and-dash structures of tartaric acid are labeled 2R,3R; 2S,3S; 2R,3S; and 2S,3R. Blue panels marked “Mirror” separate the structures into two mirror-image pairs, illustrating stereoisomers with two chirality centers.

ch05/prob-5-16c.description: A five-membered ring has OH groups on adjacent carbons, both shown on solid wedges, and H atoms on dashed bonds. The drawing illustrates one stereochemical structure in a problem asking which structures are meso compounds.

ch05/we-5.5.description: A perspective drawing of a cyclobutane ring shows methyl and hydrogen groups on two adjacent carbons, numbered 1 and 2. A blue plane labeled “Symmetry plane” bisects the ring, illustrating that the structure is a meso compound.

ch05/prob-5-16a.description: A stereochemical drawing shows two bonded tetrahedral carbons, each attached to a bromine atom, a hydrogen atom, and a methyl group. Solid wedges and dashed bonds indicate the groups’ three-dimensional orientations; the problem asks whether the structure is meso.

ch05/p164b.description: A generic carboxylic acid, RCO₂H, reacts with an amine base, RNH₂, to form a carboxylate–ammonium salt. The diagram highlights transfer of the acid’s hydrogen to the amine.

ch05/prob-5-16d.description: A five-membered ring has OH and H attached at each of two adjacent carbons. The OH bonds are shown as a solid wedge at one carbon and a dashed wedge at the other, indicating opposite orientations.

ch05/fig-5.13.description: The diagram shows a 50:50 mixture of wedge-and-dash (R)- and (S)-lactic acid reacting with methylamine to give a 50:50 mixture of the corresponding ammonium salts. A mirror and arrows indicate that the R and S salts are enantiomers.

ch05/fig-5.14.description: The diagram shows the wedge-and-dash structures of both enantiomers of racemic lactic acid reacting with (R)-1-phenylethylamine to form two ammonium carboxylate salts, labeled R,R and S,R. Arrows identify the salts as diastereomers.

ch05/p166.description: A reaction scheme shows lactic acid and methanol forming methyl lactate and water, with “Acid catalyst” above the arrow. The structures show the hydroxyl group on the central carbon but do not specify its stereochemistry.

ch05/prob-5-16b.description: The drawing shows two five-membered rings joined at one carbon, with solid-wedge and dashed bonds indicating their three-dimensional arrangement. A carbon on the right-hand ring bears a CH₃ group on a solid wedge and an H on a dashed bond.

ch05/fig-5.15.description: A branching chart divides isomers into constitutional isomers and stereoisomers. Stereoisomers branch into enantiomers (mirror-image) and diastereomers (non-mirror-image), with the latter divided into configurational and cis–trans diastereomers.

ch05/p167a.description: The figure compares three pairs of compounds with the same molecular formula but different connections: 2-methylpropane and butane have different carbon skeletons, ethyl alcohol and dimethyl ether have different functional groups, and isopropylamine and propylamine have amino groups in different positions. Each compound is shown as a condensed structural formula with its name beneath it.

ch05/prob-5-195.description: A reaction scheme shows acetic acid and 2-butanol forming sec-butyl acetate and water with an acid catalyst over the arrow. The alcohol’s OH and the ester’s connecting oxygen are highlighted in pink; no stereochemistry is drawn.

ch05/we-5.6.description: Mirror-image (S)- and (R)-lactic acid structures react with CH₃OH under an acid catalyst to give mirror-image methyl (S)- and (R)-lactate structures. Wedge-and-dash bonds show the stereochemistry at each central carbon.

ch05/p168b.description: A phosphorus center is bonded to methyl, propyl, and phenyl groups, with a pink lone-pair lobe marked “Lowest ranked.” The figure labels the compound (R)-methylpropylphenylphosphine and calls it configurationally stable.

ch05/p168d.description: A reaction arrow connects planar 2-butanone to 2-butanol, drawn with H and OH attached at the former carbonyl carbon. Pink arrows point to that carbon in each structure, and the labels contrast “prochiral” with “chiral.”

ch05/p168c.description: The structure labeled (S)-S-Adenosylmethionine shows a sulfur center joining the bracketed methionine and adenosine portions. Wedge and dashed bonds indicate its three-dimensional arrangement, and a pink lobe with two dots highlights the sulfur lone pair.

ch05/p168a.description: Two mirror-image drawings show a nitrogen bonded to hydrogen, methyl, and ethyl groups, with its lone pair highlighted in pink. Opposing arrows labeled “Rapid” indicate interconversion between the forms.

ch05/p167b.description: The figure compares three pairs of stereoisomers: mirror-image lactic acid enantiomers, non-mirror-image configurational diastereomers of 2-amino-3-hydroxybutanoic acid, and trans and cis 1,3-dimethylcyclopentane. Wedge-and-dash bonds show how the groups are arranged around the stereocenters.

ch05/p164a.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a carbon-and-hydrogen framework with double bonds and a red oxygen bonded to hydrogen, indicating a hydroxyl group. The differently angled bonds make the molecule's three-dimensional shape visible.

ch05/p169a.description: A planar 2-butanone structure is marked with clockwise Re and counterclockwise Si faces, with its three groups numbered 1–3. An arrow points to alternative wedge-and-dash products labeled (S)-2-Butanol and (R)-2-Butanol, illustrating how addition from opposite faces gives different stereoisomers.

ch05/p169b.description: The figure shows ethanol with an arrow pointing to its CH₂OH carbon, labeled a prochirality center. An arrow leads to a structure in which one of that carbon’s hydrogens is replaced by X, and the carbon is labeled a chirality center.

ch05/p169d.description: A fumarate structure has its Re and Si faces marked at one alkene carbon, with numbered groups around it. An arrow leads to a wedge-and-dash drawing labeled (S)-Malate, showing the stereochemical outcome of adding water.

ch05/p169c.description: The figure shows the two hydrogens on ethanol’s CH₂ group marked pro-R and pro-S. Replacing the pro-R hydrogen with ²H gives the depicted (R) chiral center; replacing the pro-S hydrogen gives the (S) center.

ch05/p170a.description: A reversible reaction shows ethanol and NAD⁺ on the left and acetaldehyde and NADH on the right. Colored Hᴿ and Hˢ labels mark hydrogens on ethanol and NADH, while Re and Si arrows mark faces of the NAD⁺ ring.

ch05/prob-5-24.description: A reaction diagram shows pyruvate, drawn with a carbonyl group, a methyl group, and a carboxylate group, converting to lactate, drawn with a hydroxyl group in place of the carbonyl oxygen. The problem asks for the product’s stereochemistry if hydrogen adds to the Re face of pyruvate; the product is shown without stereochemical bonds.

ch05/prob-5-23a.description: The figure shows the structure of hydroxyacetone, with pink arrows pointing toward the carbonyl carbon from above and below. The arrows indicate the two faces to be identified in the problem.

ch05/prob-5-22a.description: The figure shows the wedge-and-dash structure of (S)-glyceraldehyde, with two pink arrows pointing to the hydrogens on its CH₂OH group. One hydrogen is drawn on a solid wedge and the other on a dashed wedge; the drawing asks the reader to distinguish them without showing an answer.

ch05/prob-5-22b.description: A wedge-and-dash structure labeled “Phenylalanine” shows a benzene ring attached to a CH₂ group and a neighboring carbon bearing NH₃⁺, CO₂⁻, and H. Pink arrows point to the two hydrogens on the CH₂ group for identification as pro-R or pro-S.

ch05/prob-5-23b.description: A structural drawing of crotyl alcohol shows CH₃–CH=CH–CH₂OH, with pink arrows pointing toward the alkene carbon next to CH₂OH from above and below. The arrows mark the two faces of that carbon for the stereochemistry problem.

ch05/p171.description: A wedge-and-dash structural formula labeled “(S)-Fluoxetine (prevents migraine)” appears beside a ball-and-stick model of the same molecule. The pair illustrates its three-dimensional, chiral structure.

ch05/p170b.description: The figure shows citrate in two equivalent drawings, with its hydrogens marked pro-S (blue) and pro-R (pink). Loss of the pink OH and pro-R hydrogen as water forms the double bond in cis-aconitate, while the blue hydrogen remains.

ch05/fig-5.16.description: Two panels show a left hand holding mirror-image arrangements of four colored shapes. In (a), the green sphere, red sphere, and gray oval align with the thumb, palm, and pinkie; in (b), a blue cube sits against the palm instead, marked “Mismatch.”

ch05/prob-5-25.description: A reaction diagram shows cis-aconitate reacting with H₂O in the presence of aconitase to form (2R,3S)-isocitrate. The product has numbered carbon positions and wedge-and-dash bonds showing its three-dimensional arrangement.

ch05/fig-5.17.description: Panel (a) shows a hand holding a generic tetrahedral model whose two red substituents are labeled pro-R and pro-S. Panel (b) shows a hand holding a coffee mug, illustrating how a chiral environment makes otherwise equivalent positions distinguishable.

ch05/p173.description: A skeletal structure of penicillin V shows its phenoxy-containing side chain, fused rings, and wedge-and-dash bonds. Pink arrows mark the three stereocenters as 2S, 5R, and 6R.

ch05/fig-5.18.description: An athlete lies on a stretcher on a running track while several medical staff attend to them. The caption connects athletic injury pain with the greater effectiveness of the S enantiomer of ibuprofen compared with the R enantiomer.

ch05/p174.description: The figure pairs a skeletal structure of (S)-ibuprofen with a ball-and-stick model beneath it. The structure marks its stereocenter with wedge and dashed bonds to CO₂H and H and labels it “an active analgesic agent.”

ch05/prob-5-26a.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a central carbon bonded to a green chlorine atom, a white hydrogen atom, a methyl group, and a carboxylic acid group. It is one of the structures in a problem asking which models are identical.

ch05/prob-5-27a.description: A ball-and-stick model labeled “Serine” shows a central carbon bonded to an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen, and a carbon side chain bearing a hydroxyl group. Nitrogen is blue, oxygen red, carbon dark gray, and hydrogen pale gray.

ch05/prob-5-26c.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a tetrahedral carbon bonded to green chlorine, hydrogen, a methyl group, and a carboxylic acid group. It is one structure from a stereochemistry problem asking which drawings are identical.

ch05/prob-5-27b.description: A ball-and-stick model labeled “Adrenaline” shows a benzene ring with two hydroxyl groups and a side chain bearing another hydroxyl group and a blue nitrogen atom. The hydroxyl-bearing side-chain carbon is shown as a tetrahedral center.

ch05/prob-5-26d.description: A ball-and-stick model shows 2-chloropropanoic acid, with a central tetrahedral carbon attached to chlorine, hydrogen, a methyl group, and a carboxylic acid group. The problem asks for the configuration of this chirality center.

ch05/prob-5-26b.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a tetrahedral carbon bonded to a green chlorine atom, a methyl group, a hydrogen atom, and a carboxylic acid group. It is one of the structures presented for comparison in a stereochemistry problem.

ch05/prob-5-30b.description: A central tetrahedral C is bonded to four numbered groups: 3 above and 4 to the right on plain lines, 2 to the left on a dashed bond, and 1 down-left on a solid wedge. The drawing illustrates the spatial arrangement used in an R/S configuration exercise.

ch05/prob-5-30a.description: A central carbon is bonded to four groups ranked 1–4: 1 is above and 3 is to the right on plain bonds, 2 is lower left on a solid wedge, and 4 is left on a dashed wedge. The drawing is for an R/S configuration exercise; no configuration is assigned.

ch05/prob-5-29.description: A ball-and-stick model of pseudoephedrine shows a benzene ring attached to a chain with a hydroxyl group and a nitrogen atom; the nitrogen is blue and the oxygen is red. The model accompanies a problem asking for the configurations of its chirality centers.

ch05/prob-5-36.description: A skeletal structure of erythronolide B is shown as a large ring containing an ester group, a ketone, several hydroxyl groups, and methyl substituents. Solid and dashed wedges mark bonds projecting toward and away from the viewer; the accompanying problem asks readers to identify its chirality centers.

ch05/prob-5-30c.description: A tetrahedral center labeled C is bonded to four numbered groups: 4 above and 2 to the right on ordinary bonds, 1 to the left on a dashed bond, and 3 at the lower left on a solid wedge. The diagram shows their three-dimensional arrangement for a stereochemistry problem without assigning a configuration.

ch05/prob-5-28a.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a five-carbon ring with hydroxyl groups attached at two ring positions. Dark gray spheres represent carbon, red spheres oxygen, and white spheres hydrogen.

ch05/prob-5-28b.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a five-carbon chain with an amino group on each of the second and fourth carbons. Carbon atoms are dark gray, nitrogen atoms blue, and hydrogen atoms pale gray.

ch05/prob-5-37b.description: Two tetrahedral carbon structures are shown side by side, each bonded to H, Br, CN, and CO₂H. Dashed bonds indicate H behind the plane and solid wedges indicate a bond projecting forward; the positions of Br, CN, and CO₂H differ between the drawings.

ch05/prob-5-28c.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a four-carbon chain with a green atom attached to each of the two central tetrahedral carbons; the smaller pale spheres represent hydrogens. The drawing presents the molecule’s three-dimensional arrangement without assigning configurations.

ch05/prob-5-41a.description: A central carbon is bonded to four numbered groups: 1 on a dashed bond to the left, 2 on a solid wedge down-left, 3 on a plain bond to the right, and 4 on a plain bond above. The drawing shows the groups’ three-dimensional arrangement for the stereochemistry problem.

ch05/prob-5-41c.description: A central tetrahedral carbon is bonded to four groups numbered 1 through 4. Group 1 is on a solid wedge toward the viewer, group 2 on a dashed wedge behind the page, and groups 3 and 4 on ordinary bonds in the plane.

ch05/prob-5-41b.description: A central C is bonded to four numbered groups: 3 above and 1 to the right by plain lines, 2 at lower left by a solid wedge, and 4 to the left by a dashed wedge. The drawing presents a tetrahedral center for a stereochemistry assignment.

ch05/prob-5-43a.description: A skeletal structure of 2-butanol shows a tetrahedral carbon bonded to H on a solid wedge, OH on a dashed bond, and two carbon chains drawn in the plane. The drawing is part of a problem asking for the chirality center’s R or S configuration.

ch05/prob-5-37c.description: Two perspective drawings show a tetrahedral carbon bonded to OH, H, CH₃, and CH₂CH₃, with solid wedges and dashed bonds indicating their spatial arrangement. The substituents are positioned differently in the two drawings.

ch05/prob-5-37a.description: Two wedge-and-dash structures show a tetrahedral carbon bonded to Br, CN, CH₃, and H. In the left drawing, H projects forward and CH₃ recedes; in the right, Br projects forward and H recedes.

ch05/prob-5-37d.description: Two wedge-and-dash structures show a tetrahedral carbon bonded to an amino group, a carboxyl group, a methyl group, and hydrogen, with the groups arranged differently in the two drawings.

ch05/prob-5-42.description: The problem shows four substituents for Cahn–Ingold–Prelog ranking: —C≡CH, —CH=CH₂, —C(CH₃)₃, and a benzene ring attached through one carbon. No rankings are shown.

ch05/prob-5-43b.description: A benzene ring is attached to a tetrahedral carbon bearing Cl, H, and an unlabeled terminal carbon. Cl is drawn on a solid wedge and H on a dashed bond, showing their three-dimensional orientation without assigning a configuration.

ch05/prob-5-43c.description: A tetrahedral carbon is bonded to H, OCH₃, HOCH₂, and CO₂H. H is shown on a solid wedge and OCH₃ on a dashed wedge; the drawing is presented for assigning the center’s R or S configuration.

ch05/prob-5-45a.description: The figure shows the labeled structure of biotin, with a carbonyl-containing ring fused to a sulfur-containing ring and a CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CO₂⁻ side chain. Solid wedges and a dashed bond indicate the three-dimensional orientations of bonds at its tetrahedral centers.

ch05/prob-5-48.description: The figure shows the structural formula of ascorbic acid, with a five-membered ring, hydroxyl groups, and a CH₂OH side chain. Solid and dashed wedge bonds mark the orientations at two chirality centers for the stereochemistry problem.

ch05/prob-5-47a.description: A wedge-and-dash drawing shows 2,3-dibromobutane with bromine and hydrogen attached to each of its two central carbons. The solid wedges and dashed bonds show the groups’ three-dimensional orientations for a stereochemistry assignment.

ch05/prob-5-45b.description: A skeletal structure labeled Prostaglandin E₁ shows a five-membered ring with a ketone and hydroxyl group, plus two side chains: one ends in CO₂H, and the other contains a double bond and an OH group. Solid and dashed wedges indicate the orientations of bonds at several tetrahedral centers.

ch05/prob-5-44c.description: A five-membered ring has two substituted carbons, each bearing an OH group on a solid wedge and a CH₃ group on a dashed bond. The drawing is part of a problem asking for the configuration of each chirality center.

ch05/prob-5-44b.description: A cyclohexane ring has an ethyl group and a methyl group at two stereogenic ring carbons separated by one carbon. Solid and dashed wedges show the ethyl group pointing behind the page and the methyl group pointing out, with the hydrogens in the opposite directions; the drawing asks for configurations but does not give them.

ch05/prob-5-47b.description: A benzene ring is attached to a chain drawn as Ph–CH₂–CH(OH)–CH(NH₂)–CO₂H. Solid and dashed wedges show the three-dimensional arrangement of H, OH, and NH₂ around the tetrahedral centers for an R/S assignment problem.

ch05/prob-5-50.description: A zigzag structure labeled (+)-Xylose runs from OHC on the left to CH₂OH on the right. Its three central carbons bear HO and H groups on solid and dashed wedge bonds, showing their three-dimensional arrangement.

ch05/prob-5-49a.description: A Newman projection shows a front carbon bonded to Cl, CH₃, and H, with the rear carbon bonded to CH₃ and two H atoms. The drawing presents the molecule for a stereochemistry assignment without indicating its configuration.

ch05/prob-5-44a.description: A cyclohexane ring has OH and Cl on adjacent carbons. Wedge and dashed bonds show the three-dimensional positions of those groups and the attached hydrogens for an R/S assignment problem.

ch05/prob-5-52a.description: A condensed structural formula shows a six-carbon chain with an OH group attached to each of the two CH groups next to the end methyl groups. No stereochemical bonds are indicated.

ch05/prob-5-52b.description: A cyclohexane ring is drawn with CH₃ groups attached at two ring carbons separated by one carbon. No wedge or dash bonds are shown.

ch05/prob-5-54.description: A labeled skeletal structure of ribose shows a five-carbon chain with a CHO group at one end, a CH2OH group at the other, and OH and H groups attached along the chain. Solid and dashed wedge bonds show the three-dimensional orientations of these groups.

ch05/prob-5-49b.description: A Newman projection shows a front carbon bearing H and two CH₃ groups, and a rear carbon bearing H, OH, and CH₃. The drawing is presented as a stereochemistry problem, without an R or S assignment shown.

ch05/prob-5-52c.description: A five-membered carbon ring has an OH group on one carbon and CH₃ groups on two adjacent carbons across the ring. No wedge or dashed bonds indicate stereochemistry.

ch05/prob-5-56b.description: A wedge-and-dash structure labeled methionine shows its sulfur-containing side chain and charged amino and carboxylate groups. Pink arrows point to the two hydrogens on each of two side-chain carbons for a pro-R/pro-S identification problem.

ch05/prob-5-57a.description: The figure shows pyruvate with its central carbonyl carbon highlighted in pink, bonded to CH₃ and CO₂⁻. Pink arrows point toward that carbon from above and below, marking the two faces to identify.

ch05/prob-5-58.description: A reaction arrow connects crotonate, with its alkene carbons marked 3 and 2, to 3-hydroxybutyrate, drawn with an OH group on carbon 3. The diagram shows the structural change but does not depict stereochemistry with wedges or dashes.

ch05/prob-5-57b.description: A skeletal structure labeled “Crotonate” shows a carboxylate group attached to a carbon–carbon double bond ending in CH₃. The right-hand alkene carbon is highlighted in pink, with arrows pointing toward it from above and below for a face-identification problem.

ch05/prob-5-55.description: The figure shows the wedge-and-dash structure of ribitol, a five-carbon chain with hydroxyl groups and CH₂OH groups at both ends. Solid and dashed wedges show the orientations of H and OH at the three inner carbons.

ch05/prob-5-56a.description: The figure shows the wedge-and-dash structure of malic acid, with pink arrows pointing to the two hydrogens on its CH₂ group. It accompanies a problem asking whether each indicated hydrogen is pro-R or pro-S.

ch05/prob-5-59.description: The figure shows citrate with its two arms colored blue and pink, followed by two alternative cis-aconitate structures. The alternatives differ in whether the double bond forms on the blue or pink arm; the problem asks which product results, without indicating an answer.

ch05/prob-5-56c.description: A wedge-and-dash structure labeled Cysteine shows an HS–CH₂ group attached to a carbon bearing H, H₃N⁺, and CO₂⁻. Pink arrows point to the two hydrogens on the CH₂ group for the pro-R/pro-S identification problem.

ch05/prob-5-60.description: A stereochemical drawing of glycerol, with two CH₂OH groups and horizontal HO and H bonds at the central carbon, points to a condensed glycerol phosphate structure. ATP and ADP are printed above the reaction arrow.

ch05/prob-5-61.description: A stereochemical drawing shows (R)-3-hydroxybutyryl ACP dehydrating to trans-crotonyl ACP, with H₂O above the reaction arrow. Colored hydrogens and an OH group mark the atoms involved, and carbons 1–4 are numbered on the reactant.

ch05/prob-5-66.description: The figure shows cephalexin as a skeletal structure with a phenyl-containing side chain attached to a fused, nitrogen- and sulfur-containing ring system. Solid and dashed wedges mark the three stereocenters for the problem; no R or S configurations are assigned.

ch05/prob-5-64.description: The figure shows two cysteine molecules reacting to form cystine, with their sulfur atoms joined by an S–S bond. Both structures show an NH₂ group attached to the carbon beside the carboxylic acid group.

ch05/prob-5-68.description: A linear structural formula labeled Mycomycin shows two carbon–carbon triple bonds, a central cumulated double-bond segment highlighted in pink, two further double bonds, and a terminal CH₂CO₂H group. The highlighted segment is the part of the structure relevant to the question about chirality.

ch05/prob-5-694.description: A cyclohexane ring has an exocyclic double bond to a carbon bearing H and CO₂H. At the opposite ring carbon, CH₃ is shown on a solid wedge and H on a dashed bond; the figure is labeled 4-Methylcyclohexylideneacetic acid.

ch05/prob-5-67.description: The figure shows chloramphenicol as a nitro-substituted benzene ring attached to a two-carbon chain bearing OH, CH₂OH, and NHCOCHCl₂ groups. Solid wedges and dashed bonds show the three-dimensional arrangement at the chain’s two chirality centers.

ch05/prob-5-76.description: A reaction scheme shows 2-butanone treated with sodium acetylide, then H₃O⁺, to give 3-methyl-1-pentyn-3-ol. The product drawing shows a central carbon attached to OH, CH₃, CH₂CH₃, and an ethynyl group.

ch05/prob-5-77.description: A reaction scheme shows (R)-2-phenylpropanal, drawn with wedge-and-dash bonds at its stereocenter, reacting with sodium acetylide followed by H₃O⁺ to give the drawn 4-phenyl-1-pentyn-3-ol. The product retains the wedge-and-dash bonds and shows an OH group and terminal alkyne on the newly formed carbon chain.

ch06/fig-6.1.description: A pole vaulter is suspended above a red crossbar, gripping a nearly vertical pole against a blue sky. The caption compares the initial push needed to clear the bar with the activation energy needed for many chemical reactions.

ch06/p185a.description: A reaction arrow shows dihydroxyacetone phosphate changing into glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, with the phosphate group retained and the positions of the carbonyl and hydroxyl groups changed. The figure presents this as formation of an isomeric product.

ch06/p184a.description: The diagram shows ethylene and H–Br reacting to give bromoethane, with the added H and Br highlighted in pink on the product. It illustrates an addition reaction across the alkene’s carbon–carbon double bond.

ch06/p184c.description: The figure shows methyl acetate and water reacting under an acid catalyst to form acetic acid and methanol. Colored atoms highlight how the two reactants become the two products.

ch06/p184b.description: A structural formula labeled ethanol (an alcohol) is connected by a reversible arrow marked “Acid catalyst” to ethylene (an alkene) and H₂O. The figure illustrates an alcohol splitting into an alkene and water.

ch06/table-6.1a.description: A table entry labeled “Alcohol” shows a carbon bonded to an OH group and three unlabeled bonds. The carbon is marked δ+ and the oxygen δ−, illustrating the polarity pattern of the C–O bond.

ch06/p186.description: Side-by-side ball-and-stick models with colored electron-distribution surfaces and structural drawings compare chloromethane and methyllithium. The drawings mark carbon as δ+ and chlorine as δ− in chloromethane, but carbon as δ− and lithium as δ+ in methyllithium.

ch06/p185c.description: Two electron-arrow diagrams show generic A and B forming an A:B bond: in the polar case, B donates both bonding electrons to A⁺; in the radical case, A and B each donate one electron.

ch06/table-6.1b.description: The table entry shows a generic alkene with a carbon–carbon double bond and matching bonds extending from each carbon. It labels the arrangement “Symmetrical, nonpolar.”

ch06/table-6.1d.description: The table row labeled “Amine” shows a generic carbon bonded to an NH₂ group. The carbon is marked δ+ and the nitrogen δ−, illustrating the polarity of the C–N bond.

ch06/table-6.1e.description: The table row labeled “Ether” shows an oxygen atom bonded between two carbon atoms, with δ− on the oxygen and δ+ on both adjacent carbons. It illustrates the polarity pattern of an ether functional group.

ch06/p185b.description: Two generic A–B bonds break: a full-headed curved arrow shows both bonding electrons moving to B, giving A⁺ and B⁻, while two fishhook arrows show one electron moving to each atom, giving A• and •B. The figure contrasts unsymmetrical (polar) and symmetrical (radical) bond-breaking.
labels_in_image: Unsymmetrical bond-breaking (polar): two bonding electrons stay with one product.
Symmetrical bond-breaking (radical): one bonding electron stays with each product.

ch06/table-6.1c.description: The table row shows a generic alkyl halide: a carbon bonded to three unlabeled groups and to X. The C–X bond is marked δ+ at carbon and δ− at X to illustrate its polarity.

ch05/prob-5-75.description: A generic alkyl bromide with wedge-and-dash bonds reacts with HS⁻ to give a sulfur-substituted product and Br⁻. The product’s wedge-and-dash bonds are reversed, illustrating inversion at the carbon center.

ch06/table-6.1g.description: A table row labeled “Grignard reagent” shows a carbon bonded to MgBr and three unlabeled groups. The carbon is marked δ− and the MgBr end δ+, illustrating bond polarity.

ch06/table-6.1i.description: A table entry labeled “Carbonyl” shows a generic C=O group with two bonds extending from carbon. The carbon is marked δ+ and the oxygen δ− to indicate the bond’s polarity.

ch06/table-6.1f.description: The table row labeled “Thiol” shows a generic carbon bonded to an –SH group, with δ+ marked at carbon and δ− at sulfur to illustrate the bond’s polarity pattern.

ch06/table-6.1m.description: A table entry shows a generic aldehyde structure with a carbonyl carbon bonded to hydrogen and an unspecified group. The oxygen is marked δ− and the carbonyl carbon δ+, illustrating the bond’s polarity.

ch06/table-6.1h.description: A table row labeled “Alkyllithium” shows a generic carbon–lithium structure, with δ− on carbon and δ+ on lithium to indicate bond polarity.

ch06/table-6.1j.description: A table row labeled “Carboxylic acid” shows a generic –C(=O)OH group, with δ+ on the carbon and δ− on both oxygens. It illustrates the polarity pattern of this functional group.

ch06/table-6.1l.description: A table row labeled “Thioester” shows a generic —C(=O)—S—R structure, with δ+ on the carbonyl carbon and δ− on the oxygen and sulfur. The partial-charge labels illustrate the functional group’s polarity pattern.

ch06/table-6.1n.description: The table row shows a generic ester group, —C(=O)—O—R, with a partial positive charge on the carbonyl carbon and partial negative charges on both oxygen atoms. It illustrates the polarity pattern of this functional group.

ch06/table-6.1o.description: A table entry labeled “Ketone” shows a generic carbonyl structure with a partial negative charge on oxygen and a partial positive charge on the carbonyl carbon, illustrating the polarity pattern of this functional group.

ch06/table-6.1k.description: A table row labeled “Carboxylic acid chloride” shows a generic acyl chloride structure with a carbonyl oxygen and chlorine attached to the same carbon. Partial-charge marks indicate δ+ on carbon and δ− on oxygen and chlorine.

ch06/p188a.description: Methanol is shown reacting with a generic acid, H–A, as its oxygen takes a proton and the H–A bond breaks to give protonated methanol and A⁻. Colored molecular surfaces and captions contrast methanol’s weakly electron-poor carbon with the strongly electron-poor carbon after protonation.

ch06/p188b.description: Two generic carbon-containing structures show a carbon bonded to an S–H group or to iodine. In both, the carbon is marked δ+ and the sulfur or iodine δ−, illustrating the polarity assigned to these bonds.

ch06/prob-6-3.description: A ball-and-stick model of BF₃, with a central boron atom bonded to three fluorine atoms, is surrounded by a colored electrostatic potential map. The figure accompanies a question asking whether BF₃ is a nucleophile or an electrophile.

ch06/p188c.description: A curved arrow points from the electron pair on generic B⁻ (the electron-rich nucleophile) to A⁺ (the electron-poor electrophile). The product shows A—B joined by a new covalent bond, where the moved electrons end up.

ch06/p190.description: The figure shows ethylene reacting with hydrogen bromide to form bromoethane, with molecular models above and structural formulas below. It labels ethylene as the nucleophile and hydrogen bromide as the electrophile.

ch06/prob-6-4.description: A cyclohexene ring is shown reacting with HBr, followed by an arrow pointing to a question mark for the unknown product. The drawing poses a reaction-product problem without showing the product.

ch06/prob-6-2a.description: A five-membered ring with two nitrogen atoms and two double bonds is shown, with a CH₃ group attached to one nitrogen. The drawing presents the structure for classification in the problem without indicating an answer.

ch06/prob-6-2b.description: The drawing shows CH₃CH=O: a carbonyl oxygen double-bonded to a carbon attached to CH₃ and hydrogen. It is one of the structures in a problem asking readers to consider nucleophilic and electrophilic behavior.

ch06/p193a.description: The figure shows 2-methylpropene reacting with HBr to form 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, with the reactant and product structures connected by a reaction arrow.

ch06/fig-6.3.description: The figure compares ethane’s carbon–carbon σ bond on the left with ethylene’s carbon–carbon π bond on the right, using molecular surfaces above and bond-electron drawings below.
