The labels show the σ bond as stronger with less accessible bonding electrons and the π bond as weaker with more accessible electrons; an arrow points to the double-bond region on ethylene’s electrostatic potential map.
labels_in_image: Carbon–carbon σ bond: stronger; less accessible bonding electrons
Carbon–carbon π bond: weaker; more accessible electrons

ch06/p193b.description: The figure shows four generic nucleophilic electron sources—an oxygen lone pair, a nitrogen lone pair, a negatively charged carbon lone pair, and a carbon–carbon double bond. Pink curved arrows point from each source toward an electrophile labeled E, illustrating the direction of electron flow.
labels_in_image: Electrons usually flow from one of these nucleophiles.

ch06/fig-6.2.description: Seven molecular models and electrostatic potential maps are arranged in two rows: four electron-rich nucleophiles above and three electron-poor electrophiles below. Pink arrows mark the nucleophilic atoms, while blue arrows mark electrophilic sites; the lower structures also show partial charges.

ch06/p193d.description: A negatively charged CH₃O⁻ group reacts with H–Br: curved arrows show an electron pair from oxygen forming an O–H bond while the H–Br bond electrons move to bromine. The products are CH₃OH, labeled “Neutral,” and Br⁻.

ch06/p193c.description: Four generic examples show curved arrows from a nucleophile (Nu) toward an electrophilic site: a positively charged carbon, a polarized carbon–halogen bond, the hydrogen of a polarized O–H bond, and the carbon of a polarized C=O bond. Additional arrows show bond electrons moving toward the halogen or oxygen.
labels_in_image: Electrons usually flow to one of these electrophiles.

ch06/p193e.description: The diagram shows ethene reacting with hydrogen bromide: curved arrows move electrons from the double bond toward H and from the H–Br bond toward Br. The products shown are a positively charged two-carbon species and bromide, illustrating the change from a neutral to a positively charged carbon.

ch06/p193f.description: Curved arrows show the double bond of ethene taking a proton from positively charged hydronium while the O–H bond electrons move onto oxygen. The products shown are an ethyl carbocation and neutral water, illustrating how a positively charged electrophile becomes neutral after accepting an electron pair.

ch06/p194b.description: The diagram shows ethene reacting with hydronium ion to form an ethyl carbocation and water. Curved arrows show the double-bond electrons moving toward a hydrogen while the H–O bond electrons move onto oxygen.
labels_in_image: This hydrogen already has two electrons. When another electron pair moves to the hydrogen from the double bond, the electron pair in the H–O bond must leave.

ch06/p194a.description: Curved arrows show the double bond of ethene forming a bond to hydrogen in HBr while the H–Br bond electrons move to bromine. The products shown are an ethyl carbocation and a negatively charged bromide ion, contrasting with the neutral bromine in HBr.

ch06/p195b.description: A reaction diagram shows a methoxide ion and methyl bromide on the left of a straight arrow, with dimethyl ether and a bromide ion on the right. Lone pairs and negative charges are drawn on the oxygen and bromide ions.

ch06/we-6.2a.description: A negatively charged carbon next to a carbonyl reacts with bromomethane to give a four-carbon ketone and bromide ion. A straight reaction arrow shows the transformation; no curved electron-flow arrows have been added.

ch06/p195a.description: A Lewis-structure reaction shows chlorine and ammonia forming a positively charged nitrogen species bonded to chlorine and three hydrogens, alongside a chloride ion. Lone pairs and formal charges are marked on the structures.

ch06/p195e.description: A generic reactant radical (Rad·) adds to an alkene double bond, forming a carbon–Rad bond and leaving an unpaired electron on the adjacent carbon. Curved arrows show the electron movements, and the product is labeled an addition product radical.

ch06/we-6.2b.description: A negatively charged carbon adjacent to a carbonyl reacts with a carbon bonded to bromine. Curved arrows show the carbon forming a new C–C bond as the C–Br bond electrons move to bromine, yielding a longer carbon chain and Br⁻.

ch06/p195c.description: A tetrahedral carbon bearing CH₃, OCH₃, Cl, and O⁻ is shown converting to a carbonyl compound bearing CH₃ and OCH₃, plus Cl⁻. The drawing uses lone pairs and a reaction arrow to show the change in bonding.

ch06/p196a.description: A chlorine molecule is shown splitting under light into two chlorine radicals. Pink single-headed arrows indicate that one electron from the Cl–Cl bond goes to each chlorine atom.

ch06/p195d.description: A generic reactant radical, Rad·, reacts with A:B to form the substitution product Rad:A and a new radical, ·B. Curved arrows show the movement of single electrons, and arrows label the unpaired electrons on the radicals.

ch06/prob-6-7.description: A substituted alkene bearing three carboxylate groups is shown reacting with water and hydronium. Pink curved arrows indicate electron flow toward the alkene and a proton, while a reaction arrow points to a question mark instead of a product.

ch06/p196d.description: A reaction scheme shows an oxygen radical on a long-chain structure adding across a double bond to form a five-membered ring and a carbon radical. A subsequent arrow leads to a structure labeled prostaglandin H₂ (PGH₂).

ch06/p196b.description: Two steps of a radical chain reaction are shown with curved arrows: a chlorine radical takes hydrogen from methane to form hydrogen chloride and a methyl radical; the methyl radical then reacts with chlorine to form chloromethane and another chlorine radical.

ch06/p198a.description: A flask of liquid has an outward arrow labeled “Keq > 1; energy out: ΔG° negative” and an inward arrow labeled “Keq < 1; energy in: ΔG° positive.” The diagram contrasts the equilibrium and energy-change labels for the two directions.

ch06/p199.description: A generic A–B bond is shown breaking into two radical fragments, A• and •B, with an arrow labeled “Bond dissociation energy.” The figure illustrates the energy associated with separating a bond into radicals.

ch06/p197.description: The figure shows ethylene reacting reversibly with HBr to form CH₃CH₂Br, with an equilibrium expression beneath the reaction. The printed equilibrium constant is 7.1 × 10⁷.

ch06/p196c.description: An iron-bound oxygen radical abstracts a hydrogen atom from arachidonic acid, forming an iron-bound O–H group and a carbon radical on the fatty-acid chain. Curved arrows highlight the reacting atoms, while the rest of the molecule is drawn in gray.

ch06/table-6.3a.description: A benzene ring is attached to a CH₃ group, with the bond between them highlighted in pink. The drawing singles out that bond in the context of bond dissociation energies.

ch06/table-6.3d.description: A benzene ring is drawn with one C–H bond highlighted in pink and its hydrogen labeled in green, illustrating the bond represented by an entry in the bond dissociation energy table.

ch06/table-6.3c.description: A structural formula for acetaldehyde shows a carbonyl carbon double-bonded to oxygen and single-bonded to CH₃ and H; the carbonyl carbon–hydrogen bond is highlighted in color in a table of bond dissociation energies.

ch06/table-6.3e.description: A skeletal structure shows a benzene ring with a chlorine substituent, illustrating the C–Cl bond in chlorobenzene.

ch06/p198b.description: A reversible reaction shows ethylene (H₂C=CH₂) and HBr forming CH₃CH₂Br. Beside it are approximate thermodynamic values at 298 K: ΔG° = −44.8 kJ/mol, ΔH° = −84.1 kJ/mol, ΔS° = −0.132 kJ/(K·mol), and Kₑq = 7.1 × 10⁷.

ch06/table-6.3i.description: A skeletal structure shows a benzene ring with a bromine atom attached to one carbon, illustrating an aryl–bromine bond.

ch06/table-6.3f.description: A benzene ring is attached to a CH₂–H group, with the bond to H highlighted in pink and the H colored green. In the bond-dissociation-energy table, the drawing singles out this C–H bond.

ch06/table-6.3h.description: A drawn acetone molecule has the bond between its carbonyl carbon and one methyl group highlighted in pink, with that methyl group colored green. It appears as an entry in a table of bond dissociation energies.

ch06/table-6.3g.description: A cropped entry from a bond dissociation energy table shows a benzene ring attached to CH₂—Cl, with the carbon–chlorine bond highlighted in pink. It illustrates the bond whose dissociation energy is tabulated.

ch06/table-6.3b.description: An ethylbenzene structure shows a benzene ring attached to CH₂–CH₃, with the bond to the green CH₃ group highlighted in pink. It marks a specific bond in the context of bond dissociation energies.

ch06/prob-6-9.description: A reaction arrow connects a peroxide-containing chain with a radical dot to a structure with a newly formed five-membered carbon ring and a radical dot on a side chain. Double bonds, hydrogen atoms, and CO₂H groups are shown; the problem asks for fishhook arrows to explain the ring formation.

ch06/fig-6.7.description: Four energy-versus-reaction-progress diagrams compare low and high activation barriers (ΔG‡) with products at lower or higher energy than reactants (negative or positive ΔG°). Panels (a) and (b) show fast and slow exergonic reactions; (c) and (d) show fast and slow endergonic reactions.

ch06/fig-6.5.description: An energy-versus-reaction-progress diagram shows ethylene and HBr rising to a transition-state peak, then falling to a higher-energy carbocation product, CH₃CH₂⁺ + Br⁻. Vertical arrows mark the activation energy (ΔG‡) and the reactant-to-product energy difference (ΔG°).

ch06/fig-6.9.description: An energy diagram compares a high, single-peaked uncatalyzed pathway with a lower, multi-peaked enzyme-catalyzed pathway. Both begin and end at the same energy levels, with energy on the vertical axis and reaction progress on the horizontal axis.

ch06/table-6.3j.description: A benzene ring with an attached OH group shows the structure of phenol, presented alongside a table of bond dissociation energies.

ch06/we-6.3.description: An energy diagram shows a magenta curve rising from reactants to a modest peak and then falling to products at much lower energy. The vertical arrows label the activation free energy ΔG‡ and the negative overall free-energy change ΔG°, illustrating a fast, highly exergonic reaction.

ch06/p202.description: A two-step reaction drawing shows ethylene reacting with HBr: curved arrows lead to a bracketed carbocation and bromide ion, followed by an arrow from bromide to the positively charged carbon to form bromoethane. The steps are numbered 1 and 2.

ch06/p204.description: The diagram shows ethylene reacting with HBr: curved arrows lead to a bracketed, positively charged carbon species and bromide ion, followed by an arrow to a bromine-containing product. The bracketed species is labeled “Reaction intermediate.”

ch06/table-6.3k.description: Two reaction diagrams compare hydrolysis of glycerol 3-phosphate to glycerol and phosphate with hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate. Arrows mark the glycerol 3-phosphate bond as “Stronger” and the ATP bond as “Weaker,” with ΔH°′ values of −9 and −30 kJ/mol, respectively.

ch06/we-6.4.description: An energy-versus-reaction-progress diagram shows a magenta curve rising through two peaks separated by a valley, then falling to a final level below the starting level. Dashed horizontal lines and vertical arrows mark ΔG‡ and ΔG°.

ch06/fig-6.6.description: The figure shows a hypothetical transition-state arrangement for ethylene reacting with HBr, with colored orbital lobes around the carbon atoms. Dashed lines depict the ethylene π bond and H–Br bond beginning to break while a C–H bond begins to form.

ch06/p206.description: A reaction diagram shows glucose converted to glucose 6-phosphate, with its CH₂OH group changing to CH₂OPO₃²⁻. Above the hexokinase-labeled arrow, ATP points into the reaction and ADP points out.

ch06/fig-6.10.description: Space-filling and wire-frame models of hexokinase show a cleft marked “Active site.” Below, a close-up of the active site shows the positions of adenosine diphosphate (ADP), lysine, and glucose.

ch06/p207.description: The figure shows the chemical structure of reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NADH), with a pink arrow pointing to one hydrogen on its nicotinamide ring. That hydrogen is highlighted as the atom transferred to a double-bond substrate.
labels_in_image: Reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, NADH (a coenzyme)

ch06/fig-6.8.description: A reaction-energy curve for H₂C=CH₂ + HBr forming CH₃CH₂Br rises through two transition states separated by a carbocation intermediate, then falls to products below the reactants. Arrows mark the activation energies for both steps and the overall free-energy change.

ch06/p210.description: A horizontal year-by-year timeline shows drug discovery, animal tests and manufacture, an IND application, three phases of clinical trials, an NDA, and ongoing oversight. Colored blocks mark the stages from before year 0 through year 10 and beyond.

ch06/prob-6-16a.description: A ball-and-stick model of formaldehyde shows a central carbon bonded to two hydrogens and double-bonded to oxygen, surrounded by a red-to-blue colored surface. It accompanies a question about whether the formaldehyde carbon is electrophilic or nucleophilic.

ch06/prob-6-18.description: An energy diagram shows a blue reaction path with four peaks and three valleys, starting at a dashed energy level and ending at a lower dashed level. An upward arrow labeled “Energy” indicates the vertical axis.

ch06/fig-6.11.description: Workers in white lab coats and gloves handle small blue-capped vials beside a blue conveyor belt, with rows of vials arranged in white trays. The photo illustrates vaccine production in the caption’s discussion of where new drugs come from.

ch06/p211.description: The figure compares two generic bond-forming reactions: in the polar example, B:⁻ donates an electron pair to A⁺, labeled nucleophile and electrophile; in the radical example, B· and ·A each contribute one electron. Curved arrows show electron movement, and both paths lead to an A:B bond.

ch06/prob-6-17.description: An energy diagram shows a magenta reaction path rising from a low starting level to a first peak, dipping to an intermediate level, rising to a higher second peak, then falling to a final level above the starting one. The axes are labeled Energy and Reaction progress, with dashed horizontal markers at the starting, intermediate, peak, and final levels.

ch06/p209.description: A 3D pie chart titled “Origin of New Drugs 1981–2014” divides new drugs into seven labeled sources. Synthetic drugs are the largest slice (31%), followed by synthetic/natural product mimics (21%); the other slices are biological macromolecules, vaccines, unaltered natural products, natural product derivatives, and botanical drugs.

ch06/prob-6-24.description: A reaction diagram shows ethylene and water in equilibrium with ethanol. Beside it are the listed thermodynamic parameters ΔH° = −44 kJ/mol, ΔS° = −0.12 kJ/(K·mol), and K_eq = 24.

ch06/prob-6-14.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a five-carbon chain with a brown atom attached to the carbon next to one end. It depicts the molecular structure of 2-bromopentane.

ch06/prob-6-25.description: The diagram shows acid-catalyzed isomerization of isopropylidenecyclohexane to 1-isopropylcyclohexene through a bracketed, positively charged intermediate. Reversible arrows show proton addition to the exocyclic double bond followed by formation of a double bond within the ring and regeneration of H⁺.

ch06/prob-6-28a.description: A bromine radical (Br·) and a cyclohexene ring with a double bond on its left side appear before a reaction arrow; no product is drawn. The figure poses a radical addition problem without showing its outcome.

ch06/prob-6-27b.description: A reaction arrow labeled HBr connects a benzene ring bearing a vinyl group to a benzene ring bearing a –CH(Br)CH₃ group. It depicts addition of HBr across the side-chain double bond.

ch06/prob-6-27a.description: A skeletal alkene, 2-methyl-1-butene, reacts with HCl to form 2-chloro-2-methylbutane, with chlorine attached to the more substituted carbon of the original double bond. The figure shows the reactant and product for a mechanism-drawing problem, without depicting mechanism steps.

ch06/prob-6-27c.description: A reaction scheme shows a branched alkene reacting with HCl to give a saturated product with Cl attached to the branched carbon. It illustrates addition across the carbon–carbon double bond.

ch06/prob-6-28b.description: A chlorine radical (Cl·) and a five-membered oxygen-containing ring with a double bond opposite the oxygen are shown to the left of a reaction arrow. The drawing presents the starting materials for a radical addition problem; no product is shown.

ch06/prob-6-29a.description: A five-membered carbon ring is bonded to an OCH₃ group, showing an ether structure for the functional-group and polarity exercise.

ch06/prob-6-29e.description: The figure shows a benzene ring bonded to an aldehyde group (–CHO), the structure of benzaldehyde. It is a single structure rather than a reaction scheme.

ch06/prob-6-31a.description: A skeletal structure labeled Testosterone shows four fused rings, a carbonyl group, an alkene, a hydroxyl group, and methyl substituents. It is presented as a structure for identifying electrophilic and nucleophilic sites, without marking those sites.

ch06/prob-6-29b.description: A condensed structure shows CH₃–C(=O)–CH₂–C(=O)–OCH₃, with two C=O bonds separated by CH₂. No polarity markings are shown.

ch06/prob-6-29d.description: A skeletal structure shows a five-carbon chain with a carbon–carbon double bond and a terminal amide group, C(=O)NH₂. It is presented as one structure in a reaction-identification problem; no reaction arrow is visible in this crop.

ch06/prob-6-29c.description: A six-membered ring has two opposite carbonyl groups and two carbon–carbon double bonds. The drawing is presented as one structure in a problem asking readers to identify functional groups and their polarity.

ch06/prob-6-30a.description: A six-membered ring bearing an OH group is shown reacting under an “Acid catalyst” arrow to form a six-membered ring with one double bond, alongside H₂O.

ch06/prob-6-16b.description: A ball-and-stick model of methanethiol shows a carbon atom bonded to three hydrogens and a sulfur atom bonded to one hydrogen, surrounded by a colored surface.

ch06/prob-6-15.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a branched hydrocarbon carbocation intermediate, with dark carbon atoms and light hydrogen atoms. The problem asks for the two alkenes that could form this intermediate on addition of HBr.

ch06/prob-6-30c.description: A reaction scheme shows cyclohexane and O₂N–NO₂ reacting under light to form a cyclohexane ring bearing an NO₂ group, with HNO₂ shown as a byproduct.

ch06/prob-6-31b.description: The figure shows the skeletal structure labeled “Methamphetamine”: a benzene ring attached to a carbon chain ending at a carbon bonded to NHCH₃, CH₃, and H. Solid and dashed wedges show the spatial orientations of CH₃ and H; the problem asks the reader to identify electrophilic and nucleophilic sites.

ch06/prob-6-30b.description: Cyclopentadiene and methyl vinyl ketone are shown reacting under heat to form a bridged bicyclic product bearing an acetyl group. The arrow connects the two starting structures to the product.

ch06/prob-6-32c.description: A reaction diagram shows cyclohexanone plus a negatively charged methyl group, with an arrow pointing to a cyclohexane ring bearing both a methyl group and a negatively charged oxygen on the former carbonyl carbon. No curved electron-flow arrows are drawn.

ch06/prob-6-32a.description: A reaction scheme shows N₃⁻ and CH₃Cl forming CH₃N₃ and Cl⁻, illustrating replacement of chlorine by an azide group.

ch06/prob-6-32b.description: Benzene and a positively charged NO₂ species are shown reacting to form a ring bearing an NO₂ group and a positive charge on the adjacent carbon. The drawing illustrates the formation of a positively charged intermediate.

ch06/prob-6-34c.description: Water is shown next to protonated acetone, with curved arrows from the water oxygen toward the carbonyl carbon and from the C=O bond toward oxygen. An equilibrium arrow points to a question mark where the other structure would go.

ch06/prob-6-34b.description: Hydroxide ion and acetone are shown with curved arrows from hydroxide toward a hydrogen on acetone’s methyl group, from that C–H bond toward the carbonyl carbon, and from the C=O bond toward oxygen. An equilibrium arrow points to a question mark in place of the products.

ch06/prob-6-33a.description: A reaction scheme shows benzene and D–Cl in equilibrium with a bracketed, positively charged ring intermediate and chloride ion, followed by deuterium-substituted benzene and H–Cl. The drawing leaves the electron-flow arrows to be added.

ch06/prob-6-33b.description: The reaction scheme shows a methyl-substituted epoxide reacting with H–Cl to form a bracketed protonated epoxide and Cl⁻, then a product with OH and Cl on adjacent carbons. Reversible arrows appear between the stages; no curved electron-flow arrows have been added.

ch06/prob-6-36a.description: The figure shows a branched alkane with a central carbon bonded to three CH₃ groups and one CH₂CH₃ group. It is one of the structures presented in a question about radical chlorination.

ch06/prob-6-34d.description: A substituted cyclohexane bearing Br, two CH₃ groups, and an adjacent H is shown reacting with methoxide; curved arrows indicate removal of H, formation of a ring double bond, and departure of Br. An equilibrium arrow points toward a question mark in place of the product.

ch06/prob-6-36b.description: A skeletal drawing shows an unsubstituted six-membered carbon ring, cyclohexane. It is one of the structures in a problem asking which compounds give a single monochloro product upon radical chlorination.

ch06/prob-6-36c.description: A benzene ring is drawn with a methyl group attached to each of its six carbon atoms. The structure appears as one example in a problem about radical monochlorination.

ch06/prob-6-36d.description: A line-angle structure shows a four-carbon zigzag chain with a one-carbon branch on the second carbon.

ch06/prob-6-39a.description: A five-membered carbon ring has a double bond along one side, depicting the structure of cyclopentene.

ch06/prob-6-36e.description: A line-angle drawing shows a five-membered carbon ring with a single terminal bond extending from one ring carbon, depicting methylcyclopentane. No stereochemical bonds or labels are shown.

ch06/prob-6-34a.description: A carbon bearing two methyl groups, an OH group, and an OCH₃ group is shown beside hydroxide. Curved arrows trace electron movement between them, and a reversible arrow points toward an unknown product marked with a question mark.

ch06/prob-6-39b.description: A skeletal structure shows a carbon–carbon double bond with two methyl groups attached to each alkene carbon. It depicts 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene as one of the structures in the problem.

ch06/prob-6-44.description: A reaction scheme shows acetyl chloride reacting with ammonia through a tetrahedral intermediate and a positively charged intermediate after chloride leaves. A second ammonia molecule leads to acetamide and ammonium chloride.

ch06/prob-6-40.description: A reversible reaction scheme shows 2-chloro-2-methylpropane forming a bracketed carbocation, then a protonated alcohol after addition of water. A further water-mediated step gives 2-methyl-2-propanol, H₃O⁺, and Cl⁻.

ch07/p220.description: The figure shows three labeled alkene structures: ethylene with a carbon–carbon double bond, bicyclic α-pinene, and a long-chain lycopene structure with many alternating double bonds. The double bonds are highlighted in pink, emphasizing the conjugated polyene in lycopene.

ch07/fig-7.1.description: A photograph shows a large display of red tomatoes of different sizes, many still attached to green vines. The caption links their red color to lycopene, stating that it has 13 double bonds.

ch06/prob-6-46a.description: A substituted, positively charged five-membered nitrogen–sulfur ring is attached to a carbon bearing OH, CH₃, and a carboxylate group. Curved arrows indicate electron flow, and a reaction arrow points to an unknown product marked with a question mark.

ch06/prob-6-43.description: The equation shows methoxide ion and bromoethane on the left, with ethene, CH₃OH, and bromide ion on the right. The reactant’s C–Br single bond is replaced in the products by a C=C double bond; no curved arrows are drawn.

ch07/p221c.description: Side-by-side structures compare ethylene (C₂H₄), with a carbon–carbon double bond and fewer hydrogens, to ethane (C₂H₆), with a single bond and more hydrogens. The labels identify ethylene as unsaturated and ethane as saturated.

ch07/fig-7.2.description: Two branching diagrams show ethylene (ethene) and propylene (propene) pointing to labeled structural formulas of industrially derived compounds, including polymers. The figure illustrates the range of products made from these two alkenes.

ch06/prob-6-46c.description: A phosphate-substituted, protonated pyridine ring is linked through an imine to a carbon bearing H, CH₃, and CO₂⁻. Pink curved arrows show a base approaching that hydrogen and electron movement through the imine and ring; the product is left as a question mark.

ch07/p221d.description: Four labeled skeletal structures show different ways to have the formula C₆H₁₀: two double bonds, a ring and a double bond, two rings, or a triple bond. The double and triple bonds are highlighted in pink.

ch06/prob-6-45.description: A drawn carbocation with two double bonds and methyl groups points to an undrawn “Isomeric carbocation,” then through an H₂O-labeled arrow to α-terpineol. The product is shown as a methyl-substituted cyclohexene bearing a side chain with an OH group and two methyl groups.

ch07/p221a.description: A generic alkane, CH₃(CH₂)ₙCH₃ (n = 0–6), is shown undergoing treatment with steam at 850–900 °C, with an arrow leading to H₂ and three small alkenes separated by plus signs. The diagram illustrates products of high-temperature cracking.

ch07/p221b.description: A butane structure shows its central bond breaking at 900 °C to form two ethyl radicals. A second arrow shows the radicals forming two ethylene molecules and H₂.

ch06/prob-6-46b.description: A carbon skeleton bearing H₃C, OPO₃²⁻, a carbonyl, O⁻, and OPP is shown with curved arrows indicating electron movement. A reaction arrow points to a question mark where the product should be drawn.

ch07/p223a.description: A skeletal structure labeled Diazepam shows a chlorine-substituted fused benzene and seven-membered ring, with a methyl group, carbonyl group, two nitrogens, and an attached phenyl ring.

ch07/p222a.description: The figure replaces the two Br atoms in BrCH₂CH=CHCH₂Br with H atoms to obtain CH₃CH=CHCH₃, equating C₄H₆Br₂ with the hydrocarbon formula C₄H₈. It identifies one degree of unsaturation, represented by the double bond.

ch07/p223c.description: Two condensed alkene structures are shown with pink numbers marking their six-carbon chains. The left chain is numbered from the end nearer the double bond; the right has a methyl branch and is numbered from the end nearer that branch when the double bond is equally distant from either end.

ch07/p224b.description: Three numbered cyclic alkene structures illustrate the placement of double bonds and methyl substituents in their names: 1-methylcyclohexene, 1,4-cyclohexadiene, and 1,5-dimethylcyclopentene. The middle example also shows the newer name “cyclohexa-1,4-diene.”

ch07/p223b.description: Two drawings of the same alkene contrast a five-carbon chain highlighted in pink that includes the double bond with a six-carbon chain highlighted in green that does not. The figure says to name it as a pentene, not a hexene.
labels_in_image: as a hexene, since the double bond is not contained in the six-carbon chain

ch07/p224c.description: Three generic alkene-derived groups are shown side by side: a methylene group (H₂C=), a vinyl group (H₂C=CH–), and an allyl group (H₂C=CH–CH₂–). Pink zigzag marks indicate where each group attaches to the rest of a structure.

ch07/p223d.description: Four numbered alkene structures illustrate naming double-bond positions and methyl or ethyl branches. Their printed names are 2-Hexene, 2-Methyl-3-hexene, 2-Ethyl-1-pentene, and 2-Methyl-1,3-butadiene.

ch07/p222b.description: The figure crosses out the O in H₂C=CHCH=CHCH₂OH and shows the corresponding hydrocarbon structure with H in its place. It equates C₅H₈O with “C₅H₈” for counting unsaturation and notes two double bonds.

ch07/p224a.description: Two numbered, condensed alkene structures show how double-bond positions and substituents are indicated in newer versus older names. The examples are 2,5-dimethylhept-3-ene and 3-propylhexa-1,4-diene, with their older naming forms printed beneath.

ch07/table-7.1a.description: The table entry shows a carbon double-bonded to CH₂ and bonded to two CH₃ groups, the structure of 2-methylpropene (isobutylene). It pairs the alkene’s systematic and common names.

molecules.name: Isobutylene
molecules.role: common name for the same example

ch07/p222c.description: An amino-substituted five-membered ring with one double bond (C₅H₉N) is shown alongside the corresponding hydrocarbon ring (C₅H₈), with the nitrogen group marked as removed and a hydrogen shown in its place. The figure counts two unsaturations: one ring and one double bond.
labels_in_image: Two unsaturations: one ring and one double bond

ch07/table-7.1b.description: The drawing shows a four-carbon chain with double bonds at both ends and a CH₃ branch on the second carbon. The nearby table text identifies it as 2-methyl-1,3-butadiene, commonly called isoprene.

ch07/prob-7-4b.description: A condensed structural formula shows CH₃CH₂CH=C(CH₃)CH₂CH₃, with a methyl group attached above the right-hand carbon of the double bond.

ch07/fig-7.3.description: Two orbital diagrams show p orbitals on adjacent carbons aligned in parallel to form a π bond, then perpendicular after one carbon rotates 90°, breaking the π bond.
labels_in_image: Broken π bond after rotation (p orbitals are perpendicular)

ch07/prob-7-6a.description: A six-membered ring has a double bond on its right side, with a CH₃ group attached to each end of the double bond.

ch07/prob-7-4c.description: A condensed hydrocarbon structure shows a chain with two carbon–carbon double bonds and two CH₃ branches. It is presented as a compound to name, without a name printed beside the structure.

ch07/prob-7-4a.description: A condensed structure shows a terminal double bond in H₂C=CH–CH(CH₃)–C(CH₃)₃, with one methyl branch on the adjacent CH and three methyl groups attached to the next carbon.

ch07/fig-7.4.description: Side-by-side structural drawings and ball-and-stick models show cis-2-Butene with its two methyl groups on the same side of the C=C bond and trans-2-Butene with them on opposite sides. The comparison illustrates cis–trans isomerism in alkenes.

ch07/prob-7-6c.description: A five-membered ring has a double bond along its upper-left edge and a CH(CH₃)₂ group attached to the adjacent upper-right carbon. The drawing is a cycloalkene structure presented for naming.

ch07/fig-7.5.description: Two pairs of generic C=C structures compare switching A and B on one carbon. When the other carbon bears two D groups, the drawings are identical (=); when it bears D and E, they are not identical (≠) and are cis–trans isomers.
labels_in_image: These two compounds are identical; they are not cis–trans isomers.
These two compounds are not identical; they are cis–trans isomers.

ch07/p227a.description: Two generic C=C diagrams compare E and Z double bonds: the E diagram places the higher-ranked groups on opposite sides, while the Z diagram places them on the same side. A dashed vertical line marks the two sides of each double bond.
