ch07/prob-7-56c.description: A methoxy-substituted allylic carbocation is drawn with a terminal double bond and a positive charge on the carbon bonded to OCH₃ and a methyl group. A resonance arrow points to a question mark for the missing resonance form.

ch07/prob-7-58a.description: A cyclohexane ring has an exocyclic double bond to a CH₂ group, depicting the alkene for an HBr-addition problem; no product is shown.

ch07/prob-7-59b.description: A six-membered carbon ring has an exocyclic double bond to a CH₂ group. The structure is one of the alkenes presented for predicting an alcohol product.

ch07/prob-7-56b.description: A six-membered ring with two double bonds has a positive charge on one carbon; the adjacent carbon bears NO₂ and H. A double-headed resonance arrow points to a question mark, indicating a missing resonance form.

ch07/prob-7-57a.description: A drawn alkene, 3-methylhex-3-ene, is shown reacting with H₂O above an arrow and H₂SO₄ below it; a question mark marks the unspecified product. A note states that addition of H₂O occurs.

ch07/prob-7-58c.description: A condensed structural formula shows a five-carbon chain with a double bond between the second and third carbons and a methyl branch on the fourth carbon. No addition product is shown.

ch07/prob-7-58b.description: The drawing shows two fused six-membered carbon rings, with a double bond between the upper ring-junction carbon and the adjacent carbon in the right ring. It is presented as an alkene for a problem about HBr addition; no product is shown.

ch07/prob-7-57c.description: A six-membered ring with one double bond and a methyl group on the neighboring carbon is shown reacting with HBr; a question mark marks the unknown product.

ch07/prob-7-59a.description: A condensed structural formula shows an alkene, CH₃CH₂C(CH₃)=CHCH₃, with a methyl group attached to one of the double-bonded carbons. It is one of the starting structures in a problem asking for the major alcohol formed by acid-catalyzed addition of water.

ch07/prob-7-64a.description: Two skeletal structures are shown side by side: fucoserratene is a zigzag chain with three double bonds, and ectocarpene has a seven-membered ring with two double bonds and a side chain containing another double bond.

ch07/prob-7-59c.description: The image shows the condensed structure CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH=CH₂, a branched alkene with a terminal double bond. It is one of the starting alkenes in a problem asking for the major alcohol formed by acid-catalyzed addition of water.

ch07/prob-7-63.description: A skeletal structure labeled “Retin A (retinoic acid)” shows a substituted six-membered ring attached to a long chain with several double bonds and a terminal CO₂H group. The accompanying problem asks about E,Z double-bond isomers.

ch07/prob-7-68.description: An arrow points from a drawn isobutyl cation, with a positively charged CH₂ group beside a carbon bearing two methyl groups, to a drawn tert-butyl cation, with the positive charge on the central carbon. The figure presents the carbocation rearrangement posed in the problem without drawing a transition state.

ch07/prob-7-71.description: A reaction drawing shows benzene and CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl on the left, an arrow labeled AlCl₃, and a benzene ring bearing a CH(CH₃)₂ group on the right. It illustrates the product shown for this reaction without depicting the reaction steps.

ch08/p256.description: A generic alkene reacts with X–Y to form a product with X and Y attached to the two formerly double-bonded carbons. Opposing arrows label the forward change “Addition” and the reverse change “Elimination.”

ch07/prob-7-60a.description: A four-carbon chain is drawn with a CH₃ branch on the second carbon and a positive charge on the adjacent CH carbon. It is one of the carbocations in a problem asking for likely rearrangement products.

ch08/fig-8.1.description: A photo shows two people in camouflage uniforms and gas masks, one handling the other’s protective vest. The caption links bulletproof vests to Spectra fiber made from ultra-high-molecular-weight polyethylene.

ch07/prob-7-60b.description: A cyclobutane ring has a CH₃ group and a CH₂⁺ group attached to the same ring carbon. It is one of the carbocations presented for a rearrangement problem; no product is shown.

ch08/fig-8.2.description: A central generic alkene is surrounded by arrows pointing to structures labeled halohydrin, alcohol, alkane, 1,2-diol, carbonyl compound, cyclopropane, epoxide, halide, and 1,2-dihalide. The diagram illustrates different products obtainable from an alkene.

ch07/prob-7-66.description: A reaction scheme shows vinylcyclopropane reacting with H–Br, with pink curved arrows indicating movement of bonds and electrons. An unknown intermediate in brackets is followed by a step involving Br⁻ and an unknown product; the question marks leave both structures unspecified.

ch07/prob-7-64b.description: A substituted alkene bearing methyl and tert-butyl ester groups is shown reacting with CF₃CO₂H to give an alkene with the tert-butyl ester replaced by a carboxylic acid, plus H₂C=C(CH₃)₂. The two alkene drawings place the upper ester and lower carbonyl group in the same positions, illustrating the problem’s apparent change in double-bond stereochemistry.

ch08/p257b.description: A reaction diagram shows 1-methylcyclohexanol forming 1-methylcyclohexene (91%) and water under aqueous sulfuric acid in THF at 50 °C. A separate bracketed drawing shows the ring structure of tetrahydrofuran (THF), labeled as a common solvent.

ch08/p258a.description: The reaction diagram shows ethylene reacting with Cl₂ to form 1,2-dichloroethane (ethylene dichloride). The carbon–carbon double bond becomes a single bond, with one chlorine attached to each carbon.

ch08/p257c.description: A reaction diagram shows β-hydroxybutyryl ACP converting to trans-crotonyl ACP plus water, with the new carbon–carbon double bond highlighted in pink. It illustrates dehydration forming an alkene.

ch08/p257a.description: Bromocyclohexane is shown reacting with KOH in CH₃CH₂OH to give cyclohexene (81%), KBr, and H₂O. Pink highlights the Br and neighboring H removed and the double bond formed in this elimination reaction.

ch08/prob-8-2.description: The problem shows the drawn structure of 3-methyl-3-hexanol followed by a reaction arrow labeled H₂SO₄ and a question mark in place of the products. It asks how many alkene products, including E/Z isomers, could result from dehydration.

ch08/p259a.description: A reaction scheme shows cyclopentene reacting with bromine to form a bridged bromonium ion, followed by bromide attack from the open top side to give trans-1,2-dibromocyclopentane. A molecular model beneath the scheme illustrates how the bromonium bridge shields the bottom side from attack.

ch08/p258c.description: Cyclopentene reacts with Br–Br to give trans-1,2-dibromocyclopentane as the sole product; the bracketed cis-1,2-dibromocyclopentane is marked “not formed.” The drawings show the bromine atoms on opposite faces of the ring in the product.

ch08/p258b.description: A proposed mechanism shows ethene reacting with bromine to form a brominated carbocation and bromide ion, followed by bromide attack to give 1,2-dibromoethane. Curved arrows trace the electron movements, and “Possible mechanism?” appears on both sides.

ch08/p258d.description: A generic alkene reacts with Br₂; curved arrows show the double bond interacting with bromine as the Br–Br bond breaks. The products shown are a three-membered bromonium ion bridging the two carbons and a separate bromide ion.

ch08/p259c.description: A reaction scheme shows a chlorinated polyene treated sequentially with 2 Br⁺ and 2 Cl⁻ to form Halomon. Two of the three double bonds gain bromine and chlorine substituents, while the rightmost double bond remains.

ch08/p259b.description: A fluorinated, brominated carbon structure reacts with SbF₅ in liquid SO₂; curved arrows show fluoride removal and formation of a three-membered bromonium ion. The product is labeled as stable in SO₂ solution and is shown alongside SbF₆⁻.

ch08/p260.description: A generic alkene reacts with X₂ in H₂O to give a halohydrin with OH and X on adjacent carbons, plus HX. Wedge and dashed bonds show the product’s three-dimensional arrangement.

ch08/fig-8.3.description: A three-step mechanism shows an alkene reacting with Br₂ to form a bromonium ion, water opening the ring, and loss of a proton to give 3-bromo-2-butanol and H₃O⁺. Curved arrows mark electron movement, and wedges and dashes show the product’s spatial arrangement.

ch08/fig-8.4b.description: The figure shows ethylene reacting with water to form ethanol, with H₃PO₄ listed as a catalyst and 250 °C below the arrow. It illustrates hydration of an alkene to an alcohol.

ch08/p261a.description: A reaction scheme shows styrene treated with NBS in water and DMSO to form 2-bromo-1-phenylethanol (70%). The drawn product has OH on the carbon next to the phenyl ring and Br on the terminal carbon.

ch08/prob-8-6.description: A reaction arrow shows CH₃CH=CH₂ treated with Br₂ and H₂O to give CH₃CH(OH)CH₂Br, with OH on the middle carbon and Br on the terminal carbon.

ch08/fig-8.4a.description: A three-step mechanism shows 2-methylpropene reacting with hydronium to form a carbocation, water adding to give a protonated alcohol, and deprotonation yielding 2-methyl-2-propanol while regenerating hydronium. Curved arrows trace electron movement, and a colored orbital marks the carbocation.

ch08/p263b.description: A reaction scheme shows 1-methylcyclopentene treated first with Hg(OAc)₂ in H₂O/THF and then with NaBH₄, producing 1-methylcyclopentanol (92%). The drawing shows OH added to the ring carbon bearing the methyl group.

ch08/p263a.description: The reaction scheme shows fumarate reacting with H₂O under fumarase at pH 7.4 to form a bracketed anion intermediate bearing OH, followed by protonation with HA to give malate. The structures depict addition of OH and H across the original double bond.

ch08/p261b.description: A reaction arrow shows an alkene bearing a phenyl group and CH₂OH reacting with H₂O₂ and Br⁻ at pH 3 in the presence of bromoperoxidase. In the product, OH and Br have added to opposite carbons of the former double bond, illustrating halohydrin formation.

ch08/prob-8-7.description: The figure shows the condensed structure CH₃C(CH₃)=CHCH₂CH₃, with a methyl group attached to one carbon of the double bond. It is presented as an alkene for an oxymercuration–demercuration product-prediction problem; no product is drawn.

ch08/fig-8.5.description: A three-step scheme shows 1-methylcyclopentene reacting with Hg(OAc)₂ to form a bridged mercurinium ion, followed by H₂O to form an organomercury compound and NaBH₄ to give 1-methylcyclopentanol (92% yield). The OH group appears on the methyl-substituted carbon, illustrating the depicted regiochemistry.

ch08/p264b.description: A model marked “Electrophilic” and an orbital sketch accompany a Lewis acid–base reaction: a curved arrow shows the oxygen lone pair of THF donating to borane, forming a BH₃–THF complex with O⁺ and B⁻ indicated.

ch08/prob-8-8a.description: The image shows the condensed structure of 2-methylhexan-2-ol, with an OH group and a methyl group attached to the second carbon of a six-carbon chain. It is presented as an alcohol for the reader to consider, with no alkene drawn.

ch08/prob-8-8b.description: A cyclohexane ring is bonded to a carbon bearing an OH group and a terminal methyl group. It is shown as an alcohol in a problem asking which alkene could have been used to prepare it.

ch08/p264c.description: The reaction scheme shows three cyclohexene molecules reacting with BH₃ in THF to form tricyclohexylborane, followed by oxidation with H₂O₂, H₂O, and NaOH to give three cyclohexanol molecules (87%) and B(OH)₃. It illustrates the two-step hydroboration–oxidation conversion of an alkene to an alcohol.

ch08/p265.description: A reaction scheme shows 1-methylcyclopentene treated with BH₃ in THF to form a bracketed organoborane intermediate, then with H₂O₂ and OH⁻ to give trans-2-methylcyclopentanol (85% yield). Wedge and dashed bonds depict the stereochemistry of the intermediate and product.

ch08/we-8.1.description: Two reaction paths start from 2-methyl-2-pentene: (a) BH₃ followed by H₂O₂ and OH⁻ gives the drawn 2-methyl-3-pentanol, while (b) Hg(OAc)₂ and H₂O followed by NaBH₄ gives the drawn 2-methyl-2-pentanol. The products show the OH group attached at different positions.

ch08/p264a.description: A reaction sequence shows 2-methyl-2-pentene treated with BH₃ in THF to form a bracketed organoborane intermediate, then treated with H₂O₂ and OH⁻ to yield 2-methyl-3-pentanol. The drawings show H and BH₂ added across the double bond, with OH replacing BH₂ in the product.

ch08/we-8.2a.description: A question mark and arrow point to a six-carbon alcohol structure bearing an OH group and a methyl branch. The worked example asks how to prepare this alcohol, without showing a starting material.

ch08/fig-8.6.description: The scheme shows BH₃ adding to 1-methylcyclopentene through two alternative bracketed transition states; the crowded pathway is marked “Not formed.” The favored pathway places boron on the less crowded carbon, and a subsequent arrow labeled H₂O₂, OH⁻ leads to trans-2-methylcyclopentanol.

ch08/prob-8-9a.description: The image shows the condensed structure CH₃C(CH₃)=CHCH₂CH₃, an alkene with a methyl branch on one carbon of the double bond. It is presented as a starting structure in a hydroboration–oxidation product problem; no product is shown.

ch08/we-8.2b.description: Two possible alkene structures, 4-methyl-2-hexene and 3-methyl-3-hexene, are shown side by side. Pink “Add –OH here” arrows point to a double-bond carbon in each structure.

ch08/we-8.2c.description: The reaction shows 3-methyl-3-hexene treated with BH₃ in THF, then H₂O₂ and OH⁻, giving an alcohol with OH on the less substituted carbon of the former double bond.

ch08/prob-8-10a.description: A condensed structural formula shows a four-carbon chain ending in an OH group, with a CH₃ branch on the third carbon from the OH end. It is one of the alcohol structures in a problem about hydroboration–oxidation.

ch08/prob-8-10b.description: A condensed structural formula shows a four-carbon chain with a methyl group attached to one middle carbon and an OH group attached to the other. It is one alcohol presented in a problem asking which alkenes could produce it by hydroboration–oxidation.

ch08/prob-8-10c.description: A six-membered saturated ring bears a CH₂OH substituent, depicting one alcohol in a problem about identifying possible alkene starting materials for hydroboration–oxidation.

ch08/prob-8-9b.description: A cyclohexane ring has an exocyclic double bond to a carbon bearing a CH₃ group. It is shown as an alkene in a hydroboration–oxidation product-prediction problem; no product is drawn.

ch08/p267a.description: A generic alkene reacts with H₂ over a catalyst to form an alkane. The two newly added hydrogens are highlighted in pink.

ch08/fig-8.7.description: A four-step ball-and-stick mechanism shows hydrogen and an alkene binding to a metal catalyst surface, followed by transfer of the two hydrogen atoms and release of the alkane. Both hydrogens are added from the same face of the alkene, illustrating syn hydrogenation.
labels_in_image: H₂ and alkene bound to catalyst

ch08/fig-8.9.description: The top sequence shows trans-Crotonyl ACP reacting with NADPH to form a bracketed anion intermediate, then reacting with HA to give Butyryl ACP; colored hydrogens mark the two additions across the former double bond. Below, a detailed NADPH structure has an arrow pointing to the hydrogen delivered in the first step.

ch08/p269a.description: The figure shows α-pinene reacting with H₂ over Pd/C to give a saturated bicyclic product, alongside a bracketed stereoisomer marked “Not formed.” A green highlight and arrow indicate that a methyl group blocks the top side of the double bond.
labels_in_image: Top side of double bond blocked by methyl group

ch08/prob-8-12a.description: The drawing shows the alkene CH₃C(CH₃)=CHCH₂CH₃, with two methyl groups attached to one carbon of the double bond. It is presented as a reactant in a catalytic hydrogenation problem; no product is shown.

ch08/p269b.description: Three reaction schemes show alkenes hydrogenated with H₂ and Pd/C in ethanol: cyclohex-2-enone becomes cyclohexanone, methyl 3-phenylpropenoate becomes methyl 3-phenylpropanoate, and cyclohexylideneacetonitrile becomes cyclohexylacetonitrile. The annotations point out that the ketone, aromatic ring, and nitrile, respectively, are not reduced.

ch08/fig-8.8.description: A generic vegetable-oil structure is shown alongside a fatty-acid chain with two cis double bonds. An arrow labeled “2 H₂, Pd/C” leads to a saturated chain, while a bracketed alternative shows a chain retaining one trans double bond.
labels_in_image: A polyunsaturated fatty acid in vegetable oil
A saturated fatty acid in margarine

ch08/p267b.description: An arrow shows 1,2-dimethylcyclohexene reacting with H₂ and PtO₂ in CH₃CO₂H solvent to give cis-1,2-dimethylcyclohexane (82%). The product drawing shows both newly added hydrogens on the same face of the ring, illustrating syn hydrogenation.

ch08/prob-8-12b.description: A five-membered ring has a double bond along its bottom edge and two CH₃ groups attached to the same ring carbon. It is shown as an alkene in a catalytic hydrogenation problem; no product is drawn.

ch08/p271a.description: The reaction diagram shows cycloheptene reacting with meta-chloroperoxybenzoic acid in CH₂Cl₂ solvent to give 1,2-epoxycycloheptane and meta-chlorobenzoic acid. The epoxide is drawn as a three-membered ring containing oxygen, with dashed C–H bonds at its two carbon atoms.

ch08/p271d.description: A generic alkene is shown undergoing epoxidation to form a three-membered epoxide ring, followed by H₃O⁺ treatment to give a 1,2-diol. Wedge and dashed bonds indicate the spatial arrangement of substituents in the epoxide and product.

ch08/p271b.description: A generic alkene reacts with a peroxyacid to form an epoxide and an acid. Curved arrows show the one-step transfer of the peroxyacid’s outer oxygen to the double bond.

ch08/prob-8-12c.description: A cyclohexene ring bearing a tert-butyl group next to the double bond is shown in two equivalent drawings: a flat ring and a puckered conformation with the hydrogen and tert-butyl group marked. It is one of the alkenes in a catalytic hydrogenation problem; no product is shown.

ch08/p271c.description: Cyclohexene reacts with Cl₂ and H₂O to form trans-2-chlorocyclohexanol, which is treated with NaOH in H₂O to yield 1,2-epoxycyclohexane (73%), H₂O, and NaCl. Curved arrows show base removing the hydroxyl proton, ring closure, and chloride departure.

ch08/p272b.description: A reaction scheme shows 1,2-dimethylcyclopentene treated with OsO₄ in pyridine to form a bracketed cyclic osmate intermediate. Treatment with NaHSO₃ and H₂O gives cis-1,2-dimethyl-1,2-cyclopentanediol (87%), with both OH groups drawn on the same face of the ring.

ch08/p272a.description: The upper mechanism uses curved arrows to show aqueous acid opening a protonated 1,2-epoxycyclohexane ring to form trans-1,2-cyclohexanediol (86%). A boxed comparison below shows cyclohexene reacting with bromine through a bridged intermediate to form trans-1,2-dibromocyclohexane.

ch08/prob-8-14b.description: The problem shows a five-carbon chain with OH groups on adjacent carbons and an additional CH₃ group attached to the carbon bearing the right-hand OH group. No stereochemistry is indicated.

ch08/prob-8-14a.description: A cyclohexane ring has OH groups on adjacent carbons, both drawn on solid wedges. A hydrogen and a CH₃ group on those carbons are drawn on dashed bonds, showing their relative stereochemistry.

ch08/prob-8-14c.description: The problem shows HOCH₂–CH(OH)–CH(OH)–CH₂OH, a four-carbon chain with an OH group on every carbon. No stereochemistry is indicated.

ch08/prob-8-11.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a five-membered cycloalkene ring with two methyl substituents. It is the starting structure for a problem asking the reader to draw the two alcohols formed after hydroboration and oxidation; the products are not shown.

ch08/p273a.description: A reaction scheme shows 1-phenylcyclohexene treated with catalytic OsO₄ in acetone and water, forming a bracketed osmate intermediate. N-Methylmorpholine N-oxide then gives cis-1-phenyl-1,2-cyclohexanediol (93%), with OsO₄ regenerated and N-methylmorpholine shown as a byproduct.

ch08/p274b.description: A reaction scheme shows 3,7-Dimethyl-1-octene treated with KMnO₄ and H₃O⁺, giving 2,6-Dimethylheptanoic acid (45%) and CO₂. It illustrates cleavage of a terminal alkene into a carboxylic acid and carbon dioxide.

ch08/p273b.description: The diagram shows oxygen converted to ozone by electric discharge, then a four-methyl-substituted alkene reacting with ozone to form a molozonide and an ozonide. Treatment with Zn in acetic acid and water gives two carbonyl molecules drawn as acetone.

ch08/p274a.description: Two examples show alkene double bonds cleaved by O₃ followed by Zn, H₃O⁺: isopropylidenecyclohexane gives cyclohexanone and acetone (84%), while methyl 9-octadecenoate gives nonanal and methyl 9-oxononanoate (78%). The figure contrasts the carbonyl products formed from a tetrasubstituted versus a disubstituted alkene.

ch08/p275.description: A generic alkene reacts with a carbene bearing two R groups to form a cyclopropane ring, with both R groups on the newly added ring carbon. The drawing shows the alkene’s double bond becoming two bonds to that carbon.

ch08/we-8.3a.description: A question mark stands for an unknown starting alkene; an arrow labeled “1. O₃” and “2. Zn, acetic acid” points to cyclopentanone and propanal. The worked-example diagram asks which alkene gives these products under the shown conditions.

ch08/fig-8.10.description: A two-step mechanism shows hydroxide removing a hydrogen from chloroform to form the trichloromethanide anion and water; the anion then loses chloride to form dichlorocarbene. Pink curved arrows mark electron movement, and numbered arrows separate the steps.

ch08/p274c.description: Two reaction schemes show 1,2-diols treated with HIO₄ in H₂O/THF, passing through bracketed cyclic periodate intermediates. Cleavage opens the six-membered ring to form 6-oxoheptanal (86%) in the first example and produces two cyclopentanone molecules (81%) in the second.

ch08/we-8.3b.description: The diagram shows cyclopentanone and propanal on the left, with their carbonyl oxygens highlighted by a dashed pink oval, and a cyclopentane ring bearing an exocyclic CHCH₂CH₃ double bond on the right. A left-pointing arrow illustrates reversing alkene cleavage by removing the oxygens and joining the two carbonyl carbons.

ch08/p278a.description: A chair-form glucose molecule is shown pointing to a cellulose chain of repeating glucose rings joined by oxygen links. Pink highlights mark the connecting oxygens and open ends of the chain.

ch08/fig-8.11.description: The figure compares dichlorocarbene with an sp²-hybridized carbocation using orbital drawings and electrostatic potential maps. Arrows mark their vacant p orbitals and the lone pair in dichlorocarbene.

ch08/prob-8-17a.description: A reaction problem shows methylenecyclohexane plus CHCl₃, with KOH over the arrow and a question mark in place of the product. The drawing asks for the product without showing its structure.

ch08/p278d.description: A structural drawing shows ethylene, a carbon–carbon double bond with four hydrogens, pointing to a long polyethylene chain of repeating carbon units. Parentheses mark a repeat unit, and pink zigzags indicate that the chain continues at both ends.

ch08/p277a.description: Two reaction schemes show cis-2-pentene and cyclohexene each reacting with CHCl₃ under KOH to form a cyclopropane ring bearing two chlorine atoms, alongside KCl. Wedge and dashed bonds depict the products’ three-dimensional arrangement.

ch08/p279a.description: A reaction scheme shows benzoyl peroxide heated to form two benzoyloxy radicals, which then give phenyl radicals and carbon dioxide. Curved arrows also show a phenyl radical adding to ethylene to form a carbon radical.

ch08/prob-8-17b.description: A branched six-carbon alkene, CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH=CHCH₃, is shown reacting with CH₂I₂ under Zn(Cu); the arrow points to a question mark rather than a drawn product.

ch08/p277b.description: The figure shows diiodomethane reacting with Zn(Cu) to form (iodomethyl)zinc iodide, depicted alongside a bracketed “:CH₂” carbene representation. Below, cyclohexene reacts with diiodomethane under Zn(Cu) in ether to give bicyclo[4.1.0]heptane (92%) and ZnI₂, illustrating cyclopropane-ring formation.

ch08/p278c.description: A diagram shows a nucleotide with a phosphate group, a sugar ring, and a blue, generically drawn base, followed by an arrow to a nucleic acid chain in which sugar rings are linked through phosphate groups. Pink marks indicate continuing bonds, and H (OH) on the sugars shows the alternatives printed in the figure.

ch08/p278b.description: A generic amino acid bearing an R group is shown leading by an arrow to a protein chain. The protein drawing shows amino acid units joined in a repeating backbone, with parentheses around one unit and zigzag marks indicating the chain continues.

ch08/p279c.description: Two reaction arrows show propylene forming polypropylene and styrene forming polystyrene. Each product is drawn as a bracketed carbon chain with methyl or phenyl groups attached to alternating backbone carbons.

ch08/we-8.4.description: The figure shows a section of a poly(vinyl chloride) chain in parentheses, with three –CH₂–CH(Cl)– units along a continuous backbone. Chlorine is attached above each CH group.

ch08/p279b.description: A phenyl-substituted carbon radical adds to ethylene, forming a longer chain with the radical at its end. An arrow labeled “Repeat many times” shows the chain extending to a repeating-unit structure while retaining the terminal radical.

ch08/p281.description: Two schemes compare additions to a generic alkene: electrophilic addition forms a carbocation that reacts with Nu⁻ and stops, while radical addition forms a carbon radical that adds to another alkene and continues. The drawings use generic E and Rad groups rather than named compounds.
labels_in_image: Electrophilic addition (Intermediate is quenched, so reaction stops.)
Radical addition (Intermediate is not quenched, so reaction does not stop.)

ch08/fig-8.12.description: A six-step pathway shows arachidonic acid converting through radical intermediates into prostaglandin H₂, with curved arrows, numbered steps, and highlighted oxygen additions and ring formation. The caption identifies steps 2 and 5 as radical additions to O₂ and steps 3 and 4 as radical additions to carbon–carbon double bonds.

ch08/prob-8-18b.description: A polymer chain is drawn in parentheses with six single-bonded CH groups, each bearing a Cl substituent. The figure is part of a problem asking for the monomer that would form this repeating structure.

ch08/p283a.description: A reaction diagram shows achiral cis-aconitate reacting with water in the presence of aconitase to form (2R,3S)-isocitrate. The product’s H and OH bonds are drawn with wedges and dashes to show its stereochemistry.

ch08/fig-8.13.description: Water approaches the achiral sec-butyl cation from either face, forming two transition states shown on opposite sides of a mirror plane with dotted, partially formed C···O bonds. The paths lead to (S)-2-butanol and (R)-2-butanol, each labeled 50%.

ch08/p284.description: The figure shows (R)-4-methyl-1-hexene reacting with H₂O under acid catalysis to give 4-methyl-2-hexanol. Pink asterisks mark the starting alkene’s chirality center and the product’s two chirality centers.

ch08/p283b.description: A reaction diagram shows cis-aconitate, with its alkene faces marked Re and Si, reacting with H₂O in the presence of aconitase to form (2R,3S)-isocitrate. The stereochemical labels illustrate addition at the Re face of the double bond.

ch08/table-8.1.description: This table excerpt shows the structure of methyl methacrylate, H₂C=C(CH₃)CO₂CH₃, beside text listing Plexiglas and Lucite and uses such as paint, sheets, and moldings.

ch08/fig-8.15.description: A close-up photograph shows green California bay laurel leaves surrounding two small, dark, wrinkled fruits. The caption links the leaves’ fragrance primarily to myrcene, a simple terpene.

ch08/p282.description: The reaction shows achiral 1-butene treated with H₂O and an acid catalyst, yielding equal amounts of (S)-2-butanol and (R)-2-butanol. Wedge-and-dash bonds show the opposite configurations of the two products.

ch08/prob-8-18a.description: A bracketed polymer segment shows three –CH₂–CH(OCH₃)– units, with a methoxy group attached to every other backbone carbon. It illustrates a polymer structure in a problem asking for the corresponding monomer.

ch08/fig-8.14.description: The diagram shows acid-catalyzed addition of water to a chiral alkene through a chiral carbocation, with water approaching from the top or bottom. The two pathways lead to the labeled (2S,4R) and (2R,4R) alcohol products.

ch08/p285.description: Four labeled skeletal structures compare the open-chain terpene myrcene, the bicyclic α-pinene, the ring-containing humulene, and the bicyclic β-santalene. Their labels give associated oils: bay, turpentine, hops, and sandalwood oil, respectively.

ch08/p279d.description: Curved arrows show a phenyl radical adding to the terminal carbon of propene, giving Ph–CH₂–CH·–CH₃, labeled “Secondary radical.” A bracketed alternative, Ph–CH(CH₃)–CH₂·, is labeled “Primary radical (Not formed).”

ch08/p286b.description: A skeletal structure labeled “Lanosterol (a triterpene, C₃₀)” shows four fused rings, a hydroxyl group, methyl groups, and an alkene-containing side chain. The nearby text identifies lanosterol as a precursor of steroid hormones.

ch08/p286c.description: Two side-by-side skeletal structures, labeled isopentenyl diphosphate and dimethylallyl diphosphate, each show a branched five-carbon chain attached to a diphosphate group. Their carbon–carbon double bonds appear at different positions.

ch08/p288b.description: A generic alkene reacts with X₂ in CH₂Cl₂ to give a product bearing one X on each formerly double-bonded carbon. Solid and dashed wedges show the two halogens added on opposite faces (anti addition).

ch08/p286a.description: A numbered, color-marked drawing of two isoprene units identifies a head and tail; an arrow points to the skeletal structure labeled Myrcene. The figure illustrates how the units connect in myrcene.

ch08/p288a.description: A generic alkene reacts with HX in ether: the double bond becomes a single bond, with H added to one carbon and X to the other. The drawing illustrates addition of a hydrogen halide across an alkene.

ch08/p288f.description: A generic alkene reacts with H₂ over Pd/C or PtO₂ to form a single-bonded product with one new hydrogen on each carbon. Both hydrogens are drawn on the same side, illustrating syn addition.

ch08/p288h.description: A generic alkene reacts with OsO₄ followed by NaHSO₃ and H₂O, or with OsO₄ and NMO, to give a product with an OH group on each formerly double-bonded carbon. The wedges show both OH groups added on the same side.

ch08/p288e.description: A generic substituted alkene reacts with BH₃ in THF, followed by H₂O₂ and OH⁻, to give a structure with H and OH added to adjacent carbons. The drawing shows their syn addition with wedge-and-dash bonds.

ch08/p288i.description: A generic alkene reacts with CHCl₃ in the presence of KOH to form a cyclopropane ring bearing two chlorine atoms on the newly added carbon. Dashed and solid wedge bonds show the substituents’ orientations on the starting alkene and product.

ch08/p288d.description: A substituted alkene is converted to an alcohol in two steps: Hg(OAc)₂ and H₂O/THF, followed by NaBH₄. The product shows HO and H added across the former double bond, illustrating oxymercuration–demercuration.

ch08/p288g.description: A generic alkene reacts with a peroxyacid to form a three-membered epoxide ring. The wedge and dashed bonds show that the substituents retain their relative arrangement.

ch08/p289a.description: A generic epoxide reacts with H₃O⁺ to give a diol with OH groups on adjacent carbons. Wedge and dashed bonds show the two OH groups on opposite sides (anti stereochemistry).

ch08/p288c.description: A generic alkene reacts with X₂ and H₂O to form a product bearing X and OH on adjacent carbons, plus HX. Dashed and solid wedges depict the product’s stereochemistry.

ch08/p288j.description: A generic alkene reacts with CH₂I₂ in the presence of Zn(Cu) and ether to form a three-membered carbon ring bearing a new CH₂ group. The wedge and dashed bonds show that the alkene’s substituent orientations are retained in the cyclopropane product.

ch08/p289b.description: A generic alkene with two R groups on each double-bond carbon reacts with O₃, followed by Zn/H₃O⁺, to form two separate carbonyl compounds. The scheme illustrates cleavage of the carbon–carbon double bond.

ch08/p289d.description: A vicinal diol with two methyl groups on each hydroxyl-bearing carbon reacts with HIO₄ in water, cleaving the central C–C bond to form two acetone molecules. The scheme illustrates cleavage of a 1,2-diol into carbonyl compounds.

ch08/p289c.description: Two generic alkenes react with KMnO₄ and H₃O⁺: the fully R-substituted alkene splits into two carbonyl compounds, while the alkene with a terminal CH₂ group yields an R-substituted carboxylic acid and CO₂. The figure illustrates two product patterns for oxidative alkene cleavage.

ch08/prob-8-23a.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a branched alcohol with a red oxygen and white hydrogen forming an OH group on the central carbon. The surrounding text asks for an alkene that would yield this alcohol by hydration.

ch08/prob-8-23b.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a five-membered carbon ring with an OH group on one ring carbon and two methyl groups attached to another. The red sphere represents oxygen; the problem asks which alkene could yield this alcohol on hydration.

ch08/prob-8-27a.description: A four-membered ring has a double bond along one edge and a methyl group attached to one of the double-bond carbons. Only this starting structure is shown; no reaction or product appears in the crop.

ch08/prob-8-24.description: A ball-and-stick molecular model shows a branched structure with dark and light spheres; a pink arrow points to a bond near the lower-right dark sphere. The nearby problem text asks which alkene could have produced the depicted 1,2-diol.

ch08/prob-8-27c.description: A six-membered ring alkene with a methyl group on one of the double-bonded carbons reacts with CF₃CO₃H; an arrow points to a question mark for the unknown product.

ch08/prob-8-22a.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a branched hydrocarbon with one carbon–carbon double bond near the left end. The figure presents an alkene to be named and used to predict reaction products; no products are shown.

ch08/prob-8-27b.description: A line-angle structure shows a benzene ring bonded to a terminal carbon–carbon double bond. It depicts styrene as a structure in a reaction problem, with no reagents or products shown in this crop.

ch08/prob-8-26b.description: A benzene ring attached to a terminal alkene is shown reacting with Cl₂; the product is left as a question mark. The figure asks for the reaction product rather than depicting it.

ch08/prob-8-25.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a methyl-substituted cyclohexane ring with hydroxyl groups on two adjacent ring carbons. Carbon atoms are gray, hydrogen atoms white, and oxygen atoms red.

ch08/prob-8-26a.description: A cyclohexene ring with a methyl group on each alkene carbon is shown reacting with Br₂; the product is left as a question mark. The figure asks for a reaction product rather than showing one.

ch08/prob-8-29a.description: The problem shows a cyclopentane ring with an epoxide bridging adjacent carbons; dashed bonds to oxygen and wedged bonds to the two hydrogens indicate stereochemistry. An arrow labeled H₃O⁺ points to a question mark for the unspecified product.

ch08/prob-8-29b.description: A three-membered epoxide ring has a methyl group on each carbon shown with a solid wedge and a hydrogen on each shown with a dashed bond. An arrow labeled H₃O⁺ points to a question mark, asking for the acid-catalyzed ring-opening product.

ch08/prob-8-27d.description: A cis-2-butene structure and a benzene ring bearing a CO₃H group are shown as reactants, with an arrow pointing to a question mark in place of the product. The problem asks for the product and mechanism of this peroxyacid reaction.

ch08/prob-8-30c.description: A skeletal alkene with a stereogenic carbon bearing a wedged CH₃ group and a dashed H is shown reacting under “1. O₃; 2. Zn, H₃O⁺” conditions. The product is left as a question mark.

ch08/prob-8-30a.description: A cyclohexane ring with an exocyclic CH₂ double bond and an opposite CH₃ substituent shown on a dashed bond (with H on a solid wedge) reacts with H₂ over Pd/C. The product is left as a question mark for the problem.

ch08/prob-8-34.description: A reaction arrow labeled “Br+” and “Bromo-peroxidase” connects the drawn structure of laurediol to prelaureatin. The product has a new oxygen-containing ring and a Br substituent, while the OH group and terminal alkyne remain drawn.

ch08/prob-8-32.description: The figure shows 1-butene reacting with iodine azide (I–N=N=N) to form a single product, CH₃CH₂CH(N=N=N)CH₂I. The product has the nitrogen chain attached to one carbon of the former double bond and iodine attached to the adjacent terminal carbon.

ch08/prob-8-38.description: A reaction diagram shows 4-penten-1-ol treated with Br₂ and H₂O to give a five-membered cyclic ether bearing a CH₂Br substituent, labeled 2-(bromomethyl)tetrahydrofuran.

ch08/prob-8-22b.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a five-carbon ring with one carbon–carbon double bond and two methyl groups attached to the same ring carbon. It depicts 3,3-dimethylcyclopentene as one of the alkenes in the naming problem.

ch08/prob-8-35.description: A reaction scheme shows sodium trichloroacetate heated to 70 °C, yielding a carbon bearing two chlorines and a lone pair, along with CO₂ and NaCl. It illustrates the formation of dichlorocarbene from the trichloroacetate salt.

ch08/prob-8-37.description: The figure shows a methyl ester–substituted cyclic compound with multiple double bonds reacting with Hg(OAc)₂ to form a fused bicyclic product bearing an AcO–Hg group. It illustrates a proposed cyclization transformation without showing mechanism steps.

ch08/prob-8-29c.description: A substituted epoxide is drawn with a methyl group on one ring carbon and an isopropyl group on the other; wedge and dashed bonds show its three-dimensional arrangement. An arrow labeled H₃O⁺ points to a question mark for the product.

ch08/prob-8-41d.description: An unknown starting material, marked with a question mark, reacts with HCl to give a seven-carbon chain bearing chlorine on carbon 2 and a methyl group on carbon 3. The figure asks for the missing reactant rather than showing it.

ch08/prob-8-30b.description: A trans-2,3-dimethyloxirane ring is shown with wedge-and-dash bonds indicating its stereochemistry. An arrow labeled H₃O⁺ points to a question mark for the unspecified product.

ch08/prob-8-392.description: The diagram shows 2-methyl-2-pentene undergoing hydroboration followed by oxidation: the 25 °C route leads to 2-methyl-3-pentanol, while the 160 °C route leads to 4-methyl-1-pentanol. It compares the products formed under the two reaction temperatures.

ch08/prob-8-41e.description: A question mark stands in for an unknown starting structure, followed by a reaction arrow labeled “1. Hg(OAc)₂, H₂O” and “2. NaBH₄.” The structure on the right is CH₃CH₂CH₂CH(OH)CH₃ (2-pentanol); the problem asks for the starting structure, rather than showing it.

ch08/prob-8-42b.description: A cyclohexene ring is shown reacting with KMnO₄ followed by H₃O⁺; a question mark marks the unspecified product.

ch08/prob-8-41c.description: A pink question mark and Br₂ appear to the left of a reaction arrow; the product is drawn as CH₃–CH(Br)–CH(Br)–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–CH₃. The diagram presents a reaction with the starting structure left unspecified.

ch08/prob-8-46.description: A cholesterol structure with an OH group, one ring double bond, and an alkyl side chain is shown beside five separate reaction arrows labeled with reagents. The arrows lead to unknown products A? through E?, making this a set of reaction-product questions rather than showing the products.

ch08/prob-8-40.description: A benzene ring bearing a vinyl group (styrene) is shown beside six reaction arrows labeled (a)–(f), each ending in a question mark. The arrows specify different reagents and ask for the corresponding products without showing them.

ch08/prob-8-45.description: Two reaction schemes show cis-CH₃CH=CHCH₃ and trans-CH₃CH=CHCH₃ separately treated with CH₂I₂ and Zn(Cu). Each arrow ends in a question mark rather than a drawn product.

ch08/prob-8-42d.description: A six-membered ring with a double bond and a CH₃ group on one of the double-bond carbons is shown reacting with 1. Hg(OAc)₂, H₂O and then 2. NaBH₄. The product is left as a question mark.

ch08/prob-8-41f.description: A question mark marks the unspecified starting material; an arrow labeled CH₂I₂, Zn/Cu leads to a product drawn as a cyclohexane and a cyclopropane sharing one carbon. The figure asks for the missing reactant rather than showing it.

ch08/prob-8-41a.description: A question mark represents an unknown alkene undergoing a reaction with H₂/Pd to give the displayed product, CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃. The diagram asks for a possible starting structure rather than showing one.

ch08/prob-8-41b.description: An unknown starting alkene, marked with a question mark, is shown reacting with H₂/Pd to form a cyclohexane ring bearing two methyl groups on the same carbon. The drawing asks for the starting structure without showing it.

ch08/prob-8-48b.description: A five-membered ring with a double bond is shown transforming into a five-membered ring bearing an OH group. A question mark above the arrow asks for the reagents; the drawing does not supply them.

ch08/prob-8-50a.description: The figure shows cyclohexanone and acetone side by side, separated by a plus sign. No reaction arrow or product is shown.

ch08/prob-8-48c.description: A problem diagram shows cyclopentene on the left and, after an arrow marked with a question mark, a cyclopentane ring fused to a cyclopropane whose outer carbon bears two chlorine atoms. Dashed bonds show hydrogens on the two shared ring carbons.

ch08/prob-8-48d.description: A reaction arrow marked with a question mark connects 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol to 1-methylcyclohexene. The figure asks for the missing conditions without showing them.

ch08/prob-8-50b.description: A condensed structural formula shows CH₃CH₂C(=O)CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CO₂H: a carbon chain with a ketone group and a terminal carboxylic acid group.

ch08/prob-8-48a.description: A reaction arrow marked with a question mark shows cyclopentene being converted to a cyclopentane ring with OH groups on adjacent carbons. Both OH bonds are drawn as solid wedges, and the corresponding H bonds as dashed lines; the figure asks for the missing reagents.

ch08/prob-8-47.description: A reaction diagram shows 1-methoxycyclohexene treated with HCl to give 1-chloro-1-methoxycyclohexane, with chlorine and methoxy attached to the same ring carbon.

ch08/prob-8-48f.description: A reaction diagram shows 2-methylpropene converting to 2-methylpropan-1-ol, with a question mark above the arrow indicating unspecified reagents or conditions.

ch08/prob-8-51a.description: A reaction arrow labeled HI connects the drawn alkene CH₃C(CH₃)=CHCH₃ to CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(I)CH₃. The product drawing shows iodine attached to one carbon of the former double bond.

ch08/prob-8-54.description: The figure shows N-vinylpyrrolidone as a five-membered ring containing nitrogen and a carbonyl group, with a CH=CH₂ group attached to the nitrogen. It is the monomer named in the accompanying polymer-drawing problem.

ch08/prob-8-51b.description: A reaction diagram shows a cyclopentene ring treated with 1. OsO₄ and 2. NaHSO₃, followed by a cyclopentane ring bearing OH and H groups on adjacent carbons. Solid wedges and dashed bonds indicate the groups’ orientations in the drawn product.

ch08/prob-8-53.description: The figure shows the structural formula of methyl methacrylate, H₂C=C(CH₃)C(=O)OCH₃, alongside its name. It accompanies a problem asking for a representative segment of Plexiglas made by polymerizing this molecule.

ch08/prob-8-52a.description: A cyclohexane ring has a methyl group and a hydroxyl group on adjacent carbons. Both groups are shown on solid wedges, while the hydrogens on those carbons are on dashed bonds.

ch08/prob-8-52b.description: A cyclohexane ring has an OH group and a CH₃ group attached to the same carbon; the adjacent ring carbon has two explicitly drawn hydrogens. Solid wedges and dashed bonds show the substituents’ orientations.

ch08/prob-8-58.description: Two isomeric cyclohexadienes are shown side by side: the left ring has double bonds separated by one single bond, while the right ring has double bonds on opposite sides. The problem asks how oxidative cleavage could distinguish them.

ch08/prob-8-55.description: The figure shows a bracketed segment of Saran with a zigzag carbon backbone and a repeating sequence of CH₂, CCl₂, CH₂, and CHCl groups. It illustrates the copolymer structure used in the problem asking which monomers formed it.

ch08/prob-8-60.description: The figure shows the structural formula OHC–CH₂–CH₂–CHO, labeled “Butanedial.” It is the ozonolysis product specified in the problem.

ch09/fig-9.1.description: A white-haired conductor gestures toward a seated musical group playing guitar and saxophones. The photo illustrates the caption’s comparison of synthesizing complex organic compounds to conducting musicians in tune.

ch08/prob-8-65.description: The figure shows the two stated ozonolysis products of α-terpinene as structural formulas: glyoxal on the left and 6-methyl-2,5-heptanedione on the right.

ch08/prob-8-52c.description: The cropped drawing shows the condensed structure CH₃CH₂CH₂CH(OH)CH₃, with the OH group drawn above the second carbon from the right. It is one of the alcohol choices in a problem about hydroboration–oxidation.

ch08/prob-8-52d.description: The image shows a condensed alcohol structure, (CH₃)₂CH–C(OH)(CH₃)₂, with the OH group drawn above the central carbon.

ch08/prob-8-51c.description: The figure shows a six-membered ring with two double bonds reacting under “1. O₃; 2. Zn” to give an open-chain structure with one double bond and a CHO group at each end.

ch08/prob-8-59.description: A five-membered ring with a carbonyl group attached at one ring carbon is shown and labeled “Cyclopentanone.”

ch08/prob-8-51d.description: A reaction diagram shows a methyl-substituted cyclohexene treated with 1. BH₃ and 2. H₂O₂, OH⁻, giving a cyclohexanol with OH on the carbon adjacent to the methyl group. In the product, the methyl and OH bonds are solid wedges, while the two newly shown C–H bonds are dashed.

ch09/prob-9-1b.description: A terminal alkyne, HC≡C–, is bonded to a carbon bearing three CH₃ groups. The drawing is one of the structures in a problem asking the reader to name alkynes.

ch09/prob-9-1c.description: A condensed structural formula shows a carbon chain with a central C≡C triple bond and two CH₃ branches attached to the same carbon on one side of it. It is presented as an alkyne to be named.

ch08/prob-8-67.description: Two HBr addition reactions are shown: a methyl-substituted cyclohexene leads to two brominated ring positions, each marked “cis, trans.” A bromine-substituted cyclohexene leads to one drawn product with adjacent bromines on opposite wedge and dashed bonds.

ch09/prob-9-1a.description: A condensed structural formula shows a carbon chain with a central carbon–carbon triple bond and a methyl group attached to the chain on each side of the triple bond.

ch08/prob-8-66.description: Two bridged-ring structures are shown side by side, labeled A (cis diol) and B (trans diol). Both have hydroxyl groups on adjacent carbons; the drawings show different orientations of those groups.

ch09/p301a.description: A reaction scheme shows 1,2-diphenylethylene (stilbene) reacting with Br₂ in CH₂Cl₂ to form 1,2-dibromo-1,2-diphenylethane, followed by treatment with 2 KOH in ethanol to give diphenylacetylene (85%), water, and KBr. It illustrates conversion of an alkene to an alkyne through a vicinal dibromide.

ch09/p302b.description: The figure shows 3-hexyne reacting with HCl in CH₃CO₂H to form (Z)-3-chloro-3-hexene, followed by a second HCl addition to form 3,3-dichlorohexane. The first product is drawn with chlorine and hydrogen on opposite sides of the double bond.

ch09/p301b.description: A reaction scheme shows (Z)-3-chloro-2-buten-1-ol converting to 2-butyn-1-ol, with “1. 2 NaNH₂” and “2. H₃O⁺” above the arrow. The drawn structures illustrate conversion of a chloro-substituted alkene into an alkyne.

ch09/p300b.description: A numbered eight-carbon chain with a methyl branch at carbon 6 and a triple bond between carbons 3 and 4 illustrates numbering from the end nearer the triple bond. The structure is labeled “6-Methyl-3-octyne” and “(New: 6-Methyloct-3-yne).”
labels_in_image: Begin numbering at the end nearer the triple bond.

ch09/prob-9-3.description: A cyclopentane ring bearing a terminal alkyne is shown reacting with 1 HBr; an arrow points to a question mark for the unspecified product. The drawing asks for the product of this addition reaction without showing it.

ch09/p304a.description: The diagram shows 1-hexyne reacting with H₂O and H₂SO₄ in the presence of HgSO₄ to form a bracketed enol, followed by an arrow to 2-hexanone (78%). It illustrates the enol intermediate and the ketone product of alkyne hydration.

ch09/p303.description: Two parallel reaction sequences show H–Br adding to an alkene and an alkyne. Pink curved arrows trace formation of an alkyl or vinylic carbocation, followed by attack by Br⁻ to give the corresponding bromide.

ch09/prob-9-1d.description: A condensed structural formula shows a branched carbon chain with a carbon–carbon triple bond. Two methyl groups branch from the carbon on one side of the triple bond, and one methyl group branches from a carbon on the other side.

ch09/prob-9-4.description: The figure shows the condensed structure CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂C≡CCH₂CH₂CH₃, an alkyne with a methyl branch. It is presented as a starting structure in a mercury-catalyzed hydration problem; no product is shown.

ch09/fig-9.2.description: Two views of linear acetylene are shown: a ball-and-stick model with a carbon–carbon triple bond and an electrostatic potential map surrounding the molecule. Arrows labeled “π bond” point to the colored region around the molecule, illustrating the negative belt created by its π bonds.

ch09/prob-9-5a.description: The figure shows the condensed structure CH₃CH₂CH₂C(=O)CH₃, a ketone presented as a target in a problem asking which alkyne to start with.

ch09/p306.description: The figure compares mercury-catalyzed hydration of a generic internal alkyne, which gives a mixture of two ketones, with hydration of a generic terminal alkyne, which gives a methyl ketone. Both reaction arrows show H₃O⁺ and HgSO₄.

ch09/prob-9-5b.description: The figure shows the condensed structure CH₃CH₂C(=O)CH₂CH₃, a ketone presented as a target in a problem asking which alkyne to start with.

ch09/fig-9.4.description: A five-step mechanism shows a generic terminal alkyne reacting with mercury(II) and water to form a mercury-containing intermediate, then an enol, which tautomerizes to a ketone. Numbered arrows and curved electron-flow arrows accompany each step.

ch09/prob-9-6a.description: A benzene ring is bonded to a CH₂–CHO group, depicting an aldehyde for the alkyne hydroboration–oxidation problem.

ch09/p308a.description: A reaction scheme shows 4-octyne hydrogenated with H₂ and Lindlar catalyst to cis-4-octene, then with H₂ and Pd/C catalyst to octane. A separate ring structure below is labeled quinoline.

ch09/p307b.description: Two reaction arrows show ethyne reacting with H₂ over a catalyst to form ethene, then ethene reacting with H₂ over a catalyst to form ethane. The listed heats of hydrogenation are −176 kJ/mol for the first step and −137 kJ/mol for the second, illustrating that the first is more exothermic.

ch09/fig-9.3.description: An electrostatic potential map and orbital drawing show a generic secondary vinylic carbocation, with a π bond and a vacant p orbital on its positively charged carbon. A second orbital drawing contrasts it with a secondary alkyl carbocation.

ch09/prob-9-7a.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a benzene ring with a bromine atom and an acetyl group attached at meta positions. The figure presents a carbonyl compound for the alkyne-preparation problem, without showing a reaction.

ch09/p308c.description: A reaction scheme shows 5-decyne treated with Li in NH₃, yielding trans-5-decene (78%). The product drawing places the two hydrogen atoms on opposite sides of the double bond.

ch09/prob-9-7b.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a five-membered carbon ring with a –CH₂–CHO side chain; the carbonyl oxygen is red. It depicts one of the carbonyl compounds in the preparation problem, without showing a reaction.

ch09/p308b.description: A reaction scheme shows an alkyne-containing chain attached to a substituted ring converted by H₂ and Lindlar catalyst into 7-cis-retinol. The product’s new cis double bond is marked “Cis,” with its carbon positions numbered 1–15.
labels_in_image: (7-cis-vitamin A; vitamin A has a trans double bond at C7)

ch09/p310a.description: Two schemes show oxidative cleavage with KMnO₄ or O₃: an internal alkyne gives two generic carboxylic acids, while a terminal alkyne gives a generic carboxylic acid and carbon dioxide.

ch09/p310b.description: A generic terminal alkyne, R–C≡C–H, reacts with sodium amide to form an R-substituted acetylide anion and ammonia. Curved arrows show the amide removing the terminal hydrogen and the C–H bond electrons moving onto carbon.

ch09/p311.description: The acetylide anion reacts with a methyl bromide structure to form propyne and NaBr. Curved arrows show the acetylide attacking the carbon as the C–Br bond breaks.

ch09/fig-9.6.description: Three labeled anions—alkyl, vinylic, and acetylide—are shown with structural drawings and electrostatic potential models, alongside sp³, sp², and sp hybridization and 25%, 33%, and 50% s character, respectively. A right-pointing stability arrow illustrates increasing stability toward the acetylide anion as the negative charge lies closer to the carbon nucleus.

ch09/table-9.1.description: A vertical arrow fades from blue at the bottom to pink at the top, pointing from “Weaker acid” toward “Stronger acid.” It indicates the direction of increasing acidity in the accompanying table of simple hydrocarbons.

ch09/fig-9.7c.description: Two reaction sequences show acetylene treated with NaNH₂ to form an acetylide anion, then reacted with a generic alkyl bromide to give a terminal alkyne. A second sequence shows that terminal alkyne undergoing the same two steps to give an internal alkyne.

ch09/we-9.1a.description: A worked-example scheme shows 1-pentyne plus a generic alkyl halide (RX) pointing through an unlabeled multistep arrow to cis-2-hexene. The alkene product is drawn with its two hydrogens on the same side of the double bond.

ch09/prob-9-10.description: A cyclohexane ring is bonded to an alkyne group, –C≡C–CH₃. The drawing shows a product for which the problem asks for possible starting materials.

ch09/p307a.description: A terminal alkyne, R–C≡C–H, branches into two reaction pathways: H₂O/H₂SO₄ and HgSO₄ lead to a methyl ketone, R–C(=O)–CH₃, while BH₃ in THF followed by H₂O₂ leads to an aldehyde, R–CH₂–C(=O)–H.

ch09/fig-9.5.description: A four-step mechanism shows lithium transferring electrons to a generic R–C≡C–R′ alkyne, with ammonia supplying protons between the electron transfers. The diagrams trace an anion radical, a vinylic radical, and a vinylic anion to a trans alkene, with curved arrows marking proton transfers.

ch09/fig-9.7b.description: A reaction scheme shows 1-hexyne treated first with NaNH₂ in NH₃, then with CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Br, to give 5-decyne (76%). It illustrates formation of a longer internal alkyne from a terminal alkyne.

ch09/prob-9-6b.description: The problem shows a ketone with the structure CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂C(=O)CH(CH₃)CH₃ and asks which alkyne could produce it by hydroboration–oxidation.

ch09/prob-9-5c.description: Two reaction sequences show an internal alkyne undergoing hydroboration–oxidation to an enol that becomes a ketone, and a terminal alkyne reacting with disiamylborane followed by oxidation to give an enol that becomes an aldehyde. The arrows label BH₃/THF or disiamylborane, then H₂O₂ and H₂O/NaOH.

ch09/p315.description: A reaction scheme shows acetylene (HC≡CH) and a generic alkyl halide (RX) pointing to 2-bromopentane, drawn as CH₃CH₂CH₂CH(Br)CH₃. It presents these as starting materials and the target product for a synthesis.

ch09/we-9.2b.description: The diagram shows CH₃CH₂CH₂C≡CH converting to CH₃CH₂CH₂CH=CH₂ with H₂ and Lindlar catalyst over the arrow. It illustrates using partial reduction of an alkyne to obtain an alkene.

ch09/we-9.2c.description: A reaction scheme shows acetylene converted to 1-pentyne using NaNH₂/NH₃ followed by CH₃CH₂CH₂Br in THF, then hydrogenated with H₂ and Lindlar catalyst to 1-pentene. Treatment with HBr in ether gives the drawn product, 2-bromopentane.

ch09/p316a.description: The figure shows 5-methyl-1-hexyne reacting with H₂ over Lindlar catalyst to form 5-methyl-1-hexene, illustrating conversion of an alkyne to an alkene.

ch09/we-9.2a.description: Two alternative starting alkenes, 1-pentene and 2-pentene, are shown to the left of an arrow labeled HBr and Ether, leading to a drawn brominated pentane. The figure compares possible alkene starting materials for making 2-bromopentane.

ch09/we-9.3b.description: A terminal alkene is shown reacting with 1. BH₃ and 2. H₂O₂, NaOH to form a primary alcohol at the end of the carbon chain. The worked example illustrates a route from a terminal alkene to a primary alcohol.

ch09/p316b.description: The reaction scheme shows acetylene treated with NaNH₂ to form sodium acetylide, which then reacts with 1-bromo-3-methylbutane to give 5-methyl-1-hexyne. It illustrates building a longer alkyne carbon chain from acetylene.

ch09/p317.description: A detailed structural formula labeled Vitamin B₁₂ shows a central Co(III) atom coordinated within a large nitrogen-containing ring, with a CN group above and a nucleotide-like group below. Numerous methyl and amide-bearing side chains extend from the ring.

ch09/p318.description: A skeletal chemical structure labeled Paclitaxel (Taxol) shows a complex fused-ring framework with attached benzene rings, oxygen-containing groups, and an amide side chain.

ch09/we-9.3c.description: A four-step synthesis shows acetylene reacting with sodium amide and 1-bromo-3-methylbutane to form 5-methyl-1-hexyne, followed by hydrogenation to 5-methyl-1-hexene and hydroboration–oxidation to 5-methyl-1-hexanol.

ch09/we-9.1b.description: A reaction diagram shows 2-hexyne converting to cis-2-hexene with H₂ over Lindlar catalyst. The product is drawn with both hydrogen atoms on the same side of the double bond.

ch09/we-9.1c.description: A two-step reaction scheme shows 1-pentyne reacting with NaNH₂ in NH₃ to form a sodium acetylide, which then reacts with CH₃I in THF to give 2-hexyne. It illustrates making a longer alkyne by alkylating a terminal alkyne.

ch09/p319b.description: A reaction scheme shows acetylene treated with NaNH₂ to form an acetylide anion paired with Na⁺, followed by reaction with RCH₂Br to give HC≡CCH₂R, labeled “A terminal alkyne.”

ch09/fig-9.8.description: A photograph shows a large outdoor sewage-treatment basin filled with foamy brown sludge, bordered by concrete walls and metal railings. The caption connects bacteria growing in the sludge with the production of vitamin B12.

ch09/p319e.description: A generic internal alkyne R–C≡C–R′ reacts with X₂ in CH₂Cl₂ to form an alkene bearing one X on each carbon. A second addition of X₂ gives a saturated product bearing two X atoms on each of those carbons.

ch09/p319f.description: A generic terminal alkyne, R–C≡CH, reacts with H₂SO₄, H₂O, and HgSO₄ to form a bracketed enol, R–C(OH)=CH₂, which is shown converting to a methyl ketone, R–C(=O)–CH₃. The arrows illustrate mercuric sulfate–catalyzed hydration followed by conversion of the enol to the ketone.

ch09/p319g.description: A generic terminal alkyne, R–C≡CH, is shown reacting with BH₃ followed by H₂O₂ to form R–CH₂–CHO, labeled “An aldehyde.” The arrow illustrates conversion of the terminal alkyne into an aldehyde.

ch09/p320a.description: Two reaction schemes show a generic alkyne (R–C≡C–R′) reacting with 2 H₂ over Pd/C to form a single-bonded product, or with H₂ and Lindlar catalyst to form a cis alkene with the R groups on the same side of the double bond.

ch09/prob-9-15a.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a branched carbon chain ending in an aldehyde group, with a red oxygen atom double-bonded to the terminal carbon. The structure is 4-methylpentanal, presented as a product in a problem asking for its alkyne precursor.

ch09/p320b.description: A generic internal alkyne, R–C≡C–R′, is shown reacting with Li in NH₃ to give an alkene with the two hydrogen atoms on opposite sides of the double bond, labeled “A trans alkene.”

ch09/p319a.description: Two reaction schemes show a vicinal dibromide and a brominated alkene each forming a generic R–C≡C–R′ alkyne under the indicated KOH/ethanol or NaNH₂/NH₃ conditions. The drawings also show H₂O and KBr among the products.

ch09/prob-9-15b.description: A ball-and-stick molecular model shows a carbon framework bearing a side-chain carbon with two green chlorine atoms attached. White spheres represent hydrogen atoms.

ch09/prob-9-14a.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a terminal carbon–carbon triple bond connected through a CH₂ group to a branched carbon chain. It illustrates one of the structures in a problem asking which alkynes could give the pictured substances.

ch09/prob-9-19b.description: The reaction shows CH₃–C≡C–CH₃ treated with 2 HBr, yielding a four-carbon chain with two bromine atoms attached to the same carbon. It illustrates the product of adding two equivalents of HBr to an alkyne; no mechanism is drawn.

ch09/prob-9-20a.description: The reaction scheme shows phenylacetylene treated with H₂O and H₂SO₄ over HgSO₄, leading to a drawn intermediate with OH on the carbon next to the benzene ring and Hg⁺ attached to the other carbon of the new double bond; SO₄²⁻ is also shown. It illustrates the intermediate whose formation the problem asks the reader to explain.

ch09/prob-9-19c.description: A reaction scheme shows phenylacetylene treated with 2 HCl to give a product with two chlorine atoms on the carbon next to the benzene ring. It illustrates addition across an alkyne.

ch09/prob-9-14b.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a branched hydrocarbon with a carbon–carbon triple bond near the center. Dark spheres represent carbon atoms and pale spheres represent hydrogen atoms.

ch09/prob-9-16a.description: A ball-and-stick molecular model shows a short carbon chain bearing an oxygen–hydrogen group and attached to a small, three-carbon ring. Dark spheres represent carbon, red represents oxygen, and pale spheres represent hydrogen.

ch09/prob-9-21a.description: A reaction arrow labeled H₃O⁺ connects an enol, with a phenyl group attached to C(OH)=CH₂, to a ketone with the same phenyl group attached to C(=O)CH₃. It depicts the acid-assisted tautomerization posed in the problem.

ch09/prob-9-20c.description: A terminal alkyne with a branched carbon chain reacts under H₂O, H₂SO₄, and HgSO₄ conditions to give a drawn alkene bearing OH on one double-bond carbon and a mercury sulfate group on the other. The figure illustrates a step in acid-catalyzed alkyne hydration.

ch09/prob-9-22a.description: The problem shows the alkyne CH₃C≡CCH₂CH₃ with a reaction arrow labeled Li above and NH₃ below. No product or mechanism is drawn.

ch09/prob-9-22c.description: A benzene ring bonded to a C≡C–CH₃ group is shown with a reaction arrow labeled Li above and NH₃ below. No product is depicted.

ch09/prob-9-21b.description: A reaction arrow labeled H₃O⁺ connects the enol CH₃C(OH)=CH₂ to the ketone CH₃C(=O)CH₃. The drawing illustrates the enol-to-ketone tautomerization posed in the problem.

ch09/prob-9-25.description: A reaction diagram shows acetone, CH₃C(=O)CH₃, converted to hexadeuterioacetone, CD₃C(=O)CD₃, with D₃O⁺ above the arrow. It illustrates replacement of the hydrogen atoms on both methyl groups with deuterium.

ch09/prob-9-24b.description: A terminal alkyne ester, HC≡C–C(=O)–OCH₂CH₃, is shown with a two-step reagent sequence over a rightward arrow: 1. NaNH₂, then 2. CH₃CH₂I. The figure asks for a product and mechanism but does not show either.

ch09/prob-9-23a.description: The reaction diagram shows CH₃CH₂C≡CCH₂CH₃ converting to an alkene with the two ethyl groups on opposite sides of the double bond, with Li and NH₃ written over and under the arrow. It illustrates the reaction posed for mechanism classification without showing a mechanism.

ch09/prob-9-22b.description: A branched terminal alkyne, (CH₃)₂CH–C≡CH, is shown with a reaction arrow labeled Li above and ND₃ below. No product or mechanism is drawn.

ch09/prob-9-20b.description: Propyne (H₃C–C≡C–H) reacts under an arrow labeled H₂O, H₂SO₄, and HgSO₄ to give a drawn intermediate with a C=C bond, an OH group, and a mercury-containing group at the other alkene carbon.

ch09/prob-9-26b.description: A condensed structural formula shows a branched carbon chain with a double bond near the left end and a triple bond farther to the right. Methyl groups branch from the carbon just after the double bond and from a CH group near the right end.

ch09/prob-9-26a.description: The drawing shows an alkyne with the condensed structure CH₃CH₂–C≡C–C(CH₃)₃. Three methyl groups are attached to the carbon next to the triple bond.

ch09/prob-9-23c.description: A reaction diagram shows CH₃CH₂C≡CCH₂CH₃ reacting with 2 HBr to give a six-carbon chain bearing two bromine atoms on the same carbon. It illustrates addition to an alkyne.

ch09/prob-9-24c.description: The figure shows CH₃CH₂C≡CH reacting in two steps: first with NaNH₂, then with PhCH₂Br. The reaction arrow points toward an unspecified product.

ch09/prob-9-26d.description: A branched hydrocarbon structure shows a central carbon–carbon triple bond, with ethyl groups attached to the carbon chains on both sides and a methyl branch near the right end.

ch09/prob-9-30.description: A phenyl-substituted chain containing a C=C bond and a terminal C≡C bond is shown with two separate reaction arrows, one labeled H₂, Pd/C and the other H₂/Lindlar. The products are left blank as A? and B? for prediction.

ch09/prob-9-26c.description: The drawing shows a carbon chain with a terminal carbon–carbon triple bond at each end. The carbon next to the left-hand triple bond bears two CH₃ groups and connects through CH₂ to the right-hand triple bond.

ch09/prob-9-34a.description: The figure shows CH₃CO₂H and a benzene ring bearing a CO₂H group, separated by a plus sign, as products in an oxidative-cleavage problem.

ch09/prob-9-37b.description: A reaction arrow marked with a question mark shows CH₃CH₂C≡CH converting to CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO. The problem asks what reagents would carry out this transformation.

ch09/prob-9-29.description: A phenyl-substituted terminal alkyne is shown reacting with Br₂ and H₂O to form a phenyl ketone bearing a CH₂Br group. The figure illustrates the bromo ketone product of this alkyne reaction without showing a mechanism.

ch09/prob-9-34b.description: Three molecular structures are shown side by side, separated by plus signs: CH₃CHO, CH₃C(=O)CH₂CH₂CO₂H, and CO₂. No reaction arrow or reagents are shown in the crop.

ch09/prob-9-37d.description: A reaction arrow marked with a question mark connects a phenyl-substituted alkyne to a phenyl-substituted alkene. The product is drawn with both hydrogen atoms on the same side of the double bond.

ch09/prob-9-37c.description: A reaction arrow with a question mark shows phenylacetylene (a benzene ring attached to C≡CH) being converted to a benzene ring attached to C≡C–CH₃. The drawing asks for the missing transformation without showing reagents.

ch09/prob-9-35.description: A reaction scheme shows a terminal alkyne converted to an internal alkyne, then a cis alkene, and finally a cyclopropane bearing isopropyl and ethyl groups on the same face. The arrows are marked a, b, and c for the reagents to be identified.

ch09/prob-9-38a.description: A reaction arrow with a question mark above it shows CH₃CH₂CH₂C≡CH being converted to CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO. The drawing asks for the unspecified steps of this synthesis.

ch09/prob-9-36.description: A central generic terminal alkyne, R–C≡CH, has arrows pointing outward to eight possible products: an aldehyde, a chloroalkane, an alcohol, an internal alkyne, a ketone, an epoxide, an alkene, and an alkane. The diagram poses these as transformations without showing reagents or conditions.

ch09/prob-9-38b.description: A terminal alkyne, (CH₃)₂CHCH₂C≡CH, points through an arrow marked with a pink question mark to an alkene bearing an ethyl group; the larger carbon groups are drawn on opposite sides of the double bond. The question mark indicates that the synthesis steps are to be supplied.

ch09/prob-9-39.description: A reaction arrow marked with a question mark leads from CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂C≡CH to a cyclopropane bearing a butyl group and a methyl group on adjacent carbons. Solid wedges show the two carbon substituents on the same side of the ring, while dashed wedges show their hydrogens on the opposite side.

ch09/prob-9-43a.description: The figure shows CH₃CH₂C≡CCH₂CH₃ reacting under an unspecified reagent, marked “?”, to give an alkene with a deuterium atom on each double-bond carbon. Both deuterium atoms are drawn on the same side of the double bond.

ch09/prob-9-37f.description: A two-step synthesis problem shows CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH=CH₂ changing to CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂C≡CH. The arrow is marked with a question mark, leaving the steps unspecified.

ch09/prob-9-43b.description: A reaction arrow marked with a question mark connects an alkyne with an ethyl group on each end to an alkene bearing two deuterium atoms on opposite sides of the double bond. The problem asks how to carry out this deuterium-introducing transformation.

ch09/prob-9-40b.description: A reaction arrow marked with a question mark shows styrene being converted to 1-phenylprop-1-ene, with the double bond retained and a methyl group added at its far end. The figure asks for a multistep conversion without showing reagents.

ch09/prob-9-51.description: The figure shows the labeled structure of Mestranol: four fused rings with a methoxy group, a methyl group, and an OH and ethynyl group attached to the same carbon. It accompanies a problem asking for the ketone used to synthesize it.

ch09/prob-9-43c.description: A reaction arrow marked with a question mark connects CH₃CH₂CH₂C≡CH to CH₃CH₂CH₂C≡CD, showing replacement of the terminal alkyne hydrogen by deuterium. The question mark indicates that the reagents or conditions are to be supplied.

ch09/prob-9-42a.description: A condensed structural formula shows a five-carbon chain with a terminal double bond and a methyl branch on the fourth carbon: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH=CH₂.

ch09/prob-9-45.description: The figure shows the structural formula labeled Muscalure: a carbon–carbon double bond with a long hydrocarbon chain attached to each carbon and both hydrogens drawn on the same side.

ch09/prob-9-43d.description: A benzene ring attached to a terminal alkyne (C≡CH) points through a reaction arrow marked with a question mark to a benzene ring attached to CD=CD₂. The drawing asks for the unspecified conversion between these structures.

ch09/prob-9-54.description: The structure labeled E shows a central CH bonded to three CH₂CO₂H groups, forming a branched tricarboxylic acid.

ch09/prob-9-40a.description: A reaction scheme shows a benzene ring bearing a vinyl group on the left and a benzene ring bearing a –CH₂–CHO group on the right, connected by an arrow marked with a question mark for the unspecified conversion.

ch09/prob-9-50.description: Acetone is shown reacting with sodium acetylide, followed by H₃O⁺, to form an alcohol whose central carbon bears an OH group and a terminal alkyne group. Solid and dashed wedges depict its two methyl bonds.

ch09/prob-9-52.description: The figure shows the condensed structure of 1-octen-3-ol, with a terminal carbon–carbon double bond and an OH group on the third carbon. It identifies the compound whose preparation is asked about in the problem.

ch10/p330a.description: Four labeled structural formulas show trichloroethylene, halothane, tetrafluoropropene, and bromomethane, with chlorine, fluorine, and bromine atoms highlighted in pink. Their captions identify uses as a solvent, inhaled anesthetic, refrigerant, and fumigant, respectively.

ch09/prob-9-57a.description: Three five-membered rings each contain a double bond along the left side and a positive charge at a different position: the rightmost vertex, the upper-left double-bond carbon, or the upper-right carbon. The problem asks for their order of increasing carbocation stability.

ch10/fig-10.1.description: A volcano on an island sends a towering dark plume across an orange sky above the sea. The caption notes that volcanic gases contain organohalides, although no molecules are shown.

ch10/p330b.description: A skeletal structure labeled Sucralose shows two linked oxygen-containing rings with several hydroxyl groups. Three chlorine atoms are highlighted in pink.

ch09/prob-9-57b.description: Three five-carbon carbocations are drawn, each with a terminal double bond. The positive charge is on the carbon next to the double bond in the left structure, on a double-bond carbon in the middle structure, and farther from the double bond in the right structure.

ch09/prob-9-55.description: The figure shows a generic cumulene with four carbons joined by three consecutive double bonds, R₂C=C=C=CR₂. Each terminal carbon bears two unspecified R groups.

ch09/prob-9-56a.description: The drawing shows Na⁺ beside a negatively charged CH₂ group bonded to S(=O)–CH₃. It is one of the proposed bases in a problem about deprotonating 1-butyne.

ch10/p331c.description: Three alkyl halide structures are shown side by side: CH₃I, a three-carbon chain with Cl on its middle carbon, and a cyclohexane ring bonded to Br. Each structure has its systematic name and a parenthesized common name beneath it.

ch10/p331b.description: A six-carbon chain has a bromine substituent at carbon 2 and a methyl substituent at carbon 5, with the carbons numbered from right to left. The figure labels it “2-Bromo-5-methylhexane” and explicitly rejects “5-bromo-2-methylhexane.”

ch09/prob-9-56b.description: The drawing shows Na⁺ next to a negatively charged CH₂ group bonded to C(=O)–CH₃. It is presented as one candidate base in a problem about deprotonating 1-butyne.

ch10/p330c.description: Two seven-carbon chain structures are numbered 1–7, with their bromo and methyl substituents highlighted. The printed names show how the positions of those substituents are included in each name.

ch10/p332.description: A ball-and-stick model within a colored surface appears beside a generic carbon–halogen structure. The diagram marks X as δ− and C as δ+, with an arrow identifying the carbon as electrophilic.

ch10/prob-10-1a.description: A condensed structural formula shows a four-carbon chain ending in Cl, with a CH₃ group attached to the second carbon from the left. It is one of the alkyl halides presented for naming.

ch10/prob-10-1d.description: The drawing shows a five-carbon chain, CH₃–CH–CH–CH₂–CH₃, with iodine attached to the second carbon and a –CH₂CH₂Cl group attached to the third. It illustrates a branched alkyl halide structure in a nomenclature problem.

ch10/prob-10-1b.description: The drawing shows a five-carbon chain with a bromine attached to each end and two methyl groups attached to the carbon next to one end. It is one of the alkyl halide structures presented for naming.

ch10/prob-10-1e.description: A six-carbon chain is drawn with Br attached to the second carbon and Cl attached to the fifth carbon. It is a condensed structural formula illustrating an alkyl halide with two different halogen substituents.

ch10/fig-10.2.description: The diagram shows methane reacting with chlorine under light: initiation produces chlorine radicals, two repeating propagation steps form hydrogen chloride and chloromethane, and termination steps combine radicals. An overall reaction is shown beneath the mechanism.

ch10/p333b.description: The figure shows butane reacting with Cl₂ under hν to form 1-chlorobutane and 2-chlorobutane in a 30:70 ratio, alongside dichloro-, trichloro-, tetrachloro-, and further chlorinated products. It illustrates that chlorination produces a mixture rather than a single product.
