ch09/prob-9-57c.description: Three drawings show the same methyl-substituted cyclohexene ring with a double bond on the left side. A plus sign appears at the lower-left ring carbon in the first, the methyl-bearing upper-right carbon in the second, and the lower-right carbon in the third.

ch10/p334a.description: Three generic carbon radicals are shown with one, two, or three R groups, labeled Primary, Secondary, and Tertiary. Less-than signs and a right-pointing Stability arrow show stability increasing from primary to tertiary.

ch10/p333a.description: A stepped reaction scheme shows methane reacting with chlorine under light, followed by successive chlorinations to give CH₃Cl, CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃, and CCl₄; each step also produces HCl. It illustrates that chlorination can continue beyond the first substitution.

ch10/p333d.description: Three generic carbon centers bearing one, two, or three R groups are labeled primary, secondary, and tertiary, with relative values of 1.0, 3.5, and 5.0. A right-pointing “Reactivity” arrow shows increasing reactivity toward radical chlorination from primary to tertiary.

ch10/p335a.description: A cyclohexene ring has three highlighted hydrogens at alkyl, allylic, and vinylic positions, labeled 410, 370, and 465 kJ/mol, respectively. The comparison illustrates the lower value for the allylic position.

ch10/fig-10.4.description: An orbital diagram and molecular model show p orbitals overlapping across the three carbons of the allyl radical. At right, two equivalent resonance structures place the double bond and radical on opposite ends of the chain.

ch10/p334c.description: Cyclohexene is shown with its allylic hydrogen positions marked, then reacting with NBS under light in CCl₄ to give 3-bromocyclohexene (85%) and a cyclic byproduct. The diagram illustrates bromination next to, rather than on, the double bond.

ch10/p334b.description: A methyl-substituted cyclopentene is shown reacting along two paths: X₂ adds halogens to both carbons of the double bond, while HX adds H to one carbon and X to the methyl-substituted carbon. The labels specify X = Cl or Br for X₂ and X = Cl, Br, or I for HX.

ch10/p335b.description: Six generic carbon radicals, each marked by a dot in a green orbital, are arranged in the printed order Vinylic < Methyl < Primary < Secondary < Tertiary < Allylic. A right-pointing arrow labeled “Stability” shows that stability increases from left to right.

ch10/prob-10-5.description: A six-membered ring has two double bonds along its left side and a radical dot beside its upper-right carbon. The drawing is labeled “Cyclohexadienyl radical.”

ch10/p337b.description: The scheme shows cyclohexene converted to 3-bromocyclohexene with hν, NBS, and CCl₄, followed by conversion to 1,3-cyclohexadiene with KOH. It illustrates allylic bromination followed by formation of a second double bond.

ch10/p337a.description: The scheme shows 1-octene treated with NBS in CCl₄ under light, forming two resonance-related allylic radicals and then two brominated products. It labels 3-bromo-1-octene as 17% and 1-bromo-2-octene as 83%, with a 53:47 trans:cis ratio for the latter.

ch10/prob-10-61.description: A reaction scheme shows methylenecyclohexane treated with NBS under light in CCl₄, forming a cyclohexene ring bearing a CH₂Br group, labeled “Major product.” It illustrates the stated major product of this reaction without showing the mechanism.

ch10/p333c.description: A reaction scheme shows 2-methylpropane reacting with Cl₂ under light (hν) to form 2-chloro-2-methylpropane and 1-chloro-2-methylpropane in a 35:65 ratio, alongside dichloro-, trichloro-, tetrachloro-, and further chlorinated products.

ch10/prob-10-8a.description: The drawing shows a central carbon bonded to chlorine and three CH₃ groups, an alkyl chloride in a preparation problem.

ch10/fig-10.5.description: A ball-and-stick model of the allyl radical is surrounded by a multicolored spin-density surface. Two arrows point to matching regions around the terminal carbons, illustrating that they share the unpaired electron equally.

ch10/p338a.description: A generic tertiary alcohol reacts with H–X to form a tertiary alkyl halide and H₂O. Below, methyl, primary, secondary, and tertiary alcohol structures are arranged left to right with an arrow showing increasing reactivity.

ch10/we-10.1.description: A dimethylcyclohexene ring is marked with positions A, A′, B, and B′; arrows labeled NBS lead to brominated ring structures. ch10/p339c.description: A reaction scheme shows primary, secondary, and tertiary alkyl, alkenyl, and aryl halides represented as R–X, with X listed as Cl, Br, or I. An arrow labeled Mg, with ether or THF, leads to the corresponding generic R–Mg–X structure.

ch10/prob-10-7a.description: The drawing shows a seven-membered ring with a double bond on its lower-left side and a CH₃ group attached near the upper right. It is presented as an alkene for the NBS reaction problem, with no products shown.

ch10/prob-10-8d.description: The problem shows a condensed structural formula for a branched alkyl bromide, with bromine at one end and a methyl branch near the other. It asks how to prepare the compound from its corresponding alcohol.

ch10/prob-10-8b.description: A cyclopentane ring has a fluorine substituent at one carbon and two methyl groups attached to another ring carbon. The drawing is one alkyl halide in a problem asking for preparation from the corresponding alcohol.

ch10/p341b.description: The reaction shows lithium dimethylcopper and 1-iododecane forming undecane (90%) in ether at 0 °C, with LiI and CH₃Cu also shown as products. It illustrates carbon–carbon bond formation in an organometallic coupling reaction.

ch10/p339b.description: A reaction arrow shows cyclohexanol, drawn as a ring bearing OH, converted to fluorocyclohexane, with HF above the arrow and pyridine below it. The product is labeled with a 99% yield.

ch10/prob-10-8c.description: The problem shows a five-carbon chain with bromine attached to the second carbon and a methyl branch on the fourth carbon. It asks for preparation of this alkyl halide from the corresponding alcohol, without showing the preparation.

ch10/p341c.description: Two organocopper coupling reactions are shown: trans-1-iodo-1-nonene reacts with (n-C₄H₉)₂CuLi to give trans-5-tridecene (71%), and iodobenzene reacts with (CH₃)₂CuLi to give toluene (91%). Each scheme also shows an organocopper byproduct and LiI.

ch10/p340a.description: Iodomethane reacts with Mg in ether to form methylmagnesium iodide. Partial-charge labels mark magnesium δ+ and carbon δ−; an arrow labeled “Basic and nucleophilic” points to that carbon in both the structure and a colored molecular model.

ch10/p341d.description: A coupling reaction converts cis-1-bromo-9-octadecene to muscalure (9Z-tricosene) using the organocopper reagent [CH₃(CH₂)₄]₂CuLi. The drawings show the bromine-bearing chain replaced by a longer carbon chain while the double bond remains cis.

ch10/p340b.description: A reaction scheme shows 1-bromohexane reacting with magnesium in ether to form 1-hexylmagnesium bromide, followed by reaction with water to give hexane. It illustrates formation of a Grignard reagent and its conversion to a hydrocarbon by water.

ch10/p341e.description: A generic organohalide R–X reacts with a lithium diorganocopper reagent, passing through a bracketed copper species bearing R and two R′ groups. The arrows show formation of R–R′ and R′–Cu, illustrating coupling with loss of mono-organocopper.

ch10/p341f.description: A trimethyl-substituted phenylboronic acid reacts with iodobenzene under Pd(PPh₃)₄, CaCO₃, and THF conditions to form a biaryl product, shown in 92% yield. An inset defines Ph as phenyl.

ch10/prob-10-11a.description: A cyclohexene ring is shown transforming into a cyclohexene ring bearing a methyl group on the carbon adjacent to the double bond. A question mark above the reaction arrow indicates that the required steps or reagents are to be supplied.

ch10/p341a.description: A reaction scheme shows two equivalents of methyllithium reacting with CuI in ether to form lithium dimethylcopper (a Gilman reagent) and LiI. It illustrates preparation of a lithium diorganocopper reagent.

ch10/p340c.description: The reaction shows 1-bromobutane treated with 2 Li in pentane to form butyllithium and LiBr. A molecular model of butyllithium beside it has an arrow labeled “Basic and nucleophilic” pointing toward its lithium-bearing end.

ch10/prob-10-11c.description: A reaction problem shows CH₃CH₂CH₂CH=CH₂ converting to a longer straight-chain alkane, CH₃(CH₂)₈CH₃. A pink question mark above the arrow asks for the missing reaction conditions.

ch10/p343b.description: Two reaction schemes show ethylene reacting with Br₂ to form 1,2-dibromoethane, and with HBr to form bromoethane. The first is labeled oxidation because two carbon–bromine bonds form; the second is labeled neither oxidation nor reduction because one carbon–hydrogen and one carbon–bromine bond form.

ch10/prob-10-11b.description: A problem diagram shows CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Br converting to CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃, with a question mark above the reaction arrow indicating missing steps or reagents.

ch10/p342.description: A Suzuki–Miyaura coupling scheme shows para-methylbenzeneboronic acid and ortho-chlorobenzonitrile forming a methyl-substituted biphenyl nitrile with a Pd catalyst and K₂CO₃; a second arrow points to the drawn structure of valsartan (Diovan).

ch10/fig-10.8.description: A colorful underwater photograph shows pink, orange, red, purple, and yellow corals on a reef. The caption says marine corals secrete organohalogen compounds that deter fish from feeding.

ch10/we-10.2a.description: Four condensed structures—propene, 2-propanol, acetone, and propane—are shown side by side for a worked example asking readers to compare their oxidation levels; no ranking is shown.

ch10/p345.description: The figure shows Halomon as a skeletal chemical structure beside a color-coded ball-and-stick model. Both depict the same carbon chain with bromine and chlorine substituents.

ch10/fig-10.6.description: A three-step circular mechanism shows an aromatic halide (Ar–X) reacting with a palladium catalyst, then an aromatic boronic acid (Ar′–B(OH)₂), to form a diarylpalladium intermediate that releases a biaryl product (Ar–Ar′) and regenerates the catalyst. The diagram also shows ligand L and X–B(OH)₂ leaving during the cycle.

ch10/fig-10.7.description: Rows of molecular formulas are arranged from left to right above an arrow running from “Low oxidation level” to “High oxidation level.” The arrangement illustrates the relative oxidation levels of several common carbon compounds.

ch10/prob-10-13b.description: A reaction drawing shows cyclohexene converting to cyclohexanol, with “1. BH₃” and “2. NaOH, H₂O₂” written over the arrow. The accompanying problem asks the reader to classify the reaction as oxidation, reduction, or neither.

ch10/p346a.description: A substituted alkene reacts with NBS under light in CCl₄; the product retains the double bond while Br replaces the highlighted H on the adjacent carbon. The scheme illustrates allylic bromination.

ch10/p346c.description: A wedge-and-dash drawing shows a generic alcohol, with OH and H attached to the central carbon, reacting with SOCl₂ in pyridine to give the corresponding structure with Cl in place of OH.

ch10/prob-10-13a.description: A reaction arrow shows propanal (CH₃CH₂CHO) becoming 1-propanol (CH₃CH₂CH₂OH), with NaBH₄ above the arrow and H₂O below it. The problem asks the reader to classify the reaction without giving the answer.

ch10/p347c.description: A reaction scheme shows a generic organohalide, R–X, reacting with 2 Li in pentane to form R–Li and LiX. It illustrates the formation of an organolithium reagent.

ch10/p347d.description: Phenylboronic acid and iodobenzene are shown reacting under Pd(PPh₃)₄, CaCO₃, and THF conditions to form biphenyl. The scheme illustrates a palladium-catalyzed Suzuki–Miyaura coupling.

ch10/p347b.description: A generic R–X structure reacts with Mg in ether to form R–Mg–X, showing formation of an organomagnesium reagent from an alkyl halide.

ch10/p346d.description: A generic alcohol bearing OH on a tetrahedral carbon reacts with PBr₃ in ether to give the corresponding structure with Br replacing OH. Solid-wedge and dashed bonds show the carbon’s three-dimensional arrangement on both sides of the arrow.

ch10/prob-10-18b.description: A six-carbon chain is shown as CH₃CH=CHCH₂CH(I)CH₃, with a double bond near one end and an iodine atom attached near the other.

ch10/prob-10-15a.description: A ball-and-stick model shows an alkene with two methyl groups attached to one carbon of the double bond and a three-carbon chain attached to the other. It is one of the alkenes in a problem asking for products of reaction with NBS.

ch10/prob-10-18a.description: The figure shows a seven-carbon chain with bromine atoms on two adjacent carbons and methyl branches near each end. It is presented as an alkyl halide to be named.

ch10/p347a.description: A reaction arrow shows cyclohexanol converting to fluorocyclohexane, with HF above the arrow and pyridine below it. A boxed ring structure at the right depicts pyridine.

ch10/prob-10-14b.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a branched carbon chain with a double bond near the left end and a green chlorine atom attached to the carbon next to it. Gray spheres represent carbon and small pale spheres represent hydrogen.

ch10/prob-10-15b.description: A ball-and-stick model shows two five-membered carbon rings joined by a carbon–carbon double bond. It is one of the alkenes presented for the NBS product-prediction problem.

ch10/prob-10-18c.description: A condensed carbon-chain structure is shown with bromine and a methyl group attached to one carbon, chlorine attached farther along the chain, and another methyl group on the next carbon. It is presented as an alkyl halide naming problem.

ch10/prob-10-22a.description: A cyclohexane ring bearing a methyl group and an OH group on the same carbon is shown reacting with HBr in ether. The product is left as a question mark.

ch10/prob-10-22c.description: A cyclohexane ring bearing an OH group is shown to the left of a reaction arrow labeled PBr₃ above and Ether below; a question mark marks the unspecified product.

ch10/prob-10-22b.description: A pair of fused six-membered carbon rings with a double bond along their shared edge is shown reacting with NBS under hν in CCl₄; a question mark marks the unspecified product.

ch10/prob-10-22f.description: The problem shows CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Br reacting with (CH₃)₂CuLi in ether, with a question mark in place of the product. It asks for the missing product without depicting its structure.

ch10/prob-10-18d.description: A condensed structure shows a six-carbon chain with a CH₂Br branch attached to its third carbon, illustrating a branched organohalide.

ch10/prob-10-16.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a five-carbon chain with a bromine atom attached to the second carbon from one end, representing 2-bromopentane.

ch10/prob-10-14a.description: A ball-and-stick model shows an alkyl halide with a green chlorine atom bonded to a gray carbon framework; the pale spheres represent hydrogen atoms.

ch10/prob-10-27b.description: Four condensed structures are shown side by side for an oxidation-level ranking problem: a propyl amine, a propyl bromide, a chloromethyl ketone, and a three-carbon chain bearing bromine and chlorine at opposite ends.

ch10/prob-10-29b.description: The figure shows CH₃CH₂OH on the left of an arrow labeled CrO₃ and CH₃CHO, with its carbonyl double bond drawn, on the right.

ch10/prob-10-28.description: Five numbered structures are shown for comparison of oxidation levels: an ethyl-substituted epoxide, an unsaturated alcohol, an unsaturated ketone, a five-membered cyclic ether, and a conjugated diene. The figure asks the reader to compare them but does not indicate an answer.

ch10/prob-10-29a.description: A reaction drawing shows H₂C=CHC(=O)CH₃ and NH₃ forming H₂NCH₂CH₂C(=O)CH₃. The carbon–carbon double bond in the starting ketone is replaced by a chain bearing an amino group in the product.

ch10/prob-10-29c.description: A reaction scheme shows CH₃CH₂CH(Br)CH₃ treated first with Mg and then H₂O, yielding CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃. It illustrates replacement of the bromine substituent with hydrogen.

ch10/prob-10-26.description: A skeletal structure shows a benzene ring attached to a four-carbon chain with a double bond between the second and third carbons. It is labeled “1-Phenyl-2-butene” and accompanies a question about its reaction with NBS.

ch10/prob-10-27a.description: Four condensed structures are shown side by side for an oxidation-level ranking problem: two butenes, an aldehyde, and a carboxylic acid. No ranking is given in the figure.

ch10/prob-10-36.description: Three arrows show cyclohexene, cyclohexanol, and cyclohexane as separate starting materials leading to the same drawn product, butylcyclohexane. A pink question mark above each arrow marks the unspecified synthesis.

ch10/prob-10-31.description: A reaction diagram shows a benzene ring bearing CH₃ converted to one bearing CH₂Br, with NBS above the arrow and hν, CCl₄ below it. The change is shown at the carbon next to the aromatic ring.

ch10/prob-10-30b.description: Three line-angle structures show a branched five-carbon skeleton, each with a dot at a different position: an internal carbon, the branch point, or a terminal carbon. The drawings compare three possible carbon-centered radicals.

ch10/prob-10-40.description: A three-step scheme shows an alkene attached to a cyclohexane ring changing to an alcohol, then a bromide, and finally a hydrocarbon. The arrows are labeled a, b, and c for reagents to be identified; the figure does not give their identities.

ch10/prob-10-33.description: A five-membered ring has two double bonds and a lone pair with a negative charge on the remaining carbon. It is presented as a species for which the problem asks the reader to draw resonance structures.

ch10/prob-10-37a.description: Part (c) shows CH₃CH₂CH₂F reacting with 1. Mg, then 2. H₃O⁺, to give CH₃CH₂CH₃. It is presented as a proposed synthesis in a problem asking what is wrong with the reactions shown.

ch10/prob-10-43a.description: The drawing shows a biaryl compound with a methoxy group on each benzene ring and a methyl ester group adjacent to the bond joining the rings. It is presented as a target for a Suzuki–Miyaura reaction problem; no reaction partners are shown.

ch10/prob-10-37b.description: A methyl-substituted cyclohexane ring with an exocyclic CH₂ double bond is shown reacting with NBS under light in CCl₄. The drawn product retains the double bond and methyl group and has Br attached to the adjacent ring carbon.

ch10/prob-10-43c.description: A skeletal structure shows two benzene rings joined by a single bond. One ring bears three methoxy groups, while the other has two oxygens linked by a methylene group to form a five-membered ring.

ch10/prob-10-45a.description: Two three-carbon alcohol structures are shown side by side, separated by “or”: a straight-chain alcohol with OH at an end and a branched drawing with OH on the middle carbon. The problem asks which reacts faster with HX, but the figure does not indicate an answer.

ch10/prob-10-38.description: The drawing shows 4-bromo-1-pentanol on the left and a proposed product in which MgBr replaces Br on the same carbon. An arrow labeled Mg is crossed out, indicating that this conversion is not expected.

ch10/prob-10-45c.description: Two skeletal alcohol structures are shown as alternatives, separated by “or”: 2,2-dimethylpropan-1-ol on the left and 2-methylbutan-2-ol on the right. The hydroxyl group is at the end of the left structure and attached to the central carbon of the right structure.

ch10/prob-10-46a.description: The problem shows 4-bromobenzoic acid and phenylboronic acid separated by a plus sign, with a reaction arrow labeled Pd(OAc)₂. It asks for the product and catalytic cycle of this Suzuki–Miyaura reaction, but neither is drawn.

ch11/p355.description: A chiral, phenyl-containing alkyl tosylate reacts with acetate ion to form the corresponding acetate ester and tosylate ion. Wedge and dashed bonds at the starred carbon show the inversion of configuration indicated beneath the arrow.

ch10/prob-10-46b.description: A brominated benzene ring bearing two methyl groups is shown reacting with a benzene ring bearing a boronic acid group and two methoxy groups. Pd(OAc)₂ is written above the reaction arrow; no product is shown.

ch10/prob-10-43b.description: The drawing shows a biphenyl with an NH₂ group para to the bond joining the rings on one ring and a CH₃ group para to that bond on the other. No reaction partners are shown.

ch11/we-11.1b.description: A reaction scheme shows (R)-1-bromo-1-phenylethane reacting with cyanide to give (S)-2-phenylpropanenitrile. Wedge and dashed bonds show the change in stereochemistry as Br is replaced by a cyano group.

ch11/we-11.1a.description: A benzylic alkyl bromide with a phenyl group and methyl group on the bromine-bearing carbon reacts with sodium cyanide; the arrow points to a question mark in place of the product. The worked example asks for the substitution product without showing it.

ch10/prob-10-45b.description: Two cyclopentane-ring alcohol structures are shown side by side, separated by “or”: the left has a methyl group and OH on the same ring carbon, while the right has them on adjacent ring carbons. The problem asks which alcohol reacts faster with HX to form an alkyl halide.

ch11/fig-11.6.description: Two energy-versus-reaction-progress diagrams compare black and pink reaction curves. In (a), the pink curve starts at higher reactant energy and has a smaller activation-energy barrier; in (b), it has a higher transition-state peak and a larger barrier.

ch11/fig-11.1.description: A photograph shows two bull moose facing each other with their antlers locked in a grassy landscape. The caption uses their contest to illustrate competition between alternative reaction pathways.

ch11/p360c.description: Two generic substitution schemes show Nu attacking R–Y as the R–Y bond breaks, indicated by curved arrows. A negatively charged nucleophile gives a neutral R–Nu product, while a neutral nucleophile gives a positively charged R–Nu product; both schemes show Y⁻ leaving.

ch11/p360b.description: A generic vinylic halide and an aryl halide are shown with a nucleophile approaching their chlorine-bearing carbons. Pink crossed-out arrows and “No reaction” labels indicate that neither undergoes the depicted displacement.

ch11/p362a.description: A chart compares relative leaving-group reactivity: OH⁻, NH₂⁻, and OR⁻ are grouped at ≪1, followed by F⁻ (1), Cl⁻ (200), Br⁻ (10,000), I⁻ (30,000), and TosO⁻ (60,000). A right-pointing arrow indicates increasing leaving-group reactivity.

ch11/fig-11.4.description: A two-stage drawing shows hydroxide attacking (S)-2-bromobutane opposite the bromine, passing through a transition state with partial C–OH and C–Br bonds. Bromide then departs to give (R)-2-butanol, illustrating inversion of stereochemistry in an SN2 reaction.

ch11/prob-11-3.description: A ball-and-stick model shows 2-bromo-4-methylpentane, with a reddish-brown bromine atom attached to a carbon near one end of the branched chain. The problem asks for its configuration and the product of substitution with HS⁻; no product is shown.

ch11/prob-11-6.description: A generic anion X⁻ is surrounded by four ROH molecules, with dotted lines showing hydrogen bonds from their H atoms to the anion. The figure labels this a solvated anion with reduced nucleophilicity due to enhanced ground-state stability.
labels_in_image: A solvated anion (reduced nucleophilicity due to enhanced ground-state stability)

ch11/p360a.description: A generic substitution shows R–Br reacting with Cl⁻ to give R–Cl and Br⁻. Below, five alkyl bromide structures are arranged by increasing S_N2 reactivity from tertiary (<1) through neopentyl (1), secondary (500), and primary (40,000) to methyl (2,000,000).

ch11/p362c.description: A primary or secondary alcohol reacts with the drawn sulfonyl chloride in ether and pyridine to form a tosylate. The wedge-and-dash bonds at the oxygen-bearing carbon are unchanged in the product.

ch11/fig-11.5.description: Three stages of a generic SN2 substitution are shown as electrostatic-potential models and structural sketches: a tetrahedral carbon bonded to X reacts with Nu⁻, passes through a planar, bracketed transition state, and forms a tetrahedral carbon bonded to Nu as X⁻ departs. The transition state shows partial negative charge at both Nu and X.

ch11/fig-11.8.description: Four paired energy diagrams compare SN2 reaction profiles for hindered versus unhindered substrates, good versus poor nucleophiles, good versus poor leaving groups, and polar aprotic versus protic solvents. They illustrate how each factor changes the activation barrier, with substrate and leaving-group effects shown mainly near the peak and nucleophile and solvent effects mainly at the starting energy level.

ch11/p362b.description: Two parallel schemes show a primary or secondary alcohol reacting with SOCl₂ or PBr₃ in ether to form a chlorosulfite or dibromophosphite intermediate, respectively. Each then undergoes a labeled SN2 step with chloride or bromide to give an alkyl chloride or bromide; wedge-and-dash bonds show the change in stereochemistry.

ch11/fig-11.9.description: A three-step SN1 mechanism shows 2-bromo-2-methylpropane slowly losing bromide to form a carbocation, followed by fast attack by water and loss of a proton to give an alcohol and H₃O⁺. Curved arrows trace bond breaking, water attack, and proton transfer; the first step is marked rate-limiting.

ch11/fig-11.11.description: Ball-and-stick models show a chiral substrate dissociating into a planar, achiral carbocation intermediate. A generic nucleophile (Nu) attacks from either side, giving 50% inversion and 50% retention of configuration.

ch11/p362d.description: Propene oxide reacts with H–Cl: curved arrows show protonation of the epoxide oxygen, followed by chloride attack at the less substituted carbon and ring opening. The product is labeled 1-chloro-2-propanol.

ch11/p360d.description: An acetylide anion, R–C≡C⁻, reacts with CH₃Br in an SN2 reaction to form R–C≡C–CH₃ and Br⁻. The diagram illustrates the acetylide replacing bromide while leaving the R group unspecified.

ch11/p363.description: The reaction scheme shows 1-bromobutane reacting with azide ion to form an alkyl azide and bromide ion. A table gives relative reactivities of 1, 7, 1300, 2800, 5000, and 200,000 in CH₃OH, H₂O, DMSO, DMF, CH₃CN, and HMPA, respectively, with a right-pointing arrow indicating increasing solvent reactivity.

ch11/p368.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a benzene ring attached to a carbon bonded to bromine, a methyl group, and an ethyl group. It illustrates the three-dimensional structure of a tertiary alkyl bromide.

ch11/prob-11-9.description: A chiral benzylic tosylate, drawn with dashed H and wedged tert-butyl bonds, reacts with CH₃COOH to give the corresponding acetate and TosOH. The figure compares the starting material’s optical rotation (−30.3) with the observed product rotation (+5.3) and the optically pure acetate’s rotation (+53.6).

ch11/p364.description: A generic reaction shows an alkyl bromide reacting with water to form an alcohol and HBr. Below, methyl, primary, secondary, and tertiary alkyl bromide structures have relative reactivities of <1, 1, 12, and 1,200,000, respectively, with a right-pointing reactivity arrow.

ch11/fig-11.13.description: Two resonance structures of the allyl carbocation and five of the benzyl carbocation are linked by double-headed arrows, with pink curved arrows showing shifts in π bonds. Colored models at right show the delocalized regions, and blue arrows mark electron-poor atoms.

ch11/fig-11.12.description: A ball-and-stick alkyl halide loses its leaving group to form an ion pair, whose nearby anion shields one side of the carbocation so the nucleophile approaches from the open side and produces inversion. A second path shows a free carbocation open to attack from either side, leading to racemization.

ch11/fig-11.10.description: An SN1 energy diagram plots energy against reaction progress: generic RX and Nu⁻ rise over a high, rate-limiting barrier to a carbocation intermediate, R⁺, and X⁻, then cross a smaller barrier to form RNu and X⁻. The two peaks show that carbocation formation is slower than the subsequent nucleophile reaction.

ch11/p369b.description: Three structures show C–Cl bonds marked with arrows: CH₃CH₂–Cl at 338 kJ/mol (81 kcal/mol), H₂C=CHCH₂–Cl at 289 kJ/mol (69 kcal/mol), and a benzene ring–CH₂–Cl at 293 kJ/mol (70 kcal/mol). The figure compares the bond energies of a saturated, an allylic, and a benzylic C–Cl bond.

ch11/prob-11-11.description: Four condensed structures are shown for an SN1 reactivity ranking problem: CH₃CH₂Br, CH₂=CHCH(Br)CH₃, CH₂=CHBr, and CH₃CH(Br)CH₃. The bromine atoms on the second and fourth structures are drawn above their attachment points.

ch11/p371.description: The figure shows tert-butyl chloride reacting with generic ROH to form a tert-butyl ether (OR) and HCl. A table below shows relative reactivity rising from 1 in ethanol to 100 in 40% water/60% ethanol, 14,000 in 80% water/20% ethanol, and 100,000 in water, alongside a right-pointing “Solvent reactivity” arrow.

ch11/prob-11-13b.description: A reaction arrow shows H₂C=C(CH₃)CH₂Br reacting with Na⁺ ⁻SCH₃ in CH₃CN to give H₂C=C(CH₃)CH₂SCH₃. The problem asks the reader to classify the substitution reaction as SN1 or SN2.

ch11/fig-11.14a.description: A three-step SN1 mechanism shows a tertiary alcohol reacting with HBr: protonation of its OH group, slow departure of water to form a carbocation, and attack by bromide to form the alkyl bromide. Curved arrows indicate electron movement, and the steps are numbered beside the structures.

ch11/prob-11-13a.description: A cyclohexene ring bearing a –CH(OH)CH₃ substituent is shown reacting with HCl in CH₃OH to give the corresponding –CH(Cl)CH₃ substituent; the ring double bond remains drawn in the same position. The problem asks whether this substitution is SN1 or SN2.

ch11/fig-11.15.description: Six water molecules surround a positively charged carbon center, with their oxygen atoms and lone pairs directed toward it. The arrangement illustrates how water solvates and stabilizes a carbocation.

ch11/p375b.description: An E1 reaction diagram shows a generic C–X bond breaking to form a bracketed carbocation and X⁻. Curved arrows then show a base removing a neighboring hydrogen as a C=C bond forms, yielding an alkene and protonated base.

ch11/prob-11-14.description: The figure shows a chain structure labeled linalyl diphosphate, with an OPP group and two double bonds, pointing by an arrow to a ring structure labeled limonene with a double bond in the ring and another in a side group. It presents the biosynthesis transformation as a problem without showing a mechanism.

ch11/p375a.description: Two elimination reactions show 2-bromobutane forming 2-butene (81%) and 1-butene (19%), and 2-bromo-2-methylbutane forming 2-methyl-2-butene (70%) and 2-methyl-1-butene (30%), with sodium ethoxide in ethanol shown above and below each reaction arrow. In both examples, the more substituted alkene is the major product.

ch11/p372.description: Two substitution schemes show (a) a chlorine-bearing carbon next to a phenyl ring changing to an OAc-bearing carbon with sodium acetate in acetic acid and water, and (b) a terminal CH₂Br group on a three-carbon phenylalkyl chain changing to CH₂OCH₃ with sodium methoxide in DMF. The drawings illustrate replacement of the halogen by an oxygen-containing group under two different sets of conditions.

ch11/we-11.3a.description: A cyclohexane ring bearing Cl and CH₃ on the same carbon is shown reacting with KOH in ethanol; the arrow points to a question mark instead of a product, posing an elimination-product prediction.

ch11/p374.description: Two rows compare reactions of a brominated alkane with hydroxide: substitution replaces Br with OH, while elimination removes Br and a neighboring H to form a C=C double bond, water, and bromide.

ch11/prob-11-15b.description: The problem shows a branched alkyl chloride: its central carbon bears Cl and a CH₃ group, with CH₂–CH(CH₃)–CH₃ on one side and CH(CH₃)–CH₃ on the other. The surrounding prompt asks for possible elimination products and the major product, without showing the products.

ch11/p375d.description: An E1cB reaction diagram shows a base removing H from a generic carbon chain to form a bracketed carbanion intermediate, followed by loss of X⁻ to form a C=C double bond. Pink curved arrows mark the electron movements, and B–H⁺ appears beside the intermediate.

ch11/prob-11-16a.description: A condensed structural formula shows a seven-carbon chain ending in a double bond, with methyl branches on two of its CH groups. The accompanying problem asks which alkyl halides could have produced this alkene.

ch11/prob-11-16b.description: A five-membered ring has a double bond on its lower-left side and a CH₃ group attached to each of the two right-hand ring carbons. It is one of the alkenes in a problem asking what alkyl halide it might have been made from.

ch11/fig-11.19.description: Three stages show an anti-periplanar alkyl halide reacting with a base: the bracketed transition state has a dotted bond to H, a departing X, and overlapping colored orbitals that form the alkene product. Arrows connect the reactant, transition state, and product.

ch11/fig-11.18a.description: A two-stage drawing depicts a one-step E2 elimination: a base removes a neighboring H as the C=C bond forms and X leaves through a bracketed transition state. The products shown are a generic alkene, B–H⁺, and X⁻.

ch11/p375c.description: An E2 reaction diagram shows a base removing H from one carbon as the adjacent C–X bond breaks, forming a C=C bond in a single step. Curved arrows trace the electron movement, and the products include B⁺–H and X⁻.

ch11/we-11.3b.description: The scheme shows 1-chloro-1-methylcyclohexane reacting with KOH in ethanol to give two alkene products: 1-methylcyclohexene, labelled major, and methylenecyclohexane, labelled minor. It illustrates the preference for the more substituted double bond in this elimination.

ch11/prob-11-15a.description: The problem shows a five-carbon chain with a bromine attached to one middle carbon and a methyl group attached to the adjacent carbon. It asks about elimination products, but no products are drawn.

ch11/we-11.4.description: A base removes a hydrogen from a dibromo, diphenyl-substituted two-carbon structure as a bromine leaves, with curved arrows showing formation of the double bond. The product shown is (Z)-1-bromo-1,2-diphenylethylene.

ch11/p378a.description: The figure compares anti-periplanar (staggered, lower-energy) and syn-periplanar (eclipsed, higher-energy) arrangements of H and X on adjacent carbons. Each arrangement is shown as a bond-line drawing, a Newman projection, and a ball-and-stick model.

ch11/fig-11.22b.description: 2-Chloro-2-methylpropane reacts in water and ethanol at 65 °C to give 2-methyl-2-propanol (64%) and 2-methylpropene (36%). The diagram shows the alcohol and alkene products side by side, without drawing the intermediate steps mentioned in the caption.

ch11/prob-11-15c.description: A cyclohexane ring is bonded to a CH(Br)CH₃ group, showing an alkyl halide for the elimination-products problem. No reaction products are drawn.

ch11/fig-11.20.description: Two chair conformations show that an axial chlorine and neighboring axial hydrogen are anti periplanar, allowing an E2 reaction with base to form a cyclohexene ring and HCl. With equatorial chlorine, the diagram says “No reaction from this conformation.”
labels_in_image: Axial chlorine: H and Cl are anti periplanar
Equatorial chlorine: H and Cl are not anti periplanar

ch11/p382.description: A base removes the hydrogen next to a carbonyl group in a generic X-substituted structure, forming an anion shown in two resonance forms. Curved arrows then show loss of X and formation of a carbon–carbon double bond beside the carbonyl.

ch11/fig-11.18b.description: A base converts a brominated phenethyl structure into a phenyl-substituted alkene, with H or D shown at the carbon next to the CH₂Br group. The labels indicate that elimination of H is faster than elimination of D.

ch11/we-11.5a.description: Two reaction prompts show chlorocyclopentane treated with sodium methoxide in methanol (a), and a benzene ring bearing a CH(Br)CH₃ group treated with formic acid in water (b). Each reaction arrow ends in a question mark rather than a product.

ch11/p378b.description: Side-by-side diagrams compare an S_N2 reaction, where a nucleophile attacks a carbon from the side opposite X, with an E2 reaction, where electrons from a neighboring C–H bond move toward the C–C bond as X leaves. Curved arrows show the electron movement, and the E2 arrangement is labeled anti periplanar.

ch11/p383.description: A curved-arrow mechanism shows 3-hydroxybutyryl thioester converting through a charged intermediate to crotonyl thioester, with H₂O leaving. A blue nitrogen-containing ring participates in proton transfers as the double bond forms.

ch11/p379.description: A curved-arrow scheme shows meso-1,2-dibromo-1,2-diphenylethane reacting with KOH in ethanol to form (E)-1-bromo-1,2-diphenylethylene. Newman-style projections below show the reactant’s anti-periplanar geometry and the product’s arrangement; a key identifies Ph as a phenyl group.

ch11/prob-11-18.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a five-carbon chain with a bromine atom on the second carbon and a methyl branch on the third. The problem asks about the stereochemistry of the alkene formed by E2 elimination, but the product is not shown.

ch11/prob-11-20a.description: A reaction scheme shows CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Br treated with NaN₃ in THF, giving CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂N=N=N. It is presented as one reaction to classify by mechanism, without a mechanism shown.

ch11/p384.description: A benzylic bromide reacts with HCO₂H in H₂O to give a formate ester labeled Sₙ1 and an alkene labeled E1. The drawing illustrates competing substitution and elimination products.

ch11/we-11.5b.description: The diagram shows chlorocyclopentane reacting with sodium methoxide in methanol to form cyclopentene. The arrow is labeled “E2 reaction,” illustrating an elimination.

ch11/p387e.description: A base removes H from the carbon next to a carbonyl, forming a bracketed carbanion intermediate. Curved arrows then show a C=C bond forming as X leaves, giving an alkene beside the carbonyl and HX.

ch11/prob-11-20b.description: The reaction drawing shows CH₃CH₂CH(Cl)CH₂CH₃ converting to CH₃CH₂CH=CHCH₃, with KOH over the arrow and ethanol below it. The figure is a problem asking the reader to classify the reaction mechanism.

ch11/p387b.description: A generic alkyl halide, R₃C–X, loses X to form a bracketed carbocation, R₃C⁺; a nucleophile then bonds to the carbon, yielding R₃C–Nu and X⁻. The two arrows illustrate the stepwise SN1 substitution shown in the section heading.

ch11/p387c.description: A nucleophile (Nu:) attacks a generic carbon bonded to X as the C–X bond breaks, forming a C–Nu bond and X⁻. Wedge and dashed bonds show the carbon’s three-dimensional arrangement before and after substitution.

ch11/prob-11-20c.description: A reaction arrow labeled CH₃CO₂H connects 1-chloro-1-methylcyclohexane to a cyclohexane product in which the chlorine has been replaced by an acetate group; the methyl group remains on the same ring carbon.

ch11/p387d.description: A generic E1 elimination scheme shows X leaving a substituted carbon to form a carbocation, followed by formation of a C=C double bond between adjacent carbons. The products shown are a generic alkene and HX.

ch11/prob-11-21a.description: A ball-and-stick model shows two bonded carbon atoms: one bears three hydrogens, and the other bears two hydrogens and a green atom. It illustrates the structure of a two-carbon alkyl halide.

ch11/p386.description: A sequence of structures shows isobutylbenzene converted to ibuprofen through a ketone and then an alcohol intermediate. The arrows list acetic anhydride and HF, H₂ with a Ni catalyst, and CO with a Pd catalyst.

ch11/p387f.description: Curved arrows show a base removing a hydrogen from the carbon adjacent to a brominated carbon as the C–H bond forms a double bond and the C–Br bond breaks. The reaction arrow is labeled KOH in ethanol, and the product is an alkene.

ch11/prob-11-20d.description: A cyclohexanone ring attached at its α-carbon to an OH-bearing carbon of a second cyclohexane ring is shown converting, with NaOH in ethanol over the arrow, to a structure with a double bond between the two rings. The drawing illustrates loss of the OH group and formation of that double bond.

ch11/prob-11-21b.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a green halogen atom attached to a central carbon that also bears two methyl groups and an ethyl group. Gray spheres represent carbon atoms, and small pale spheres represent hydrogens.

ch11/prob-11-22.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a branched alkyl acetate, with gray carbon atoms, pale hydrogen atoms, and two red oxygen atoms in the acetate group. The problem asks for the alkyl bromide that would form this product by an SN2 reaction, with stereochemistry shown.

ch11/prob-11-24.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a benzene ring attached to a carbon bearing a green chlorine atom; the adjacent carbon bears methyl and ethyl groups. The problem asks for the structure and Z/E stereochemistry of its E2 product with NaOH, but no product is shown.

ch11/prob-11-25b.description: A cyclohexane ring bearing an iodomethyl group is shown reacting with KCN; an arrow labeled DMSO points right, with no product shown. The drawing is a reaction-mechanism problem.

ch11/prob-11-26a.description: A reaction drawing shows a branched alcohol converted to the corresponding alkyl chloride, with HCl above the arrow and H₂O below it. The carbon skeleton remains the same while the OH group is replaced by Cl.

ch11/prob-11-25a.description: The figure shows 1-bromo-4-methylpentane plus a lithium acetylide, CH₃C≡C⁻ Li⁺, with THF written beneath a right-pointing reaction arrow. No product is shown.

ch11/prob-11-27b.description: The problem shows CH₂=CH–CH(Cl)–CH₃ reacting with CH₃CO₂Na in CH₃CO₂H, indicated above and below a right-pointing arrow. It asks for elimination products and a mechanism, but no products are drawn.

ch11/prob-11-26b.description: An allylic chloride, CH₂=CH–CH(Cl)–CH₃, reacts with CH₃CO₂Na in CH₃CO₂H to give CH₂=CH–CH(OCOCH₃)–CH₃. The drawing shows the chlorine-bearing position replaced by an acetate group while the double bond remains in place.

ch11/prob-11-27c.description: A cyclohexane chair bears an OH and CH₃ on one carbon, with another CH₃ and H on the adjacent carbon. An arrow marked H₂SO₄ indicates the conditions for the elimination reaction; no product is shown.

ch11/prob-11-26c.description: A reaction arrow labeled CH₃OH connects a cyclohexyl-substituted chain bearing Br to the same chain bearing OCH₃ in its place. The figure illustrates replacement of bromine by a methoxy group.

ch11/prob-11-27a.description: A skeletal structure of 2-methylbutan-2-ol is shown to the left of a reaction arrow labeled H₂SO₄; no product is drawn.

ch11/prob-11-28b.description: A skeletal structure of a branched alkyl bromide is shown reacting with (CH₃)₃COK in THF, with an arrow pointing to an unspecified product. The figure presents an elimination-reaction problem without showing its outcome.

ch11/prob-11-29b.description: A cyclohexanone ring bearing a methyl group next to the carbonyl and an OH group on the following carbon is shown reacting with NaOH in water; the product is left blank for the problem.

ch11/prob-11-29c.description: A reaction scheme shows 3-hydroxy-2-methylbutanal on the left and an arrow labeled CH₃ONa above and CH₃OH below; no product is drawn. It is presented as an elimination-reaction problem.

ch11/prob-11-29a.description: A hydroxy ketone is drawn with an arrow labeled CH₃ONa above and CH₃OH below; no product is shown. The figure presents a reaction for which the product and mechanism are to be predicted.

ch11/prob-11-21c.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a six-carbon ring with a green atom attached to one carbon; the carbon atoms are dark gray and the hydrogen atoms are pale. It illustrates the three-dimensional structure of chlorocyclohexane.

ch11/prob-11-30b.description: A reaction scheme shows sodium phenoxide and CH₃CH₂I separated by a plus sign, with an arrow labeled DMF. The product is left blank for the problem.

ch11/prob-11-35.description: A structural drawing shows argininosuccinate reacting with a base to give arginine and fumarate; fumarate is drawn as a carbon–carbon double bond with a carboxylate group at each end. The figure presents the reaction as a mechanism problem without showing the mechanism.

ch11/prob-11-30c.description: A reaction scheme shows a branched alkyl iodide with wedge-and-dash bonds at the iodine-bearing carbon, plus CH₃OH, followed by an arrow with no product shown.

ch11/prob-11-32.description: A skeletal drawing shows a bridged bicyclic structure with Br attached to the lower bridgehead carbon. It is presented as the tertiary alkyl bromide in the problem statement, with no reaction or products drawn.

ch11/prob-11-28a.description: A cyclohexane ring has chlorine on a solid wedge and a methyl group on a dashed bond at adjacent carbons. An arrow labeled CH₃ONa above and CH₃OH below presents elimination conditions; no product is shown.

ch11/prob-11-30d.description: A cyclopropane ring bearing bromine and an ethyl group on the same carbon is shown reacting with CH3CH2ONa; the arrow lists CH3CH2OH beneath it. No product is drawn.

ch11/prob-11-37.description: A reaction arrow shows 2-bromopropanoic acid treated with 1% NaOH in water, then H₃O⁺, to give 2-hydroxypropanoic acid. Wedge and dashed bonds show that the stereocenter retains its configuration as Br is replaced by OH.

ch11/prob-11-31.description: A bromohydrin with OH and Br on adjacent carbons is shown converting to a three-membered epoxide ring under NaOH in ethanol. Solid and dashed wedges indicate the substituents’ spatial orientation in both structures.

ch11/prob-11-45a.description: The drawing shows CH₃–C≡C–CH(CH₃)–CH₃, an alkyne with a methyl branch adjacent to one end of the carbon chain. It is one of the target structures in a nucleophilic-substitution preparation problem.

ch11/prob-11-38.description: A generic tert-butyl carbamate bearing an N–H and an R group reacts under CF₃CO₂H to give 2-methylpropene and a bracketed R-substituted carbamic acid. The figure presents the reaction as a mechanism problem but shows no mechanistic steps.

ch11/prob-11-54c.description: A reaction arrow shows a cyclohexane ring bearing OH and CH₃ on the same carbon converted to the corresponding ring structure bearing Cl and CH₃, with SOCl₂ above the arrow and “Pyridine (a base)” below it. It illustrates replacement of the hydroxyl group by chlorine.

ch11/prob-11-52.description: The problem shows CH₃CH(CH₃)C(Br)(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ reacting under an arrow labeled HOAc and Heat, with a question mark in place of the product. It asks for the major alkene product of an E1 reaction but does not draw the product.

ch11/prob-11-36.description: A cyclohexane ring bearing a methyl ester reacts with LiI in DMF to give the corresponding lithium carboxylate and CH3I. The diagram illustrates the ester cleavage reaction stated in the problem without showing a mechanism.

ch11/prob-11-51.description: A reaction scheme shows 1-chloro-1,2-diphenylethane treated with −OCH₃ to form trans-1,2-diphenylethylene. The drawing illustrates elimination of HCl to produce a carbon–carbon double bond between the phenyl-bearing carbons.

answer_key/ans-10-5.description: This figure displays three resonance structures of a cyclohexadienyl radical, illustrating the delocalization of the radical electron within the conjugated system.

ch08/prob-8-36.description: The reaction scheme shows cyclohexene treated with Hg(OAc)₂ in CH₃OH, then NaBH₄, to form cyclohexyl methyl ether with an OCH₃ substituent. The figure asks the reader to suggest a mechanism for this transformation.

ch08/prob-8-33.description: The scheme shows γ-bisabolene converted by “Br⁺” and bromo-peroxidase through labeled bromonium-ion and cyclic-carbocation stages, then treatment with base (−H⁺) to give 10-bromo-α-chamigrene. The intermediate structures are not drawn; the problem asks the reader to draw them and propose the route.

ch08/prob-8-42a.description: A problem reaction shows 1-methylcyclohexene treated with 1. O₃ and 2. Zn, H₃O⁺, with a question mark at the product side. It asks for the product without depicting one.

ch08/prob-8-48e.description: A branched alkene, CH₃CH=CHCH(CH₃)CH₃, is shown in a reaction scheme with a question mark above the arrow, yielding CH₃CHO and CH₃CH(CH₃)CHO. It illustrates a problem asking about the alkene reaction and its carbonyl products; the nearby text mentions ozonolysis.

ch08/prob-8-68.description: A branched terminal alkyne, 5-methyl-1-hexyne, is shown for three product-prediction reactions: (a) 1 equiv Br₂, (b) 2 equiv H₂ with Pd/C, and (c) 1 equiv HBr. Each reaction arrow ends with a pink question mark; no products are drawn.

ch08/prob-8-42c.description: A methyl-substituted cyclohexene is shown undergoing a two-step reaction, with “1. BH₃” and “2. H₂O₂, −OH” above the arrow and a question mark at the product position. The product is left unspecified, illustrating a problem asking the viewer to predict it.

ch09/p300a.description: A long, hydrogen-terminated carbon chain with alternating triple and single bonds is shown. The caption identifies it as a polyyne detected in interstellar space.
labels_in_image: A polyyne detected in interstellar space

ch09/p300d.description: The figure compares three four-carbon substituent structures: butyl with only single bonds, 1-butenyl with a double bond, and 1-butynyl with a triple bond; each has a marked attachment point. It illustrates the corresponding alkyl, alkenyl, and alkynyl group names, with newer forms shown in parentheses for the latter two.

ch09/p300c.description: Two numbered alkyne–alkene structures illustrate numbering and naming when a molecule contains both a double and a triple bond, including examples with the older and newer naming formats. The second structure also has a methyl substituent.

ch09/p302c.description: The figure shows 1-butyne undergoing two successive Br₂ additions in CH₂Cl₂, first forming (E)-1,2-dibromo-1-butene and then 1,1,2,2-tetrabromobutane. It illustrates trans stereochemistry in the first halogen-addition product and further addition across the double bond.

ch09/p302a.description: The reaction scheme shows two successive HBr additions to 1-hexyne, first forming 2-bromo-1-hexene and then 2,2-dibromohexane, with CH₃CO₂H shown beneath each arrow. It illustrates addition of HX to an alkyne.

ch09/we-9.1d.description: A three-step synthesis converts 1-pentyne to 2-hexyne using NaNH₂/NH₃ followed by CH₃I/THF, then reduces it with H₂ and Lindlar catalyst to cis-2-hexene. The figure illustrates preparation of a cis alkene from an alkyne.

ch09/fig-9.7a.description: The mechanism shows the acetylide anion attacking bromomethane as the C–C bond forms and the C–Br bond breaks through a transition state, yielding propyne and NaBr. It illustrates alkylation by simultaneous bond formation and bond cleavage.

ch09/p313.description: Bromocyclohexane reacts with sodium methylacetylide, with the illustrated outcome giving cyclohexene, propyne (CH₃C≡CH), and NaBr; the alternative cyclohexyl alkyne product is crossed out and marked “Not formed.” The figure contrasts the shown elimination outcome with the unformed substitution product for a secondary alkyl halide.

ch09/p304b.description: An enol tautomer and a keto tautomer are shown in equilibrium, with the enol labeled less favored and the keto form more favored. The structures illustrate the preference for the keto form in the keto–enol tautomeric equilibrium.

ch09/we-9.3a.description: The reaction scheme shows acetylene (HC≡CH) and a generic alkyl halide (RX) leading to 5-methyl-1-hexanol. It illustrates a synthesis target from acetylene and an alkyl halide.

ch09/p319c.description: A generic terminal alkyne (RC≡CH) is treated with NaNH₂ to form a sodium acetylide, which reacts with R′CH₂Br to give an internal alkyne (RC≡CCH₂R′). The figure illustrates alkylation of an acetylide anion.

ch09/p319d.description: A generic alkyne undergoes two successive additions of HX in ether: the first gives an alkene bearing X and H, and the second gives a saturated product with both X groups on one carbon. It illustrates addition of hydrogen halides to alkynes.

molecules.name: R-substituted alkene bearing X and H
R-substituted saturated product bearing two X groups and two H atoms

ch09/p320c.description: A generic terminal alkyne, R—C≡C—H, reacts with NaNH₂ in NH₃ to form the acetylide anion R—C≡C:⁻ paired with Na⁺, along with NH₃. The figure illustrates conversion of a terminal alkyne into an acetylide anion.

ch09/prob-9-17.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a five-membered carbon ring with a triple bond as one side. The problem identifies it as a cycloalkyne and asks why it is too unstable to exist.

ch09/prob-9-21c.description: An enol with a branched alkyl group is shown reacting with H₃O⁺ to give the corresponding ketone, illustrating enol-to-ketone tautomerization. The product has a carbonyl group and a methyl group where the enol had a terminal CH₂ group.

ch09/prob-9-16b.description: A ball-and-stick model of the cycloalkyne in the problem shows a carbon framework with a triple bond, a carbonyl group, and attached hydrogens. The figure presents the structure whose instability the problem asks the reader to explain.

ch09/prob-9-19a.description: A terminal alkyne reacts with 2 HCl to give a product with two chlorine atoms attached to the same carbon. The reaction drawing is presented as a problem asking for a mechanism.

ch09/prob-9-24a.description: The problem shows phenylacetylene treated sequentially with 1. NaNH₂ and 2. CH₃I, with an arrow indicating a reaction whose product is left blank. It asks the reader to predict the product and provide the complete electron-pushing mechanism.

ch09/prob-9-23b.description: A reaction scheme shows CH₃CH₂C≡CCH₂CH₃ reacting with Br₂ to form an alkene bearing a Br and an ethyl group on each double-bond carbon; the two ethyl groups are drawn on opposite sides of the double bond. The scheme is presented as part of a problem asking readers to classify the reaction mechanism.

ch09/prob-9-37a.description: The problem shows CH₃CH₂C≡CH converting to CH₃CH₂COCH₃, with a question mark above the reaction arrow for the missing conditions. It illustrates a reaction to be completed, without specifying the reagent.

ch09/prob-9-37e.description: A generic reaction arrow with a question mark shows CH₃CH₂C≡CH converting to CH₃CH₂CO₂H; it is a problem asking for the missing reaction condition or reagent.

ch09/prob-9-34c.description: The scheme shows a carbon chain with an aldehyde at one end and a carbonyl-bearing carboxylic-acid group at the other, alongside CO₂. It is a problem prompt asking for reagents a–c; no reagents or solution are shown in this crop.

ch09/prob-9-42b.description: The figure shows the condensed structure of octan-4-one, with a carbonyl group between a propyl group and a butyl group. It is one of the organic structures in a problem about introducing deuterium into molecules.

ch10/p331a.description: A numbered pentane chain is shown with Br on carbon 1, Cl on carbon 3, and a CH₃ branch on carbon 4. The figure illustrates the structure corresponding to the printed name “1-Bromo-3-chloro-4-methylpentane.”

ch10/p338b.description: 1-Methylcyclohexanol reacts with HCl gas in ether at 0 °C to form 1-chloro-1-methylcyclohexane and water; the product is labeled 90%.

ch10/prob-10-1c.description: The problem shows a condensed structural formula with a central carbon bonded to two CH₃ groups, a Cl atom, and a –CH₂–CH₂–Cl chain. It is one of the alkyl-halide structures for which the exercise asks for an IUPAC name; the name is not supplied here.

ch10/prob-10-7b.description: The figure shows a linearly written alkene, CH₃CH(CH₃)CH=CHCH₂CH₃, with a methyl branch on the second carbon. It is a problem structure for predicting products with NBS; no products are shown.

ch10/fig-10.3.description: The mechanism shows a Br· radical abstracting an allylic hydrogen from cyclohexene to form an allylic radical and HBr; HBr reacts with NBS to form Br₂, which brominates the allylic radical and regenerates Br·. The numbered steps and dashed pink arrows illustrate the radical chain process.

ch10/prob-10-10.description: A reaction scheme shows CH₃CH(Br)CH₂CH₃ converting to CH₃CH(D)CH₂CH₃, with a question mark above the arrow. It illustrates the problem of replacing a halogen substituent with deuterium; no reaction conditions are provided.

ch10/p343a.description: The figure shows methane reacting with Cl₂ to form chloromethane and HCl, marked as oxidation because a C–H bond is broken and a C–Cl bond is formed. In the reverse conversion, chloromethane treated with Mg in ether followed by H₃O⁺ gives methane, marked as reduction because a C–Cl bond is broken and a C–H bond is formed.

ch10/p339a.description: Two alcohol-to-alkyl-halide reactions are shown: benzoin is converted to the corresponding chloro ketone using SOCl₂/pyridine, and 2-butanol is converted to 2-bromobutane using PBr₃. The examples illustrate preparation of alkyl halides from alcohols and report 86% yields for both products.

ch10/we-10.2b.description: The structures are arranged in increasing oxidation level as propane < propene = 2-propanol < acetone. The equal sign indicates that propene and 2-propanol have the same oxidation level in this comparison.

ch10/p346b.description: A generic alcohol reacts with HX in ether to form the corresponding carbon–X product; the figure gives the reactivity order as 3° > 2° > 1°.

ch10/prob-10-22d.description: The problem shows CH₃CH₂CHBrCH₃ treated with Mg in ether to form an unknown A, followed by H₂O to form an unknown B. It illustrates a two-step reaction sequence with the intermediate and product left for the student to determine.

ch10/prob-10-17.description: The reaction shows tert-butyl bromide treated with H₂O at 50 °C to give tert-butanol and HBr. It is presented as a problem asking for a mechanism; no mechanism is drawn.

ch10/prob-10-12.description: Four skeletal structures are shown in a row: cyclohexane, benzene, cyclohexanone, and 1-chlorocyclohexene, as compounds in an oxidation-level ranking problem. The figure presents the structures without showing a ranking.

ch10/prob-10-23.description: A reaction scheme shows 2-pentene treated with NBS under hν in CCl₄, with the proposed product drawn as CH₃CH₂CH=CHCH₂Br. It is presented as a problem asking what is wrong with the proposed plan and what side products would form; the scheme itself does not show an answer.

ch10/prob-10-22e.description: A reaction problem shows CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂Br treated with Li in pentane to give an unknown A, followed by CuI to give an unknown B. It asks the reader to identify the structures represented by A and B.

ch10/prob-10-24.description: A skeletal structure of 1-methylcyclohexene is shown reacting with NBS under hν in CCl₄, with a magenta question mark where the product(s) would be. The figure poses a problem asking what product(s) to expect; no product is shown.

ch10/prob-10-37c.description: A cyclohexane ring bearing fluorine reacts with lithium dimethylcuprate, (CH₃)₂CuLi, in ether to give a cyclohexane ring bearing a methyl group. The reaction illustrates replacement of the ring’s fluorine substituent by methyl.

ch10/prob-10-39.description: The figure shows 1-methoxycyclohexene reacting with HBr to give a cyclohexane bearing OCH₃ and Br on the same carbon. It illustrates the observed product in an electrophilic addition problem about carbocation intermediates and resonance.

ch10/prob-10-30a.description: Three six-membered cyclohexene-ring radicals are shown, with the radical dot at different positions relative to the double bond. The figure presents them as structures to be ranked from most stable to least stable.

ch11/fig-11.2.description: The cycle shows (+)-malic acid converted to (+)-chlorosuccinic acid with PCl₅ in ether, then to (–)-malic acid with Ag₂O and H₂O; the reverse sequence connects (–)-malic acid and (–)-chlorosuccinic acid. It illustrates interconversion of the two malic-acid forms through chlorosuccinic acid.

ch11/p354.description: The figure contrasts two reactions of a brominated alkane with hydroxide: substitution replaces Br with OH, while elimination forms an alkene and produces water and bromide. It illustrates the competing substitution and elimination pathways described in the surrounding text.

ch11/p356.description: The diagram shows hydroxide ion attacking the methyl carbon of bromomethane as the C–Br bond electrons move to bromine, forming methanol and bromide ion. It illustrates the bond-making and bond-breaking steps of an SN2 substitution.

ch11/fig-11.3.description: A three-step Walden cycle interconverts (+)- and (−)-1-phenyl-2-propanol through tosylate and acetate derivatives, with rotation values shown beside the structures. The chirality center is marked with an asterisk, and step 2 shows acetate replacing tosylate with inversion at that center.

ch11/fig-11.7.description: Four alkyl bromides are shown as structural formulas and space-filling models, with arrows indicating approach toward the carbon bonded to bromine. From (a) to (d), increasing crowding around that carbon illustrates progressively greater steric hindrance and slower SN2 reactions.

ch11/p367.description: (R)-6-chloro-2,6-dimethyloctane reacts with water in ethanol to give the alcohol in two stereochemical forms: 60% (S), labeled inversion, and 40% (R), labeled retention. The figure illustrates that the SN1 reaction gives incomplete racemization, with more inversion than retention.

ch11/p369a.description: The figure compares carbocation stability, showing the order methyl < primary < allylic ≈ benzylic ≈ secondary < tertiary, with an arrow indicating increasing stability to the right. Each category is illustrated with a carbocation structure.

ch11/prob-11-12.description: The chart orders leaving-group reactivity as HO⁻ < Cl⁻ < Br⁻ < I⁻ ≈ TosO⁻ < H₂O, with the arrow indicating increasing reactivity to the right. It illustrates the relative reactivity order shown for leaving groups in the SN1 context.

ch11/fig-11.14b.description: The figure shows 2-methyl-2-propanol reacting with HX to form a tertiary alkyl halide and water, with a note that the rate is the same for X = Cl, Br, or I. It illustrates the overall SN1 reaction of a tertiary alcohol with HBr; the caption identifies neutral water as the leaving group in step 2.
labels_in_image: Same rate for X = Cl, Br, I

ch11/fig-11.17.description: The figure shows norepinephrine reacting with S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) in an SN2 substitution to form epinephrine (adrenaline) and S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH). The methyl group transfers to norepinephrine’s nitrogen as the sulfur-containing leaving group departs.

ch11/p373.description: Two dissociation diagrams show a generic alkyl chloride, R–Cl, forming R⁺ and Cl⁻, and a generic organodiphosphate forming R⁺ and a diphosphate ion (PPᵢ), with Mg²⁺ shown coordinating the phosphate groups. The figure illustrates ionization of different leaving groups in biological substitution reactions.

ch11/fig-11.16.description: The reaction scheme shows dimethylallyl diphosphate reacting with isopentenyl diphosphate through carbocation intermediates to form geranyl diphosphate, then geraniol. Curved arrows illustrate two SN1 substitutions with diphosphate leaving groups, followed by water attack and deprotonation.

ch11/fig-11.21.description: The figure compares E2 dehydrochlorination of neomenthyl chloride, which eliminates from a trans-diaxial conformation to form 3-menthene, with menthyl chloride, which must ring-flip from a trans-diequatorial conformation before elimination to form 2-menthene. Newman projections and chair conformations illustrate how cyclohexane ring orientation affects whether the required geometry for elimination is available.

ch11/fig-11.22a.description: The figure shows a two-step E1 elimination: tertiary alkyl chloride dissociates in the slow, rate-limiting first step to form a carbocation and chloride, then a base removes a neighboring proton in a fast step as a C–H bond electron pair forms the alkene π bond. It illustrates the carbocation intermediate and the difference in rates between the two steps.

ch11/fig-11.23.description: The figure shows menthyl chloride chair conformations and compares elimination outcomes: E2 conditions produce 2-menthene (100%), while E1 conditions produce 2-menthene (32%) and 3-menthene (68%). It illustrates how the conditions affect the alkene product mixture, with the E2 pathway shown as an anti-periplanar elimination.

ch11/p387a.description: A three-row summary shows primary RCH₂X substrates giving mostly Sₙ2 substitution, secondary R₂CHX substrates giving Sₙ2 substitution with nonbasic nucleophiles or E2 elimination with strong bases, and tertiary R₃CX substrates giving mostly E2 elimination, with Sₙ1/E1 noted in nonbasic solvents. It illustrates how substitution and elimination outcomes vary with substrate class and conditions.

ch11/prob-11-28c.description: A branched alkyl tosylate, with OTs on the carbon next to a tert-butyl-like group, is shown reacting under CH₃ONa in CH₃OH; no products or mechanism are drawn. The figure is an elimination-reaction problem asking the reader to predict the products and show the mechanism.

ch11/prob-11-30a.description: A hydroxyl-substituted cyclohexane bearing an adjacent acetyl group is shown reacting with NaOH in H₂O, with an arrow toward an unspecified product. The image presents a reaction-prediction problem without showing its answer.

ch11/prob-11-25c.description: A stereochemical chlorinated cyclic ether is shown reacting with sodium methanethiolate (CH₃S⁻ Na⁺) in DMF, with a reaction arrow and no product drawn. The problem asks for the reaction mechanism; the image provides the structures but does not show a solution.

ch11/prob-11-23.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a chloro-substituted carbon in a chain bearing a terminal alkene and a terminal hydroxyl group; the chlorine is green. The problem asks for the molecule’s R/S configuration and the expected product and configuration in an SN2 reaction with NaCN.

ch11/prob-11-45b.description: The structure shown is methyl tert-butyl ether, with an oxygen linking a methyl group to a carbon bearing three methyl groups. It is one of the target structures in the nucleophilic-substitution preparation problem.

ch11/prob-11-33.description: The scheme shows S-adenosylhomocysteine oxidized by NAD⁺ to a carbonyl-containing intermediate, with NADH and H⁺ formed; treatment with base then gives homocysteine and an adenine-containing ring product bearing an exocyclic double bond. It illustrates the two-step conversion shown by the arrows, without specifying the identity of the base.

ch11/prob-11-40.description: The diagram shows a chiral benzylic-chain alcohol converted to its tosylate and then, with ethanol and heat, to an ethyl ether; a second route converts the alcohol to its potassium alkoxide and reacts it with bromoethane to give the ether. The positive and negative optical-rotation values illustrate the Walden cycle, whose accompanying prompt asks where inversion occurs.

ch11/prob-11-54a.description: The reaction scheme shows 2-bromobutane treated with potassium tert-butoxide in tert-butanol, with the depicted product having an OC(CH₃)₃ group attached at the same carbon that bore bromine. It illustrates one of the proposed reactions in a problem asking what is wrong with the scheme and what the actual product is; this description does not resolve the problem.

ch11/prob-11-54b.description: A reaction scheme shows a cyclohexane ring bearing F treated with Na⁺ OH⁻, with a cyclohexane ring bearing OH drawn as the product. It illustrates a proposed substitution in a problem asking what is wrong with the reaction as written and what the actual product would be.

ch11/prob-11-56a.description: The figure shows three structures: tert-butyl chloride, 2-chloro-2-phenylpropane, and butan-2-amine. They are presented as compounds to compare for SN1 reactivity; no ordering is shown.

ch11/prob-11-55a.description: Three five-membered ring carbocations are shown, each with a double bond along the lower-left ring edge; the positive charge and presence or position of a methyl substituent differ among them. The figure asks the reader to arrange the carbocations in order of increasing stability.

ch11/prob-11-55c.description: Three skeletal alkenyl-containing carbocations are shown, each with the positive charge at a different carbon along the framework. They are presented as a problem set to order by SN1 reactivity; no ranking is supplied in the figure.

molecules.name: alkenyl-containing carbocation (positive charge on the carbon adjacent to the alkene)
alkenyl-containing carbocation (positive charge farther along the carbon chain)
alkenyl-containing carbocation (positive charge on the terminal branch)

ch11/prob-11-56b.description: The figure shows benzyl bromide, 1-bromo-1-phenylethane, and triphenylmethyl bromide as three structures in an SN2-reactivity ordering problem. It presents the compounds to compare without giving an order.

ch11/prob-11-57a.description: Three alkyl chlorides are shown: tert-butyl chloride, 1-chloropropane, and 2-chlorobutane. They are presented as a set to be ordered by SN2 reactivity; no ordering is provided in the figure.

ch11/prob-11-55b.description: The figure shows three branched-chain skeletal carbocations, with the positive charge at a terminal carbon, an internal carbon, and a branched carbon, respectively. It presents them for comparison in a problem asking for increasing stability; no ordering is supplied in the drawing.

ch11/prob-11-57b.description: Problem 11-57(a) shows three condensed structural formulas of alkyl bromides, arranged side by side: 2-bromo-3-methylbutane, 1-bromo-2-methylpropane, and 1-bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane. They are presented as a set to be ordered by SN2 reactivity; no ordering is shown.

ch11/prob-11-58a.description: A cyclohexane bearing OTs and CH₃ at opposite ring positions, both shown with solid wedges, is shown with KCN in DMSO and an arrow to an unfilled product side. The problem asks for the major product(s) and whether the product mixture would rotate plane-polarized light.

ch11/prob-11-58b.description: A stereochemically drawn bromoalkane with a wedge H and dashed methyl group is shown reacting with sodium methoxide in methanol; the product is not shown, and the prompt asks the reader to predict it. The figure is a problem about an alkyl-halide reaction, not a worked solution.

ch11/prob-11-59.description: The problem shows a chiral alkyl tosylate, CH₃–CH(OTos)–CH₂OCH₃, with the hydrogen and OTs bonds drawn as wedge and dashed bonds and “(S stereochemistry)” printed below. An arrow labeled NaCN points toward a question mark for the product; the product is not shown.

ch11/prob-11-58c.description: A stereochemical skeletal structure of 1-chloro-1,2-dimethylcyclopentane is shown with a reaction arrow and CH₃OH beneath it; the product side is blank. The drawing illustrates a reaction prompt with the substrate’s substituent orientations indicated by solid and dashed wedges.

ch11/prob-11-61.description: The problem shows trans-1-bromo-2-methylcyclohexane reacting with KOH, with an arrow to a drawn methylcyclohexene product; the reactant’s wedge-and-dash bonds and the product’s double bond are shown. It illustrates a reaction-product prediction problem that asks for stereochemistry where necessary.

ch11/prob-11-60.description: The problem diagram compares two possible reactant pairs—cyclohexoxide with CH₃I, or iodocyclohexane with CH₃O⁻—both shown leading to cyclohexyl methyl ether. It illustrates alternative routes to the same ether without indicating which route to choose.

ch11/prob-11-62.description: The problem shows a substituted cyclohexane bearing Br and CH₃ on one ring carbon and CH₃ and H on the opposite ring carbon, with wedge-and-dash stereochemistry; it is treated with H₂O in ethanol, and the product is left as a question mark. The figure asks the reader to predict the product(s) and indicate stereochemistry where necessary, without showing a solution.

ch11/prob-11-64a.description: The reaction scheme shows (E)-1-chlorobut-1-ene, with ethyl and chlorine on opposite sides of the double bond, treated first with Na⁺ NH₂⁻ and then H₃O⁺. The product side is left blank for the problem to be completed.

ch11/prob-11-63.description: A vinylic chloride bearing a carboxyl group on each alkene carbon is shown reacting with 1. Na⁺ NH₂⁻ and 2. H₃O⁺ to give the corresponding alkyne. The problem asks for products and mechanisms in the follow-up; the figure itself shows the starting material and product.

ch11/prob-11-66.description: A condensed structural formula shows a central carbon bonded to OH, CH₃, a propyl group, and an ethyl group. It is labeled “3-Methyl-3-hexanol.”

ch11/prob-11-65.description: The figure shows the structure of 2-butanol, with an OH group attached to the second carbon of the four-carbon chain. It illustrates the alcohol referenced in the racemization problem.

ch11/prob-11-64b.description: A substituted alkene bearing Br and Ph on one carbon and CH₃ and H on the other is shown with an arrow and the sequence 1. Na⁺ NH₂⁻, 2. H₃O⁺; no product is drawn. It is a reaction problem asking for the product(s) and mechanism.

ch11/prob-11-64c.description: The drawing shows (Z)-1-chloroprop-1-ene, with H atoms on the same side of the double bond, followed by an arrow labeled “1. Na⁺ −NH₂” and “2. H₃O⁺”; no product is shown. It illustrates a two-step reaction sequence with sodium amide followed by acidic workup.

ch11/prob-11-72.description: The reaction scheme shows benzyl alcohol converted to benzyl chloride with TosCl and pyridine at 60 °C. It is presented as a problem about the product formed under these conditions.

ch11/prob-11-67.description: 1-Bromo-2-deuterio-2-phenylethane reacts with tert-butoxide to give two phenylethylene structures: one with D and one with H on the phenyl-substituted alkene carbon. The products are bracketed as a 7:1 ratio.

ch11/prob-11-73.description: A reaction scheme shows homocysteine converted to methionine by methionine synthase, with the transferred methyl group labeled with H, D, and T isotopes to pose a question about inversion versus retention of configuration. Below, N-methyltetrahydrofolate is shown alongside a separate nitrogen-containing structure, with a plus sign between them.

ch11/prob-11-74.description: The scheme shows pentylamine treated with excess CH₃I, then Ag₂O and H₂O, to give 1-pentene. It illustrates an elimination reaction of an amine-derived substrate.

ch11/prob-11-69.description: A deuterated bridged bicyclic bromo compound reacts with “Base” to form a bridged bicyclic alkene; the product is shown without deuterium. The figure illustrates the stated syn elimination that gives an undeuterated alkene.

ch12/fig-12.1.description: A glass cup of espresso on a saucer sits among scattered coffee beans. The photograph introduces the idea that many compounds isolated from coffee have had their structures determined using spectroscopic techniques.

ch12/p398a.description: A flow diagram shows a sample entering an ionization source, followed by a mass analyzer and detector, with the detector sending output to a display. It illustrates the main stages and example options in a mass spectrometer.

ch12/p398b.description: The diagram shows an organic molecule labeled RH struck by an electron, forming the cation radical RH⁺• and a separate electron. It illustrates electron bombardment producing a positively charged radical.

ch12/fig-12.2.description: A schematic shows a sample entering an ionization chamber, where a heated filament produces an electron beam that ionizes and fragments molecules; the ions pass through slits and a magnetic sector that deflects them according to m/z before reaching a detector and LCD display. It illustrates how an electron-ionization magnetic-sector mass spectrometer sorts charged fragments by mass-to-charge ratio.

ch12/fig-12.3.description: A quadrupole mass analyzer is shown with an ion beam entering from the ionization chamber and passing between four charged rods. Ions with the correct m/z pass through to the detector, while ions with an incorrect m/z collide with the rods and cannot reach it.
labels_in_image: m/z correct; ion passes through quadrupole mass filter
m/z incorrect; ion cannot reach detector

ch12/fig-12.4.description: A mass spectrum of propane plots relative abundance (%) against m/z, with the tallest peak at m/z = 29 and another labeled peak at m/z = 44. It illustrates the distribution of ion abundances by mass-to-charge ratio.

ch11/prob-11-75.description: The scheme shows amine A reacting with an unspecified alkyl chloride B to form C, followed by treatment with SOCl₂ and Mg in ether to give D; D then reacts with the labeled sulfur-containing compound E to form F, which is shown leading to Flupentixol. The problem asks for the structure of B; it is not specified in the figure.

ch12/fig-12.5.description: A mass spectrum of 2,2-dimethylpropane plots relative abundance against m/z, with labeled peaks at m/z 29, 41, and 57; the peak at m/z 57 is the tallest, while no molecular-ion peak is observed. The figure illustrates fragmentation under electron-impact ionization and asks the reader to infer the m/z 57 ion’s formula and structure.

ch12/fig-12.6.description: The mass spectrum of hexane shows relative abundance versus m/z, with a base peak at m/z 57 and prominent peaks at 43, 29, and the molecular ion at 86. It illustrates the mixture of fragment ions formed when hexane’s similar carbon–carbon bonds break.

ch12/fig-12.8.description: Two stacked mass spectra compare unlabeled Sample A and Sample B, plotting relative abundance (%) against m/z with distinct peaks in each spectrum. The figure illustrates using mass-spectrum peak patterns to distinguish the two samples.

ch12/p401.description: The radical cation of 2,2-dimethylpropane fragments to form a tert-butyl cation and a methyl radical. The tert-butyl cation is marked as the m/z = 57 peak.

ch12/fig-12.9a.description: A mass spectrum plots relative abundance (%) against m/z, with prominent peaks near m/z 41, 69, and 84 and smaller peaks elsewhere. It is panel (a) of the paired spectra used in the problem to distinguish 2-methyl-2-pentene from 2-hexene.
