ch12/fig-12.10.description: Mass spectrum of 2-pentanol, with relative abundance plotted against m/z and a base peak at 45; a small structural drawing of 2-pentanol appears in the upper right with formula C₅H₁₂O and molecular weight 88.15. The figure illustrates the characteristic mass-spectrum peaks of the compound, including the molecular ion marked M (88).

ch12/fig-12.9b.description: A mass spectrum plots relative abundance (%) against m/z, with the tallest peak near m/z 55 and smaller peaks around 27, 39–43, 50–56, 69, and 84. It illustrates the fragment-mass pattern shown for Problem 12-2.

ch12/p404a.description: A generic alcohol radical cation undergoes alpha cleavage, producing an RCH₂ radical and a resonance-stabilized oxygen-containing carbocation. The diagram illustrates bond cleavage adjacent to the carbon bearing OH and the two resonance forms of the resulting ion.

ch12/p404c.description: The diagram shows alpha cleavage of a generic amine, breaking a C–C bond next to nitrogen to form an alkyl radical and a nitrogen-containing cation. Two resonance forms of the cation are shown.

ch12/fig-12.11.description: A mass spectrum plots relative abundance against m/z, with a base peak at 86 and a molecular ion marked M (101); a triethylamine structure labeled MW = 101 appears above the spectrum. It illustrates the mass spectrum of triethylamine.

ch12/fig-12.12.description: A mass spectrum of chloroethane (CH₃CH₂Cl) plots relative abundance (%) against m/z, with the molecular ion peak M at 64 and an M + 2 peak at 66. It illustrates the chlorine isotope pattern, with the M and M + 2 peaks in an approximately 3:1 abundance ratio.

ch12/fig-12.13.description: A mass spectrum of 1-bromohexane plots relative abundance (%) against m/z, with the strongest peak at 43, notable peaks at 85 and 135/137, and molecular-ion markers M (164) and M + 2 near the high-mass end. It illustrates the characteristic spectrum shown for 1-bromohexane.

ch12/fig-12.7.description: The diagram shows hexane ionized to a molecular ion, which fragments along several pathways into smaller positive ions. The fragments are listed with their m/z values and relative abundances, with m/z 57 marked as the base peak.

ch12/p406a.description: A generic carbonyl ion undergoes a McLafferty rearrangement: a hydrogen shifts to the oxygen as a C–C bond breaks, producing an alkene and a positively charged oxygen-containing fragment. The diagram illustrates this mass-spectrometric fragmentation pathway.

ch12/p404b.description: A bracketed alcohol radical cation undergoes dehydration, losing H₂O to form a bracketed alkene radical cation. The figure illustrates loss of water from an alcohol in mass spectrometry.

ch12/p406b.description: A bracketed carbonyl molecular ion with generic R and R′ groups undergoes alpha cleavage, forming an R radical and a resonance-stabilized acyl cation shown in two resonance forms. The figure illustrates fragmentation adjacent to the carbonyl carbon.

ch12/p406c.description: A generic carbonyl group is shown at the end of a carbon chain, with the successive chain positions labeled α, β, γ, and δ. The figure illustrates the Greek-letter naming of positions relative to a carbonyl group.

ch12/fig-12.15.description: A mass spectrum plots relative abundance (%) against m/z, with multiple fragment peaks and a base peak near m/z 59; a structural formula of 2-methyl-3-pentanol is shown at the right. The figure illustrates the fragmentation pattern used to identify fragments in the compound’s mass spectrum.

ch12/fig-12.17.description: A spectrum diagram lays out gamma rays, X rays, ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, microwaves, and radio waves along frequency and wavelength scales, with an arrow showing energy increasing toward the high-frequency end. A magnified visible band displays wavelengths from 380 to 780 nm in a color gradient, illustrating that visible light occupies only a small part of the electromagnetic spectrum.

ch12/we-12.2.description: The skeletal structure of 2-methylpentan-3-ol is annotated with two α-cleavage losses: loss of C₃H₇ gives a peak at mass 59, and loss of C₂H₅ gives a peak at mass 73. The molecular ion is marked M⁺ = 102.

ch12/fig-12.16.description: The MALDI–TOF mass spectrum of chicken egg-white lysozyme plots intensity (%) against mass-to-charge ratio (m/z), with peaks at 14,306.7578 and 28,614.2188 and additional lower-m/z protonated species. It illustrates the protein’s monoprotonated peak and a dimer impurity, alongside other multiply protonated species.

ch12/fig-12.19.description: An infrared spectrum for ethanol is plotted as transmittance (%) versus wavenumber (cm⁻¹), with multiple downward spikes indicating where energy is absorbed. The figure illustrates that lower transmittance corresponds to absorption.

ch12/fig-12.18.description: Three diagrams show sinusoidal electromagnetic waves with wavelength measured between successive maxima and amplitude measured from the centerline to a peak; violet light is illustrated with a 400 nm wavelength and infrared radiation with an 800 nm wavelength. The figure illustrates that electromagnetic radiation types differ in wavelength and frequency.

ch12/fig-12.20.description: A wavelength-scale diagram divides the electromagnetic spectrum into ultraviolet, visible, near infrared, infrared, far infrared, and microwave regions, with boundaries at 2.5 μm (4000 cm⁻¹) and 25 μm (400 cm⁻¹) marking the useful IR range. An arrow indicates energy increases toward shorter wavelengths, illustrating the infrared region’s position relative to adjacent spectrum bands.

ch12/fig-12.22.description: A transmittance-versus-wavenumber chart divides the infrared spectrum into four regions: single bonds to hydrogen (C—H, O—H, N—H), triple bonds (C≡C, C≡N), double bonds (C=C, C=N, C=O), and the fingerprint region. Dashed vertical lines mark the boundaries near 2500, 2000, and 1500 cm⁻¹.

ch12/fig-12.21.description: Three IR spectra plot transmittance against wavenumber for (a) hexane, (b) 1-hexene, and (c) 1-hexyne; arrows highlight the alkene- and alkyne-related absorptions in the latter spectra. The figure illustrates how the spectra differ among an alkane, an alkene, and a terminal alkyne.

ch12/p412.description: Four ball-and-stick diagrams show a central atom with attached lighter atoms moving in symmetric stretching, antisymmetric stretching, in-plane bending, and out-of-plane bending motions, indicated by pink arrows. The figure illustrates several allowed molecular vibration modes.

ch12/prob-12-4.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a carbon-and-hydrogen framework with a red oxygen bonded to a hydrogen, representing a hydroxyl group. It is the molecule given in Problem 12-4 for predicting parent-ion and fragment masses; no molecule name is printed.

ch12/p416a.description: The figure shows generic alkane C–H and C–C bonds alongside their indicated infrared absorption ranges: 2850–2960 cm⁻¹ and 800–1300 cm⁻¹, respectively. It illustrates characteristic IR absorptions associated with alkanes.

ch12/p416b.description: A table titled “Alkenes” pairs generic alkene structures with infrared absorption values: 3020–3100, 1640–1680, 910 and 990, and 890 cm⁻¹. It illustrates characteristic IR bands associated with alkene structures and substitution patterns.

ch12/p417a.description: A chart labeled “Alkynes” shows a generic internal C≡C bond associated with an absorption at 2100–2260 cm⁻¹ and a terminal ≡C—H group associated with an absorption at 3300 cm⁻¹. It illustrates characteristic infrared absorption positions for alkyne bonds.

ch12/fig-12.23.description: A chart compares infrared absorption ranges for C–H out-of-plane bending in generic mono-, cis-1,2-, trans-1,2-, 1,1-di-, tri-, and tetrasubstituted alkenes, with example structures and ranges plotted against wavelength (μm) and wavenumber (cm⁻¹). The marked ranges are labeled strong (s) or medium (m), illustrating how the absorption range varies with alkene substitution pattern.

ch12/fig-12.25.description: The figure shows an infrared spectrum of cyclohexanol, with transmittance plotted against wavenumber. Arrows mark the broad O–H stretch and the C–O stretch absorption bands.

ch12/p417b.description: Under “Aromatic compounds,” a generic alkene C–H fragment is paired with a weak band at 3030 cm⁻¹, and a benzene ring is paired with weak 1660–2000 cm⁻¹ and medium 1450–1600 cm⁻¹ bands. The figure illustrates characteristic infrared absorptions associated with aromatic compounds.

ch12/fig-12.26.description: The figure shows an IR spectrum of cyclohexylamine, with transmittance plotted against wavenumber and an NH₂ label with an arrow highlighting a dip in the spectrum. A skeletal drawing of the cyclohexylamine structure appears beneath the spectrum.

ch12/fig-12.24.description: A chart shows C–H out-of-plane bending absorption ranges from 900 to 700 cm⁻¹ for benzene rings with mono-, ortho-, meta-, para-, 1,2,4-, 1,2,3-, and 1,3,5-substitution patterns. Blue and red bars mark the ranges, with adjacent “s” and “m” annotations indicating strong and medium bands.

ch12/p418.description: A generic amine N–H bond is shown beside its 3300–3500 cm⁻¹ infrared absorption range, described as sharp and medium intensity. The figure illustrates the characteristic N–H stretching absorption of amines.

ch12/fig-12.27.description: An infrared spectrum plots transmittance against wavenumber, with a prominent absorption near the carbonyl region and weaker absorptions around 2750 and 2850 cm⁻¹ highlighted by arrows and structural sketches. The figure illustrates the characteristic IR features of benzaldehyde, including aldehyde C–H absorptions useful for distinguishing an aldehyde from a ketone.

ch12/p419a.description: The figure shows three aldehyde structures—propanal, but-2-enal, and benzaldehyde—with carbonyl IR absorbances labeled 1730 cm⁻¹, 1705 cm⁻¹, and 1705 cm⁻¹, respectively. It illustrates the characteristic IR absorbance associated with aldehydes.

ch12/p419b.description: The figure compares four ketone structures with their carbonyl IR absorption values: acetone (1715 cm⁻¹), cyclopentanone (1750 cm⁻¹), an unsaturated ketone (1690 cm⁻¹), and acetophenone (1690 cm⁻¹). It illustrates how the reported carbonyl absorption varies among these ketones.

ch12/p420.description: The figure shows three ester structures: methyl acetate with an absorption at 1735 cm⁻¹, an unsaturated ester and an aromatic ester each at 1715 cm⁻¹. It illustrates that a neighboring double bond or aromatic ring corresponds to a lower carbonyl absorption frequency than the saturated ester shown.

ch12/fig-12.28.description: An IR spectrum plots transmittance (%) against wavenumber (cm⁻¹), with numerous absorption dips across the range. It illustrates the spectral data for an unknown compound in Worked Example 12.6.

ch12/we-12.5.description: The worked example shows two skeletal structures: (a) a cyclohexene ring bearing a –CH₂OH group, and (b) a terminal alkyne-containing ketone with a methyl branch. It asks where these compounds might absorb in an IR spectrum, illustrating prediction of absorptions from functional groups.

ch12/we-12.6.description: A skeletal structure of phenylacetaldehyde shows a benzene ring attached to a –CH₂–CHO group, with the aldehyde oxygen drawn above the carbonyl carbon. It illustrates the structure of the compound discussed in the worked example.

ch12/fig-12.29.description: An infrared spectrum plots transmittance (%) against wavenumber (cm⁻¹), with a structural drawing of phenylacetylene inset. It illustrates the absorption bands in phenylacetylene’s IR spectrum.

ch12/prob-12-10a.description: The figure shows a cyclohexene ring with an acetyl group attached to one of the alkene carbons. It is a problem structure for identifying where the compound might absorb in an IR spectrum.

ch12/prob-12-10b.description: The figure shows HC≡C–CH₂–CH₂–CHO, a terminal alkyne chain ending in an aldehyde (4-pentynal). It is one of the structures in an IR-absorption problem.

ch12/fig-12.30.description: A multicolored ribbon model shows the folded, multi-subunit structure of human muscle fructose-1,6-bisphosphate aldolase. It illustrates the three-dimensional protein structure determined by X-ray crystallography.

ch12/prob-12-10c.description: The structure shows a benzene ring bearing adjacent CO₂H and CH₂OH substituents, identified as 2-(hydroxymethyl)benzoic acid. It is presented as a problem asking where the compound might have IR absorptions.

ch12/prob-12-11.description: A ball-and-stick model of an unnamed organic compound with a nitrile group, carbon–carbon double bonds, and a carbonyl group. It is presented in Problem 12-11 as a structure for predicting where IR absorptions might occur.

ch12/prob-12-12c.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a branched hydroxy ketone, with gray carbon atoms, red oxygen atoms, and white hydrogen atoms. It is one of the molecules in a problem asking where the molecules would absorb in an IR spectrum.

ch12/prob-12-12b.description: A ball-and-stick model shows methyl 2-methylbut-3-enoate, with a methyl ester group and a terminal alkene. It is one of the molecules in a problem asking where each would absorb in an IR spectrum.

ch12/prob-12-12a.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a carbon-ring structure bearing an aldehyde group on one side and a nitro group on the other. It is one of the structures in Problem 12-12, which asks where the molecules would absorb in an IR spectrum.

ch12/prob-12-24.description: A mass spectrum plots relative abundance (%) against m/z, with the tallest peak near m/z 43 and smaller peaks including those near 29, 41, 57, and 71. ch12/prob-12-13a.description: A ball-and-stick model shows a branched ketone, with a red oxygen double-bonded to the carbonyl carbon. It is one of the molecules in a problem asking for expected mass-spectrometry fragments.

ch12/prob-12-26a.description: A skeletal structure shows a benzene ring bonded directly to a carbonyl carbon, which is attached to a three-carbon chain. It depicts 1-phenylbutan-1-one as an infrared-spectroscopy problem structure.

ch12/prob-12-26c.description: A five-membered saturated carbon ring is bonded to a nitrogen bearing H and CH₃ groups. The problem figure shows this secondary amine structure for an infrared spectroscopy question.

ch12/prob-12-32a.description: An infrared spectrum labeled (a) plots transmittance (%) against wavenumber (cm⁻¹), with prominent absorption dips near 3000 cm⁻¹ and around 1450 cm⁻¹. ch12/prob-12-33a.description: The structure is a benzene ring bearing a CO₂H group, shown as one of the compounds in an IR-absorption-position problem. It illustrates a compound for which the reader is asked to estimate approximate IR absorption positions.

ch12/prob-12-33b.description: A benzene ring bearing a CO₂CH₃ substituent is shown as one of the compounds in a problem asking for approximate IR absorption positions.

ch12/prob-12-32b.description: An IR spectrum plots transmittance (%) against wavenumber (cm⁻¹), with numerous downward absorption bands, especially in the regions around 3000 cm⁻¹ and below 1500 cm⁻¹. It illustrates the pattern of absorptions in a spectrum labeled “(b).”

ch12/prob-12-33c.description: A benzene ring bears an –OH group and a –C≡N group at opposite positions (4-hydroxybenzonitrile). It is one of the structures in a problem asking for approximate IR absorption positions.

ch12/prob-12-33e.description: The figure shows CH₃C(=O)CH₂CH₂C(=O)CH₃, a molecule with two ketone carbonyl groups. It is labeled “(e)” as part of an infrared-spectroscopy problem asking how to distinguish pairs of compounds.

ch12/prob-12-33d.description: A skeletal structure of a six-membered ring containing a ketone carbonyl and one C=C bond. It is one of the compounds in a problem asking for approximate IR absorption positions.

ch12/prob-12-35a.description: The figure shows the structural formula of a ketone, CH₃CH₂C(=O)CH₃, as one compound in a problem asking where its IR absorptions might occur. It illustrates a structure to be analyzed, without giving the absorption positions.

ch12/prob-12-34.description: The figure shows two condensed ketone structures: CH₃C(=O)CH=CHCH₃ and CH₃C(=O)CH₂CH=CH₂, joined by “and.” They illustrate a pair of structures being compared in a constitutional-isomer problem.

ch12/prob-12-35b.description: The structure is 4-methyl-1-pentyne, shown as a branched carbon chain ending in a terminal C≡C–H bond. It is one of the compounds in a problem asking where its IR absorptions might occur.

ch12/prob-12-35c.description: The figure shows the branched alkene CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH=CH₂ (4-methyl-1-pentene), labeled as part (e) of a problem asking for approximate IR absorption positions. It presents the structure without an IR spectrum or absorption positions.

ch12/prob-12-35e.description: A benzene ring is bonded to a carbonyl carbon, which is also bonded to a CH₃ group. The figure shows the skeletal structure of acetophenone.

ch12/prob-12-41b.description: An infrared spectrum (b) of an unknown hydrocarbon plots transmittance (%) against wavenumber (cm⁻¹), with numerous absorption dips, including prominent ones near 3300, 3000, 1450, and 650 cm⁻¹. It illustrates the spectral data provided for identifying the unknown.

ch12/prob-12-35d.description: The figure shows CH₃CH₂CH₂C(=O)OCH₃, an ester structure presented as part (e) of a problem asking where compounds might absorb in an IR spectrum. It illustrates a molecule to analyze, without showing an answer or spectrum.

ch12/prob-12-35f.description: A benzene ring is shown with an –OH group and a –CHO group in the meta arrangement; the structure is 3-hydroxybenzaldehyde. The figure presents the molecule without showing a reaction or solution.

ch12/prob-12-41a.description: Panel (a) is a mass spectrum with relative abundance plotted against m/z, showing its tallest peak near m/z 67 and several smaller peaks, including clusters around 38–42 and 50–53. It is presented as part of a problem about determining the structure of an unknown hydrocarbon.

ch12/prob-12-42a.description: A mass spectrum plots relative abundance (%) against m/z, with the tallest peak near m/z 55 and smaller groups of peaks around 26, 40–42, and 70. It is the mass-spectrum portion of a problem about an unknown hydrocarbon.

ch12/prob-12-44.description: The figure shows skeletal structures of 4-methyl-2-pentanone and 3-methylpentanal, labeled as isomers. It illustrates the structures to be compared by mass spectrometry and infrared spectroscopy.

ch12/prob-12-42b.description: An infrared spectrum is plotted as transmittance (%) against wavenumber (cm⁻¹), with multiple absorption dips across the range. It is presented as part (a) of a problem asking for possible structures.

ch12/prob-12-45.description: A labeled cyclohexanone structure is shown with the sequence 1. CH₃MgBr, 2. H₃O⁺ leading to a reaction arrow and a pink question mark. The figure presents a problem asking for the product structure, without showing an answer.

ch12/prob-12-46.description: A reaction scheme shows labeled 2-butanone treated first with NaBH₄ and then H₃O⁺, with a question mark at the product side. It illustrates a problem asking for the product; no product structure is shown.

ch12/prob-12-48.description: A mass spectrum plots relative abundance (%) against m/z, with the base peak at m/z 88 and a small molecular-ion peak marked M(172). The fragment pattern is presented as data for a problem asking the reader to propose a structure.

ch12/prob-12-50.description: A mass spectrum plots relative abundance (%) against m/z, with the tallest peak labeled M (112), a prominent peak at 77, and several smaller peaks. It presents spectral data for the problem asking the reader to propose a structure.

appendix_a/p432a.description: A cyclohexenyl ring bearing a ketone is connected through a three-carbon chain to a methyl ester, with arrows labeling the ketone, ester, and double bond. The printed name, “Methyl 3-(2-oxo-6-cyclohexenyl)propanoate,” is color-coded to show how parts of the name correspond to the molecule.

ch12/prob-12-49.description: A mass spectrum plots relative abundance (%) against m/z, with prominent peaks at 41 and 56, a peak at 69, and a molecular-ion peak labeled M (84). It illustrates the mass-spectral data for the compound referred to in the problem.

appendix_a/p432b.description: The figure shows two numbered condensed structures: a diketone and an amino alcohol. It illustrates choosing a single suffix for naming compounds with multiple functional groups, rather than combining suffixes.

appendix_a/p434.description: Five labeled organic structures illustrate functional-group precedence in nomenclature: each name selects a principal suffix group while other functional groups are represented as prefixes. The examples show esters with ketone or aldehyde groups, an alcohol with an amine, a carboxylic acid with amide and alcohol groups, and an aldehyde with a ketone.

appendix_a/p435a.description: Two labeled amide structures illustrate choosing the parent chain to include the principal functional groups: 5-Methyl-6-oxohexanamide and 4-Oxo-3-propylbutanamide. appendix_a/p435b.description: Four numbered structural examples show alternative parent selections in naming polyfunctional compounds, with parent portions and substituents highlighted in color. The examples contrast aromatic versus acetonitrile parent choices and cyclohexane versus propanoic-acid parent choices.

appendix_a/p435c.description: The figure shows the structure of (E)-2,5,5-trimethyl-4-oxo-2-heptenoic acid beside its name, with the prefixes and locants color-highlighted. It illustrates how the name identifies the methyl substituents, oxo group, and alkene position.

Each example includes a brief explanation of the naming choice.

answer_key/ans-1-3.description: A tetrahedral carbon is bonded to one H and three Cl atoms, illustrating the structure of CHCl₃ (chloroform).

answer_key/ans-1-4.description: A structural drawing of ethane shows two single-bonded carbon atoms, each attached to three hydrogen atoms; solid and dashed wedges indicate bonds projecting in different directions.

answer_key/ans-1-6a.description: Two representations of CHCl₃ are shown: a Lewis dot structure on the left and a line-bond structure on the right. The figure illustrates two ways to depict the same molecular connectivity.

answer_key/ans-1-6b.description: Two depictions of H₂S are shown: a Lewis dot structure with sulfur’s electron pairs and a line-bond structure, both with sulfur bonded to two hydrogens.

answer_key/ans-1-8.description: Two drawings show propane (C₃H₈): a straight-chain structural formula and a three-dimensional wedge-and-dash representation. The note states that all bond angles are near 109°.

answer_key/ans-1-6d.description: Two Lewis-style drawings show the same structure: a carbon bonded to three hydrogens and lithium, with a pair of dots between carbon and lithium in the left drawing and a line bond in the right. This illustrates two ways to represent methyllithium.

answer_key/ans-1-9.description: The figure shows an expanded structural formula of a straight six-carbon chain with single bonds and hydrogens attached to each carbon. It depicts hexane.

answer_key/ans-1-10.description: The figure shows propene (CH₃–CH=CH₂), with wedge and dashed bonds depicting the orientation of the methyl group’s hydrogens. It illustrates the different geometries around the sp³ methyl carbon and the sp² double-bond carbons, as noted in the nearby text.

answer_key/ans-1-11.description: A structural drawing of 1,3-butadiene shows a four-carbon chain with alternating double and single bonds and attached hydrogens. The nearby text states that all carbons are sp² and bond angles are near 120°.

answer_key/ans-1-12.description: A skeletal structure shows a benzene ring bearing adjacent carboxylic acid and acetoxy groups, illustrating the molecular structure of acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin).

answer_key/ans-1-13.description: The structure is propyne, H–C≡C–CH₃, with the three hydrogens on the CH₃ carbon shown in wedge, dashed, and plain bonds. The nearby text identifies the triple-bond carbons as sp and the CH₃ carbon as sp³, illustrating their different geometries and the approximately 180° bond angles at the triple-bond carbons.

answer_key/ans-1-15a.description: The skeletal structure labeled “Adrenaline—C₉H₁₃NO₃” is shown with arrows pointing to several atoms and annotations such as 0 H, 1 H, and 2 H. It illustrates hydrogen counts at different positions in the structure.

answer_key/ans-1-15b.description: The figure shows the fused-ring skeletal structure labeled Estrone, with an –OH group, a carbonyl group, and hydrogen counts marked at positions on the structure. It illustrates one possible answer structure for Problem 1-15.

answer_key/ans-1-16a.description: Three line-angle structures are shown: a straight five-carbon chain, a branched five-carbon chain, and a central carbon bonded to four terminal carbon groups. They illustrate different carbon skeletons with the same molecular formula.

answer_key/ans-1-17.description: A benzene ring bears an H₂N group and a carboxylic acid group (COOH) at opposite, para positions; the drawn structure is 4-aminobenzoic acid.

answer_key/ans-2-2.description: The figure shows H₃C—SH (methanethiol) alongside the statement that carbon and sulfur have identical electronegativities. It illustrates the stated comparison of the two atoms’ electronegativities.
labels_in_image: Carbon and sulfur have identical electronegativities.

answer_key/ans-2-4.description: A tetrahedral methylamine structure is shown with three hydrogens bonded to carbon and an NH₂ group to the right; a pink dipole arrow points from the carbon toward the nitrogen.

answer_key/ans-1-16c.description: The figure shows four skeletal structures of chlorinated butanes: straight-chain and branched arrangements with chlorine at different positions. They illustrate some of the numerous possible structures for this answer.

answer_key/ans-2-5.description: A two-carbon structure with an HO group at each end and wedge/dashed bonds to hydrogens is shown, with a magenta diagonal, double-ended arrow crossing the central C–C region. The drawing illustrates the molecule’s dipole direction or vector representation.

answer_key/ans-1-16b.description: The figure presents eight skeletal organic structures in two rows as examples of possible answers: butanal, but-3-en-1-ol, but-2-en-1-ol, methyl vinyl ether, cyclopropanol, 1,2-epoxypropane, oxetane, acetone, and prop-1-en-2-ol. The structures illustrate several different arrangements of oxygen-containing functional groups.

answer_key/ans-2-6a.description: The diagram shows allene (H₂C=C=CH₂) with arrows indicating bond dipoles and the label “No dipole moment.” It illustrates that the dipoles cancel in the symmetric molecule.

answer_key/ans-2-6b.description: A tetrahedral carbon is bonded to one H and three Cl atoms, shown with solid and dashed wedges; a magenta dipole arrow marked with a plus sign points downward beside the structure. The figure illustrates the molecule’s indicated dipole direction.

answer_key/ans-2-6c.description: A tetrahedral drawing of dichloromethane shows a central carbon bonded to two chlorine atoms and two hydrogens, with a magenta arrow pointing diagonally upward to the right. The figure illustrates the molecule’s indicated dipole direction.

answer_key/ans-2-6d.description: The structure shows H₂C=CCl₂ with a dipole arrow marked with a plus at the hydrogen-bearing end and pointing toward the carbon bearing both chlorine atoms. It illustrates the direction of the molecule’s dipole.

answer_key/ans-2-10a.description: Three resonance forms of a methyl phosphate dianion are shown, with the P=O double bond and negative charges distributed among the three non-methoxy oxygens. Double-headed arrows connect the forms.

answer_key/ans-2-10b.description: Three Lewis resonance structures of the nitrate ion are shown, connected by double-headed arrows; the N=O double bond and negative charges shift among the three oxygen atoms while nitrogen bears a positive charge.

answer_key/ans-2-8.description: A methyl group is connected through an oxygen to a phosphorus atom bonded to three additional oxygens; curved arrows indicate electron movement among the P–O bonds, with a −1 charge marked by an oxygen. It illustrates a resonance form of the structure.

answer_key/ans-2-10c.description: The figure shows two pairs of resonance structures for a phenyl-substituted carboxylate ion, with the negative charge and C=O bond interchanging between the two oxygen atoms; the benzene-ring bond placements are drawn differently in the two rows. Double-headed arrows connect the contributors.

answer_key/ans-2-17a.description: Three curved-arrow equations show ethanol, dimethylamine, and trimethylphosphine reacting with H–Cl: each atom with a lone pair bonds to H, while the H–Cl bond electrons move to chlorine, forming the corresponding positively charged protonated species and Cl⁻. The figure illustrates proton transfer to oxygen, nitrogen, and phosphorus.

answer_key/ans-2-11.description: The figure shows HNO₃ reacting with NH₃ to form NH₄⁺ and NO₃⁻, with each species labeled as acid, base, conjugate acid, or conjugate base. It illustrates the relationship between an acid–base pair and their conjugates.

answer_key/ans-2-18a.description: The imidazole ring is shown with its left nitrogen marked as “More basic (red)” and its N–H group marked as “Most acidic (blue).” The figure compares the basicity and acidity at these sites.

answer_key/ans-3-2a.description: The figure shows a benzene ring bearing a CH₃ substituent, the skeletal structure of toluene. It illustrates a methyl-substituted aromatic ring.

answer_key/ans-2-17b.description: Three Lewis-structure equations show hydroxide donating a lone pair, indicated by curved arrows, to CH₃⁺, B(CH₃)₃, and MgBr₂, with the corresponding O-bonded products drawn to the right of equilibrium arrows. The figure illustrates lone-pair donation to form bonds.

answer_key/ans-3-2b.description: The figure shows acetic acid, with a CH₃ group attached to a carbonyl carbon and an –OH group.

answer_key/ans-2-18b.description: The figure shows proton-transfer and resonance-arrow steps for a five-membered ring with two nitrogens: a generic acid (A–H) protonates the ring, and a generic base (B:) removes a proton to form a negatively charged ring. The ring is imidazole, and the drawing illustrates how charge and double bonds are redistributed in its protonated and deprotonated forms.

answer_key/ans-3-2c.description: A condensed structural formula shows CH₃–C(=O)–CH₂–NH₂, identified as 1-aminopropan-2-one (aminoacetone). It illustrates a ketone carbonyl and a primary amine in the same molecule.

answer_key/ans-3-4.description: The figure shows five condensed structural formulas for the constitutional isomers of hexane: hexane, 2-methylpentane, 3-methylpentane, 2,2-dimethylbutane, and 2,3-dimethylbutane. It illustrates how the same carbon count can be arranged in different branched and unbranched structures.

answer_key/ans-3-5b.description: The figure shows two condensed nitrile structures: CH₃CH(CH₃)C≡N and CH₃CH₂CH₂C≡N. They illustrate branched and straight-chain carbon frameworks attached to a nitrile group.

answer_key/ans-3-3.description: A six-membered nitrogen-containing ring has an N-methyl group, a double bond, and a methyl ester substituent; arrows label the amine, double bond, and ester. The molecular formula C₈H₁₃NO₂ is printed beside the structure.

answer_key/ans-3-5a.description: Three ester structures are shown in a row as condensed structural formulas: methyl butanoate, ethyl propanoate, and propan-2-yl ethanoate. They illustrate different arrangements of alkyl groups around the ester linkage.

answer_key/ans-3-5c.description: Three condensed structural formulas show disulfides with ethyl groups on both sides, methyl and propyl groups, and methyl and isopropyl groups. The branched group in the third structure is drawn with a vertical CH₃ substituent.

answer_key/ans-3-8a.description: A condensed structure shows a five-carbon chain with a CH₃ branch on the second carbon, with the letters “p,” “t,” and “s” marked above or below different positions. It illustrates the labeled positions in the answer to Problem 3-8.

answer_key/ans-3-8b.description: A branched alkane structure with two connected CH centers: the upper center is bonded to two CH₃ groups, and the lower center to two ethyl groups. The carbon positions are marked with p, s, and t labels.

answer_key/ans-3-10a.description: A condensed structural formula shows a four-carbon chain with methyl branches on the second and third carbons, illustrating 2,3-dimethylbutane.

answer_key/ans-3-7.description: The figure shows eight condensed carbon-chain structures, some straight-chain and some branched, each with a bond extending to the right as an attachment point. It illustrates different alkyl-group arrangements; no problem is solved in the figure.

answer_key/ans-3-8c.description: A branched alkane is drawn as CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–C(CH₃)₃, with the labels p, t, s, and q placed beside different parts of the structure. The figure illustrates labeling the carbon environments in the molecule.

answer_key/ans-3-10c.description: A condensed structural formula shows a central carbon bonded to three CH₃ groups and one CH₂CH₃ group, corresponding to 2,2-dimethylbutane. It illustrates a branched alkane structure.

answer_key/ans-3-12a.description: A condensed straight-chain alkane is shown with methyl groups branching from two adjacent CH groups; the structure is 4,5-dimethylnonane. The visible notation includes CH₃, CH₂, and CH groups.

answer_key/ans-3-12c.description: A condensed structural formula shows a branched carbon chain, with a propyl branch attached to the central CH and a C(CH₃)₃ group at the right end. It illustrates a branched alkyl structure in the answer to Problem 3-12.

answer_key/ans-3-10b.description: A branched alkane is shown as a condensed structural formula: a CH group in a horizontal five-carbon chain is bonded to a CH group bearing two CH₃ groups. It illustrates a branched carbon skeleton.

answer_key/ans-3-12b.description: A branched alkane is shown in condensed structural form, with a seven-carbon longest chain, an ethyl branch, and two methyl branches. The figure presents the structure for part (c).

answer_key/ans-3-14.description: A skeletal structure of 3,3,4,5-tetramethylheptane is shown beside its printed name. The structure illustrates a seven-carbon chain with four methyl branches.

answer_key/ans-3-15.description: The figure shows butane’s rotational energy profile from 0° to 360°, with energy maxima and minima and a marked difference of 14 kJ/mol. Seven Newman projections underneath show the corresponding conformations at 60° intervals.

answer_key/ans-3-12d.description: A condensed structural formula shows a branched alkane, CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂C(CH₃)₃, with methyl branches on the chain. It illustrates how the same carbon skeleton is represented with bonds and group labels.

answer_key/ans-3-16c.description: An energy-versus-angle curve runs from 0° to 360°, with minima near 60°, 180°, and 300° and maxima near 0°, 120°, 240°, and 360°; a vertical bracket marks a 16 kJ/mol energy difference. It illustrates a repeating energy profile as the angle changes.

answer_key/ans-3-16b.description: A Newman projection of butane shows the two carbon atoms’ CH₃ and H substituents, with arrows pointing to interactions labeled 4.0 kJ/mol and 6.0 kJ/mol. It illustrates energy values associated with features of the depicted conformation.

answer_key/ans-3-16a.description: A Newman projection of 2-methylpropane, with a front carbon bearing two CH₃ groups and an H, and a rear carbon bearing three H atoms. It illustrates the molecule’s arrangement when viewed along a carbon–carbon bond.

answer_key/ans-3-16d.description: An energy-versus-angle diagram shows a repeating wavelike curve with three minima and three maxima between 0° and 360°; the vertical difference between peak and trough is marked 16 kJ/mol. It illustrates how energy varies with rotation angle.

answer_key/ans-3-17.description: A Newman projection of 2,3-dimethylbutane shows two adjacent carbons, each bearing two CH₃ groups and an H, with the substituents arranged as drawn. It illustrates the molecule’s conformation when viewed along the carbon–carbon bond.

answer_key/ans-4-2a.description: An eight-membered carbon ring has two CH₃ groups attached to the same ring carbon. The drawing illustrates a geminal dimethyl-substituted cycloalkane.

answer_key/ans-3-18.description: A Newman projection of 2,3-dimethylbutane shows three indicated interactions, each labeled 3.8 kJ/mol, with a total of 11.4 kJ/mol. It illustrates the summed interaction energy for the conformation shown.

answer_key/ans-4-2c.description: A cyclopentane ring has chlorine substituents on two adjacent carbons, depicting 1,2-dichlorocyclopentane. The labels “Cl” identify both substituents.

answer_key/ans-4-2d.description: A cyclohexane ring is shown with a CH₃ group on one carbon and Br groups on two other ring carbons. It depicts 1,3-dibromo-5-methylcyclohexane, with no stereochemistry specified.

answer_key/ans-4-5a.description: A cyclohexane ring bears a methyl group and a bromine at opposite ring positions; the methyl is on a dashed bond and Br on a solid wedge, indicating they are on opposite faces. The drawing illustrates the trans relationship of the substituents.

answer_key/ans-4-5b.description: A cyclobutane ring has methyl groups on adjacent carbons, both shown on solid wedges, with the hydrogens on dashed bonds; the two methyl groups are on the same side of the ring (cis).

answer_key/ans-4-2b.description: A cyclobutane ring is attached to the fourth carbon of a six-carbon zigzag chain, depicting 4-cyclobutylhexane. The figure shows a branched alkane bearing a four-membered ring substituent.

answer_key/ans-4-12.description: Two chair conformations of cyclohexanol are shown: the left has the OH group axial (a), and the right has it equatorial (e).

answer_key/ans-4-5c.description: A cyclohexane ring has adjacent ethyl and tert-butyl groups shown on opposite faces, with wedge and dashed bonds indicating their trans relationship. The drawing illustrates stereochemistry in a substituted ring.

answer_key/ans-4-13.description: Two chair conformations of trans-1,4-dimethylcyclohexane are shown: both methyl groups are axial (a) in the left structure and equatorial (e) in the right structure, illustrating their change of position during a ring flip.

answer_key/ans-5-2a.description: A six-membered nitrogen-containing ring bears a CH₂CH₂CH₃ substituent on the carbon marked with a magenta asterisk; the drawing highlights that carbon in a structure-identification problem.

answer_key/ans-4-19.description: A chair-form drawing of 1-chloro-2,4-dimethylcyclohexane, labeled as the less stable chair form. The chlorine and one methyl group are shown axial, while the other methyl group is equatorial.

answer_key/ans-5-2b.description: A substituted cyclohexane ring is drawn with wedge-and-dash bonds, an –OH group, a methyl group, and an isopropyl group; three ring carbons are marked with pink asterisks. The figure highlights stereogenic centers in the structure.

answer_key/ans-5-3.description: Two alanine structures are shown side by side, each with a central carbon bonded to CO₂H, CH₃, H, and NH₂; the wedge and dashed bonds are arranged oppositely in the two drawings.

answer_key/ans-5-2c.description: A fused polycyclic ring structure is shown with a methoxy substituent, an N-methyl group, and three stereocenters marked with pink asterisks. The drawing illustrates the chiral centers in dextromethorphan.

answer_key/ans-5-11.description: The figure shows 2-pentanol, with the central carbon bonded to H, OH, a propyl group, and a methyl group; the methyl group is drawn on a solid wedge. It illustrates the molecule’s three-dimensional stereochemical arrangement.

answer_key/ans-5-4b.description: A stereochemical structure of a fluorinated chloroalkyl ether is shown, with one carbon marked by an asterisk and wedge/dash bonds indicating its attached H, F, and Cl groups. The nearby label reads “Levorotatory.”

answer_key/ans-5-18.description: A cyclopentane ring is drawn with two adjacent CH₃ substituents shown on solid wedges and an OH substituent at the opposite ring carbon; a dashed line marks the vertical symmetry axis, beside the label “Meso.”

answer_key/ans-5-22a.description: The structure of glyceraldehyde shows the two hydrogens on its CH₂ group labeled pro-S and pro-R. Wedge-and-dash bonds indicate the stereochemistry at the adjacent carbon.

answer_key/ans-5-23a.description: The structure of hydroxyacetone (CH₃–C(=O)–CH₂OH) is shown with arrows marking its Re and Si faces. It illustrates the two faces of the carbonyl group.

answer_key/ans-5-22b.description: A skeletal structure of 2-aminobutanoate is shown with the two hydrogens on its methylene group marked pro-R and pro-S, illustrating their distinct stereochemical designations.

answer_key/ans-6-3.description: A central boron bonded to three fluorine atoms is shown with an arrow indicating its vacant p orbital, labeled as electrophilic. The figure illustrates the electrophilic character associated with that orbital.

answer_key/ans-6-5.description: The structure shows a positively charged central carbon bonded to three methyl groups (the tert-butyl cation).

answer_key/ans-5-23b.description: A substituted alkene is shown with CH₃ and CH₂OH groups on the double bond, with arrows marking its Re and Si faces. The figure illustrates the two faces of the alkene.

answer_key/ans-5-4a.description: A stereochemical drawing of an aldotetrose, with two starred stereocenters and the label “Levorotatory”; the structure is L-erythrose. It illustrates the molecule’s stereochemistry and optical-rotation designation.

answer_key/ans-6-6b.description: The diagram shows methoxide reacting with CH₃Br, with curved arrows from oxygen to the methyl carbon and from the C–Br bond to bromine, forming CH₃OCH₃ and Br⁻. It illustrates a substitution reaction using electron-pushing arrows.

answer_key/ans-6-6a.description: The reaction shows Cl–Cl and ammonia in equilibrium with ClNH₃⁺ and Cl⁻, with curved arrows indicating electron movement from ammonia toward chlorine and from the Cl–Cl bond to the other chlorine.

answer_key/ans-6-6c.description: A tetrahedral intermediate bearing CH₃, OCH₃, O⁻, and Cl collapses as the oxygen forms a carbonyl and chloride leaves, giving methyl acetate and Cl⁻. Curved arrows indicate the bond changes.

answer_key/ans-6-13.description: An energy-versus-reaction-progress diagram shows a two-step profile with a labeled intermediate between two peaks; the product lies below the reactant in energy. It illustrates the overall free-energy change (ΔG°) and an activation free energy (ΔG‡) measured from the intermediate level to the second peak.

answer_key/ans-6-7.description: A curved-arrow mechanism shows water adding across a generic tricarboxylate alkene, with hydronium supplying a proton; the product is drawn with an attached H₂O⁺ group and wedge/dash stereochemistry. It illustrates acid-catalyzed hydration of the double bond.

answer_key/ans-6-9.description: A radical-bearing, peroxide-bridged chain with two alkenes and a terminal CO₂H group cyclizes: the curved arrows show formation of a new C–C bond and transfer of the radical to the lower chain, yielding a fused-ring product. The downward arrow indicates the transformation.

answer_key/ans-7-5a.description: A condensed structural formula shows CH₂=CH–CH₂–CH₂–C(CH₃)=CH₂, the diene 2-methyl-1,5-hexadiene. It illustrates the connectivity of a branched hydrocarbon with two double bonds.

answer_key/ans-7-5d.description: The structure shows a carbon–carbon double bond with two isopropyl groups attached to each alkene carbon. It illustrates a highly substituted alkene structure for part (d) of the answer key.

answer_key/ans-7-5c.description: A condensed hydrocarbon structure is shown as a horizontal chain with three C=C bonds and three methyl branches. It illustrates the answer-key structure for the labeled problem part.

answer_key/ans-7-14.description: A skeletal structure shows a substituted C=C bond, with a branched carbon chain on the left and CO₂CH₃ and CH₂OH groups on the right; it is labeled Z. The figure presents the answer configuration for Problem 7-14.

answer_key/ans-7-8.description: An unlabelled skeletal structure of a long-chain alkene, with the carbon–carbon double bond at the left and carbon chains extending to the right from both alkene carbons. The chains lie on the same side of the double bond, illustrating a cis arrangement.

answer_key/ans-7-5b.description: A condensed structural formula shows a branched alkene: a propyl chain on one side of the double bond and, on the other, an ethyl substituent and a carbon bearing three methyl groups. The nearby answer marker “(d)” identifies this as part (d).

answer_key/ans-7-18a.description: The condensed structure shows a carbocation bonded to an ethyl group, a methyl group, and a chain ending in a carbon bearing two methyl groups. Nearby text refers to the conformation and to a methyl-group C–H bond parallel to the carbocation p orbital.

answer_key/ans-7-18b.description: A five-membered carbon ring is bonded to a positively charged carbon, which is also bonded to an ethyl group (CH₂CH₃).

answer_key/ans-8-9b.description: A cyclohexane ring is attached to a carbon bearing an OH group and a CH₃ group, showing 1-cyclohexylethanol.

answer_key/ans-8-4.description: Two wedge-and-dash drawings show a cyclohexane ring bearing one Cl, two CH₃ groups, and one H; the two drawings differ in the wedge/dash orientation of Cl and CH₃ at one ring carbon. The word “and” separates the alternatives.

answer_key/ans-7-21.description: A curved-arrow mechanism shows HBr adding to vinylcyclohexane, followed by a hydride shift to a ring-centered carbocation and bromide capture, yielding 1-bromo-1-ethylcyclohexane. The bracketed sequence illustrates rearrangement of the carbocation before the final product forms.

answer_key/ans-8-9a.description: A condensed structural formula shows a five-carbon chain with an OH group on the middle carbon and a methyl branch on the adjacent carbon. It is 2-methylpentan-3-ol.

answer_key/ans-8-13.description: A three-membered epoxide ring has an oxygen bridging two adjacent carbon atoms, each bearing a hydrogen and a methyl group; both methyl groups are shown on solid wedges, indicating the cis arrangement. It is labeled “cis-2,3-Epoxybutane.”

answer_key/ans-8-11.description: Two wedge-and-dash drawings of 2,4-dimethylcyclopentan-1-ol are shown side by side, joined by “and”; the methyl and hydrogen orientations differ at one ring carbon. The figure illustrates two stereochemical forms of the same ring structure.

answer_key/ans-8-19.description: A reaction scheme shows two generic carbon-chain radicals with curved arrows indicating hydrogen transfer and bond rearrangement, producing a saturated chain and an alkene. It illustrates a radical disproportionation between generic structures.

answer_key/ans-8-17b.description: A cyclopropane ring is shown with a methyl group and a 2-methylpropyl group on adjacent ring carbons. The drawing illustrates a branched, substituted cycloalkane structure.

answer_key/ans-9-11.description: Propyne is treated with NaNH₂ and CH₃I to form 2-butyne, which is then hydrogenated with H₂ and Lindlar catalyst to give cis-2-butene. The figure illustrates alkylation of a terminal alkyne followed by partial reduction to a cis alkene.

answer_key/ans-8-17a.description: A skeletal structure shows a cyclohexane ring joined at one vertex to a three-membered ring, with two Cl labels on the smaller ring. It illustrates a chlorinated cyclic structure; no compound name is printed.

answer_key/ans-10-2c.description: A central carbon is bonded to bromine and three ethyl groups, representing 3-bromo-3-ethylpentane. The structure is shown as a condensed, branched formula.

answer_key/ans-10-2b.description: A condensed structural formula for 3,3-dichloro-2-methylhexane, with two chlorine atoms attached to one carbon and a methyl branch on the adjacent carbon.

answer_key/ans-10-2d.description: A cyclohexane ring is drawn with two bromine atoms attached to the same ring carbon and a branched three-carbon substituent attached at the opposite ring carbon. The figure illustrates a substituted cyclohexane structure.

answer_key/ans-10-2a.description: A condensed skeletal structure shows CH₃CH₂CH₂–C(CH₃)₂–CH(Cl)–CH₃, with two methyl groups attached to one carbon and chlorine attached to the neighboring carbon. It represents 2-chloro-3,3-dimethylhexane.

answer_key/ans-10-2f.description: A cyclohexane ring is drawn with two bromine atoms attached to the same ring carbon and a tert-butyl group attached at another ring carbon. It appears beneath the answer-key text beginning “Achiral:”.

molecules.name: cyclohexane derivative with two bromines and a tert-butyl substituent

answer_key/ans-10-3a.description: The figure shows 1-chloro-2-methylpentane as a condensed structural formula, with a methyl branch on the second carbon from the CH₂Cl end. It is presented as an example in the answer’s list of chiral compounds.

answer_key/ans-10-3b.description: The structural formula shows a carbon bonded to Cl, two CH₃ groups, and a CH₃CH₂CH₂ chain; it illustrates 2-chloro-2-methylpentane.

answer_key/ans-10-3c.description: The image shows the condensed structure CH₃CH₂CH(Cl)CH(CH₃)₂, with chlorine attached to the third carbon of the chain. It depicts 3-chloro-2-methylpentane.

answer_key/ans-10-2e.description: A condensed branched carbon-chain structure is shown, with a chlorine atom bonded to a CH near the right end and a carbon branch extending downward from a central carbon. It illustrates a molecular structure for the chirality problem; no name or conclusion is visible in the drawing itself.

answer_key/ans-10-3d.description: The structure shows CH₃–CH(Cl)–CH₂–CH(CH₃)₂, illustrating a branched alkyl chloride.

answer_key/ans-10-12.description: The figure shows cyclohexane < cyclohexanone = 1-chlorocyclohexene < benzene, with the structures linked by comparison symbols. It illustrates a relative ordering among these four structures without stating what property is being compared.

answer_key/ans-11-3.description: A reaction arrow leads from (S)-2-bromo-4-methylpentane to a skeletal/condensed structure labeled (R), with a methyl branch and an SH group on the chain. It illustrates conversion of the bromo compound to the corresponding thiol with a changed stereochemical label.

answer_key/ans-11-10.description: An arrow leads from “(S)-Bromide” to a drawn alcohol with a phenyl ring, methyl group, and ethyl group attached to the carbon bearing OH; the product is labeled “Racemic.”

answer_key/ans-11-14.description: The figure shows labeled linalyl diphosphate losing PPᵢ, followed by a cyclized carbocation intermediate and base-assisted deprotonation to form labeled limonene. Curved arrows illustrate the bond rearrangements and proton removal in the sequence.
